docs.text: REST API The http transport ( Transports ) exposes every operation of λORM on a schema as REST, with JSON in and out. The OpenAPI 3 document is served by the gateway at /doc (Swagger UI) and /api-docs . Routes The examples use a gateway at http://localhost:8080 with an API key. Each schema's methods are under its route: Gateway Schema iot/v1 Only schema at the root http://localhost:8080 http://localhost:8080/iot/v1/execute http://localhost:8080/execute With transports.http.basePath: /data-gateway , every route is under it: /data-gateway/iot/v1/execute . Every request needs the credential, except /ping , /health and /metrics (at the root and under each schema), /schemas , /version , /doc and the UI. How it is sent depends on the authentication : X-Api-Key: <key> , Authorization: Bearer <token> or Authorization: Basic <base64> . ?format=beautiful indents the JSON of the answer. data (the parameters of a query) and options (for example { "stage": "default" } ) are JSON objects; JSON text ( "data": "{\"id\": 10}" ) is also accepted. An error answers a status and { "error", "code"?, "message" } ( Errors ). Gateway methods Method Route Answers Credential GET /ping { "message": "pong", "time" } no GET /health 200 while some schema is ready , 503 if none no GET /metrics the metrics of every worker, Prometheus text no GET /version the version of the gateway no GET /schemas each schema with its state no GET /whoami the name and permissions of the credential yes curl http://localhost:8080/schemas [ { "path": "iot/v1", "status": "ready", "since": "2026-11-18T13:35:56.407Z", "restarts": 0 }, { "path": "iot/v2", "status": "error", "reason": "connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432", "since": "…", "restarts": 3 } ] The states are starting , ready , error and restarting . State of a schema Under each schema's route ( /iot/v1/… ), these answer only about that schema: Method Route Answers GET /{schema}/ping 200 if the schema is ready , 503 if not GET /{schema}/health the state of the schema; 503 if it is not ready GET /{schema}/metrics the metrics of that schema GET /{schema}/version the versions of the gateway and the schema GET /{schema}/whoami the name and permissions of the credential with the authentication of that schema, and whether it has scripts enabled curl http://localhost:8080/iot/v1/whoami -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" { "name": "reader", "permissions": ["read"], "schema": "iot/v1", "scripts": true } The secret of the credential is never answered. Query methods execute POST /{schema}/execute runs a query. The body is { query, data?, options? } . curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/execute?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => p.details)", "data": {"customerId": "CENTC"}}' [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "details": [ { "orderId": 12, "productId": 21, "unitPrice": 8, "quantity": 10 }, { "orderId": 12, "productId": 37, "unitPrice": 20.8, "quantity": 1 } ] } ] A select answers the rows; update and delete answer the number of affected rows ( 0 when nothing matched); insert answers the inserted data. With only the read permission, a query that writes ( insert , update , delete , upsert , merge , bulk* ) is refused with 403 before reaching the database. curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/execute -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "Orders.update(p => ({ freight: freight })).filter(p => p.id == id)", "data": {"id": 10248, "freight": 40}}' 1 plan POST /{schema}/plan answers how the query is executed: the dialect, the source and the sentence of each part, without running it. Body { query, options? } . curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/plan -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => p.details)"}' { "entity": "Orders", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "default", "sentence": "SELECT o.OrderID AS \"id\", o.CustomerID AS \"customerId\", o.OrderDate AS \"orderDate\", o.OrderID AS \"__id\" FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = $1 ", "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "default", "sentence": "SELECT o1.OrderID AS \"orderId\", o1.ProductID AS \"productId\", o1.UnitPrice AS \"unitPrice\", o1.Quantity AS \"quantity\", o1.OrderID AS \"LambdaOrmParentId\" FROM \"Order Details\" o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN ($1) " } ] } model POST /{schema}/model answers the shape of the result: its properties and their types. [ { "name": "id", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "customerId", "type": "string" }, { "name": "orderDate", "type": "dateTime" }, { "name": "details", "type": "Orders.details[]", "children": [ { "name": "orderId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "productId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "unitPrice", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "quantity", "type": "decimal" } ] } ] parameters POST /{schema}/parameters answers the variables the query uses, which go in data . [ { "name": "customerId", "type": "string" } ] constraints POST /{schema}/constraints answers the constraints that apply to the entities of the query. { "entity": "Orders", "constraints": [], "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "constraints": [] } ] } metadata POST /{schema}/metadata answers the analysed tree of the query: each sentence with its action ( select , insert , …), entity, columns, parameters and constraints. { "classtype": "Sentence", "name": "select", "entity": "Orders", "columns": [ { "name": "id" } ], "parameters": [ { "name": "customerId", "type": "any" } ], "constraints": [] } script POST /{schema}/script runs a script : several queries and logic in one transaction. Body { script, data?, options? } . It needs scripts.enabled (otherwise 403 ) and the script permission; the limits of scripts apply ( maxLength , timeoutMs , maxIterations ). curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/script -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ "script": "order = orm.execute(\"Orders.filter(p => p.id == id)\", { id: id }); if (order.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: \"order not found\" }; } order[0]", "data": { "id": 10248 } }' A script can choose the status of the answer with throw { status, message } . execute-queued POST /{schema}/execute-queued runs a query in the background and sends its result to a Kafka topic, in chunks. It answers at once { "queueId": "…" } ; the messages carry the keys <queueId>-<chunk> . Body { topic, query, data?, chunk?, options? } . It needs the queue permission (and write if the query writes) and an infrastructure.queue in the schema's lambdaORM.yaml . curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/execute-queued -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "Countries.map(p => [p.iso3, p.name])", "topic": "countries", "chunk": 1000}' The queue of a schema is configured in its lambdaORM.yaml ( config is the kafkajs configuration), where consumers can also be declared: infrastructure: queue: config: $QUEUE_CONFIG consumers: - name: syncInsights config: { groupId: group1 } subscribe: { topic: insights-sync, fromBeginning: true } execute: orm.execute(message.query, message.data, { stage: "insights" }) Over the WebSocket API , query.executeQueued with notify: true also tells the connection when the execution ends. Schema methods The model of the schema. They need read . The connections of the sources are never answered. Method Route Answers GET /{schema}/schema the version and the domain of the schema GET /{schema}/schema/version the version of the schema GET /{schema}/domain the domain: entities (properties, relations, keys, indexes, constraints) and enums GET /{schema}/entities the entities GET /{schema}/entities/{entity} one entity GET /{schema}/enums the enums GET /{schema}/enums/{enum} one enum GET /{schema}/sources the sources, with their name and dialect GET /{schema}/sources/{source} one source GET /{schema}/mappings the mappings (entities to tables and columns) GET /{schema}/mappings/{mapping} one mapping GET /{schema}/mappings/{mapping}/{entity} the mapping of one entity GET /{schema}/views the views GET /{schema}/stages the stages, with their sources GET /{schema}/stages/{stage} one stage GET /{schema}/typings the domain as TypeScript declarations ( text/plain ), for an editor's autocompletion curl http://localhost:8080/sources -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" [ { "name": "catalog", "dialect": "PostgreSQL" }, { "name": "accounts", "dialect": "PostgreSQL" } ] curl http://localhost:8080/entities/Categories -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" { "name": "Categories", "primaryKey": ["id"], "uniqueKey": ["name"], "properties": [ { "name": "id", "type": "integer", "required": true, "autoIncrement": true }, { "name": "name", "type": "string", "length": 80, "required": true }, { "name": "description", "type": "string", "length": 1000 } ], "relations": [] } Stage methods Method Route Answers Permission GET /{schema}/stages/{stage}/exists { "exists": true } when the stage was created and its state file exists read GET /{schema}/stages/{stage}/export the rows of every entity of the stage read POST /{schema}/stages/{stage}/import imports rows (the body is an export) into the entities of the stage stageImport curl http://localhost:8080/stages/default/export -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" > data.json curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/stages/default/import -H "X-Api-Key: $BACKEND_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @data.json Summary Operation REST MCP tool WebSocket method Permission execute POST /execute orm_execute query.execute read (selects) / write script POST /script orm_execute_script query.script script execute queued POST /execute-queued orm_execute_queued query.executeQueued queue plan POST /plan orm_plan query.plan read metadata POST /metadata orm_metadata query.metadata read model POST /model orm_model query.model read parameters POST /parameters orm_parameters query.parameters read constraints POST /constraints orm_constraints query.constraints read schema GET /schema schema_get schema.schema read schema version GET /schema/version schema_version schema.version read domain GET /domain schema_domain schema.domain read docs.text: The http transport ( Transports ) exposes every operation of λORM on a schema as REST, with JSON in and out. The OpenAPI 3 document is served by the gateway at /doc (Swagger UI) and /api-docs .
docs.title: REST API

docs.text: The examples use a gateway at http://localhost:8080 with an API key. Each schema's methods are under its route: Gateway Schema iot/v1 Only schema at the root http://localhost:8080 http://localhost:8080/iot/v1/execute http://localhost:8080/execute With transports.http.basePath: /data-gateway , every route is under it: /data-gateway/iot/v1/execute . Every request needs the credential, except /ping , /health and /metrics (at the root and under each schema), /schemas , /version , /doc and the UI. How it is sent depends on the authentication : X-Api-Key: <key> , Authorization: Bearer <token> or Authorization: Basic <base64> . ?format=beautiful indents the JSON of the answer. data (the parameters of a query) and options (for example { "stage": "default" } ) are JSON objects; JSON text ( "data": "{\"id\": 10}" ) is also accepted. An error answers a status and { "error", "code"?, "message" } ( Errors ).
docs.title: Routes

docs.text: Method Route Answers Credential GET /ping { "message": "pong", "time" } no GET /health 200 while some schema is ready , 503 if none no GET /metrics the metrics of every worker, Prometheus text no GET /version the version of the gateway no GET /schemas each schema with its state no GET /whoami the name and permissions of the credential yes curl http://localhost:8080/schemas [ { "path": "iot/v1", "status": "ready", "since": "2026-11-18T13:35:56.407Z", "restarts": 0 }, { "path": "iot/v2", "status": "error", "reason": "connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432", "since": "…", "restarts": 3 } ] The states are starting , ready , error and restarting .

docs.text: Under each schema's route ( /iot/v1/… ), these answer only about that schema: Method Route Answers GET /{schema}/ping 200 if the schema is ready , 503 if not GET /{schema}/health the state of the schema; 503 if it is not ready GET /{schema}/metrics the metrics of that schema GET /{schema}/version the versions of the gateway and the schema GET /{schema}/whoami the name and permissions of the credential with the authentication of that schema, and whether it has scripts enabled curl http://localhost:8080/iot/v1/whoami -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" { "name": "reader", "permissions": ["read"], "schema": "iot/v1", "scripts": true } The secret of the credential is never answered.

docs.text: Security Authentication The authentication block has three levels: global, per transport ( transports.<t>.authentication ) and per schema ( orm.schemas[].authentication ). The most specific replaces the others (schema → transport → global). It is applied by the edge worker before anything reaches the schema. adapter One credential (every permission) Several credentials with permissions The client sends none (default) — — nothing: an anonymous credential with every permission local , type: bearer token tokens: [{ name, value, permissions }] Authorization: Bearer <token> local , type: apikey value (and header , default X-Api-Key ) keys: [{ name, value, permissions }] <header>: <key> local , type: basic username , password users: [{ username, password, permissions }] Authorization: Basic <base64(user:password)> authentication: adapter: local type: bearer tokens: - { name: reports, value: $REPORTS_TOKEN, permissions: [ read ] } - { name: backend, value: $BACKEND_TOKEN, permissions: [ read, write, script, queue, stageImport ] } A local credential without its secret (or whose $VAR is not defined) stops the start. Open access is only adapter: none , written on purpose. Secrets are compared in constant time. The secret never travels to the schema workers: only the name and the permissions of the credential. Without a credential (or with a wrong one) the answer is 401 ; the WebSocket upgrades are refused. /ping , /health , /metrics , /version , /schemas , /doc and the UI's files need no credential. Permissions Permission Allows read the schema, the domain, plan, metadata, model, parameters, constraints, stage exists and export, and execute only when every sentence is a select write execute that writes ( insert , update , delete , upsert , merge , bulk* , …) script scripts ( POST /script , orm_execute_script , query.script ): a script can do anything inside, so it is a permission of its own queue execute-queued (and write if the query writes) stageImport importing a stage Authorization happens in the schema's worker, before running anything, the same for REST, MCP and WebSocket. To know whether a query writes, the gateway analyses it (its metadata ): with only read , a query with any sentence that is not a select , also inside an include , is refused. Without the permission: 403 in REST, status: 403 in WebSocket, isError: true in MCP, with the message the credential "reader" does not have the "write" permission . GET /whoami answers the name and permissions of the credential, never its secret. Audit Every operation that changes data, or may, leaves an audit entry: a JSON line with "type": "audit" on the standard output, so the log collector (Loki, ELK, CloudWatch, …) can keep it apart. Operation Audited execute when some sentence is not a select script always execute queued always (when queued) stage import always { "type": "audit", "time": "2026-11-17T14:03:22.114Z", "schema": "iot/v1", "transport": "mcpHttp", "credential": "agent", "operation": "execute", "actions": ["insert"], "entities": ["Devices"], "query": "Devices.insert()", "rows": 1, "durationMs": 42, "result": "ok" } It is written after running, also when it fails ( "result": "error" with the message). It has the credential's name, never its secret. The parameters ( data ) are added only with audit.includeData: true , because they can have personal data. audit.enabled: false turns it off. Limits Limit Key When it is reached Requests per window ( http only) rateLimit.windowMs , rateLimit.max ( 0 = off) 429 Simultaneous operations per schema server.maxConcurrent 429 with Retry-After (MCP: isError ; WebSocket: status: 429 ) Time of an operation server.timeout error, the operation is abandoned Size of a body server.requestBodySize 413 Size of an answer server.maxResponseBytes 413 : use .page(1, n) or aggregate in the query Scripts scripts.maxLength , timeoutMs , maxIterations 413 (length) or an error of the script Rows of a result for MCP mcp.maxRows cut, with a hint ( MCP ) Errors A failed request answers a status a client can map and a JSON body: { "error": "ExecutionError", "code": "23505", "message": "ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint \"device_types_pkey\" …" } Field Meaning error the name of the error: ExecutionError , ValidationError , ForbiddenError , ScriptDisabledError , … code the database's error code when there is one (Postgres SQLSTATE such as 23505 , MySQL ER_DUP_ENTRY ) message the message Status Cause 400 an invalid query or model ( ValidationError , SchemaError , SintaxisError , LanguageError ), a not null or check violation, invalid data (Postgres 22xxx ) 401 no credential, or a wrong one 403 the credential lacks the permission; scripts disabled 404 a schema not exposed on that transport, an unknown route 409 a unique or foreign key violation (Postgres 23505 , 23503 ; MySQL ER_DUP_ENTRY , ER_NO_REFERENCED_ROW_2 , ER_ROW_IS_REFERENCED_2 ) 413 a body, an answer or a script too large 429 rate limit, or too many simultaneous operations on the schema 503 the schema is not ready (starting, in error, restarting) n a script ran throw { status: n, message } (400–599) 500 anything else

docs.text: Transports The gateway has four transports. Each one listens on its own port, only when the port is configured ( Configuration ), and each one reaches every schema by its route. Transport What it is Routes of the schema iot/v1 Routes of the gateway http REST API, OpenAPI 3 POST /iot/v1/execute , GET /iot/v1/entities , … /ping , /health , /metrics , /version , /schemas , /doc , /api-docs , /ui mcpHttp MCP for AI agents POST/GET/DELETE /iot/v1/mcp (Streamable HTTP); GET /iot/v1/sse + POST /iot/v1/messages?sessionId= (HTTP+SSE) GET /status mcpWebSocket MCP over WebSocket upgrade at /iot/v1/mcp GET /status , /asyncapi webSocket JSON-RPC API with notifications connection to ws://host:port/iot/v1 connection to the root: general.* and gateway.schemas ; /asyncapi {basePath} ( transports.<t>.basePath ) goes before every route: with basePath: /data-gateway , /data-gateway/iot/v1/execute and /data-gateway/ui/ . With a single schema at the root, its routes have no prefix ( /execute , /mcp , ws://host:port/ ). A schema that is not exposed on a transport ( schemas[].transports ) answers 404 there. A schema that is not ready answers 503 with the reason. Each transport authenticates every request (or the WebSocket upgrade) with the effective authentication of the schema ( Security ). http The REST API: every operation of λORM on a schema (queries, scripts, the schema, stages), plus the routes of the gateway. JSON in and out. Methods and examples in REST API . transports: http: port: 8080 basePath: /data-gateway # optional swagger: { enabled: true } # /doc and /api-docs (Swagger UI, OpenAPI 3) ui: { enabled: true } # the web UI at /ui GET /doc (and /api-docs ) serves Swagger UI with the OpenAPI document. Its Authorize button asks for the credential as the schemas are configured: an API key in its header, a bearer token or a user and password. /ping , /health and /metrics need no credential (Kubernetes probes, Prometheus). The rate limit ( rateLimit ) applies to this transport only. mcpHttp Model Context Protocol for AI agents: a server per schema, with a tool per operation. See MCP . transports: mcpHttp: port: 8081 legacySse: true # also the older HTTP+SSE transport, for older clients stateful: false # stateless: any replica answers any request, no session affinity needed Route Protocol Clients POST/GET/DELETE {basePath}/{schema}/mcp Streamable HTTP Claude Code ( --transport http ), current clients GET {basePath}/{schema}/sse + POST {basePath}/{schema}/messages?sessionId=<id> HTTP+SSE (deprecated), with legacySse: true older clients GET {basePath}/status the state, the schemas and the open SSE sessions operations The credential goes in every request (Streamable HTTP) or in the GET and every POST (SSE). HTTP+SSE keeps a session in memory: with several replicas it needs session affinity. mcpWebSocket The same MCP servers over WebSocket. It is not a standard MCP transport : it is offered for clients and gateways that support it on their own; most clients use mcpHttp . transports: mcpWebSocket: port: 8082 maxConnections: 100 The connection is an upgrade at {basePath}/{schema}/mcp , authenticated in the handshake (without a credential it answers 401 and closes). The messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 with the MCP methods ( initialize , ping , tools/list , tools/call , resources/* , …). GET {basePath}/status and GET {basePath}/asyncapi (the AsyncAPI document) are plain HTTP. webSocket A JSON-RPC 2.0 API over one persistent connection, with the same operations as REST, plus notifications that REST cannot give: the end of a queued execution and the changes of state of the schema. See WebSocket API . transports: webSocket: port: 8083 maxConnections: 100 asyncapi: { enabled: true } # GET /asyncapi, /asyncapi.json

docs.text: UI A step by step tour, from the login to a diagram, is in Getting started . The gateway serves a web interface to explore its schemas and query them: an explorer of the schemas and their entities, the form of each entity, query tabs with the autocompletion of the domain, saved queries and diagrams of the domain. It is useful to try queries, to learn the language and to check what an agent does through MCP. transports: http: port: 8080 ui: { enabled: true } # off by default It is at http://localhost:8080/ui/ (with basePath: /data-gateway , at /data-gateway/ui/ ). It is served by the same http transport and calls its REST API with the credential that is entered: it has no other access. Pages Home. What the Data Gateway is, its version, the schemas of the instance with their state ( ready , error , …), a link to the API documentation (Swagger) and the Login button. Login. The authentication of the instance and the credential: Authentication Asks for API key the header (default X-Api-Key ) and the key Bearer token the token Basic the user and the password None nothing The Show / Hide button shows what was typed. The credential is checked against a schema ( /whoami ): a wrong one says so and stays on the page. The credential is kept only in that browser tab : closing it or reloading forgets it, and it is never stored. Queries. The workspace, after the login: at the top, the name and permissions of the credential, the API docs and Logout (back to the home page). At the top of every page there are two selectors: Theme: System (as the operating system), Light or Dark. Language: English, Español, Português, Français, Italiano, Deutsch, Nederlands, Català, Galego, Euskara. Both are remembered by the browser. Explorer On the left, the schemas of the instance. It can be resized by dragging its edge and hidden with the panel button of the tab bar. For each schema: Domain (YAML). The domain of the schema (entities, properties, relations, keys, enums) in a read-only editor, with syntax highlighting, search and folding. It shows only the domain: never the sources, the connections nor the rest of the configuration. Entities. Each entity unfolds into: Properties , with their types (the primary key in bold); Relations , with the related entity and the cardinality ( customer → Customers · N — 1 ); the Open button of a relation opens the related entity. The Open button (↗) of an entity, a double click or Enter open its form . What is saved in the schema: folders, queries and diagrams ( below ). Entity form Like a table in a database IDE, in its own tab, with these sections: Section Shows Properties each property: type (or enum), length, required, primary key (and unique), auto increment, default, the entity and property a foreign key references (a link to it), and its read / write expressions Relations its relations (name, type, entity, from, to, cardinality, weak) and Referenced by : the relations of other entities that point to it; each entity is a link to its form Keys and indexes primary key, unique key, indexes with their fields, constraints with their message and condition Data its rows in a table, read only , 50 per page, with Previous / Next; they can be copied and exported like any result Diagram the entity and its neighbours The Query button opens a query tab with Entity.page(1, 10) . Queries Each query is a tab, with its own schema, text, data, options and result; switching tabs loses nothing. A tab is opened with + , from an entity ( Query ) or from a saved query, and closed with its ×. Editor with the autocompletion of the schema's domain (entities, properties, relations and functions) and the errors of λORM marked in the text while typing. Mode: query or script (scripts only when the schema has them enabled and the credential has script ). Data and options (JSON), and for queued executions the topic and the chunk . Actions: plan , metadata , model , parameters (fills the data with the query's variables), constraints , execute (Ctrl+Enter), execute queued and, in script mode, execute script . An action the credential cannot use is disabled, and its tooltip says why. Result: status, operation, time, rows and size, and four views: tree , table (when the result is a list of rows), JSON and YAML . The tree and the table show up to 200 rows; the exports have all of them. The copy icon copies what is shown (the table as tab-separated text, ready to paste in a spreadsheet). Export downloads the whole result as JSON , YAML or TXT (tab-separated) . History of the last queries of each schema, to bring one back. Saved queries and diagrams The + of a schema or of a folder adds: New folder. Folders nest, to organise what is saved. New query. A query tab whose folder is that one. New diagram. See Diagrams . Each saved item has a name and a description (shown when the pointer is over it). Its row has Edit (name, description and folder) and Delete (with confirmation; a folder takes what it holds). Items are moved by dragging them onto a folder or onto the schema. Two items of the same kind cannot have the same name in a folder. A query tab has Save (Ctrl+S) and Save as… : the first save asks for the name, the description and the folder. A • in the tab marks changes that are not saved; once saved it says saved . Opening a saved query that is already open goes to its tab. Diagrams A diagram of the domain shows the chosen entities as boxes, with their properties, types, PK and FK (the required ones in bold), and the relations as lines with their cardinality ( 1 — N , 1 — 1 ); an inheritance is a dashed line. New diagram asks for the name, the description, the folder and the entities : they are searched, checked one by one, or completed with Add their neighbours (the entities related to the chosen ones). In a diagram: Action How Lay out automatic when it opens (the boxes are placed by ELK ); lay out again returns to it Move a box drag it Move a line drag it sideways; its ends stay on the rows of the fields it joins; a double click puts it back Remove an entity the × of its box (shown when the pointer is over it), or click the box and press Delete Add or remove entities Entities… Names of the relations relation names Only the names of the entities names only Zoom and move the mouse wheel; drag the background; fit shows it all Open an entity double click its box Export SVG or PNG The diagram is saved ( Save or Ctrl+S) with the place of every box and line, the names option and the entities. Where it is saved What is saved (folders, queries, diagrams) stays in the browser , in its IndexedDB, separated by gateway and by credential: what one credential saves is not seen with another. Only the name of the credential is used for this, never its secret. It is in that browser on that device: another browser or another device doesn't see it. It goes if the site data of the browser is cleared. The browser is asked to keep it, and the explorer exports everything to a JSON file (⤓) and imports it back (⤒), adding to what there is or replacing it: a backup, a way to move it to another browser or to share it with someone. In a browser that doesn't allow storing (some private windows), the explorer says so: what is saved lasts until the page is closed. In your own application The UI is built with @lambdaorm/ui , a library of React components that any web application can use against a Data Gateway: npm install @lambdaorm/ui react react-dom import { Workspace } from '@lambdaorm/ui' import '@lambdaorm/ui/styles.css' <Workspace baseUrl="https://gateway.example.com" // the http transport of the gateway headers={() => ({ 'X-Api-Key': key })} // how to authenticate; the library keeps no credential locale="es" theme="dark" workspaceKey={`gateway.example.com|${user}`} // separates what is saved /> Component What it is Workspace the whole workspace: explorer, entity forms, queries, saved items and diagrams QueryWorkbench one query editor with its actions and result QueryTabs several workbenches in tabs DomainDiagram a diagram of the domain (an entity and its neighbours, the whole model, or chosen entities) EntityView the form of an entity ResultViewer a result as tree, table, JSON or YAML, with copy and export What is saved can go to another place than the browser by giving store (a WorkspaceStore , for example a backend of your own).

docs.text: A step by step tour, from the login to a diagram, is in Getting started . The gateway serves a web interface to explore its schemas and query them: an explorer of the schemas and their entities, the form of each entity, query tabs with the autocompletion of the domain, saved queries and diagrams of the domain. It is useful to try queries, to learn the language and to check what an agent does through MCP. transports: http: port: 8080 ui: { enabled: true } # off by default It is at http://localhost:8080/ui/ (with basePath: /data-gateway , at /data-gateway/ui/ ). It is served by the same http transport and calls its REST API with the credential that is entered: it has no other access.

docs.text: Home. What the Data Gateway is, its version, the schemas of the instance with their state ( ready , error , …), a link to the API documentation (Swagger) and the Login button. Login. The authentication of the instance and the credential: Authentication Asks for API key the header (default X-Api-Key ) and the key Bearer token the token Basic the user and the password None nothing The Show / Hide button shows what was typed. The credential is checked against a schema ( /whoami ): a wrong one says so and stays on the page. The credential is kept only in that browser tab : closing it or reloading forgets it, and it is never stored. Queries. The workspace, after the login: at the top, the name and permissions of the credential, the API docs and Logout (back to the home page). At the top of every page there are two selectors: Theme: System (as the operating system), Light or Dark. Language: English, Español, Português, Français, Italiano, Deutsch, Nederlands, Català, Galego, Euskara. Both are remembered by the browser.

docs.text: On the left, the schemas of the instance. It can be resized by dragging its edge and hidden with the panel button of the tab bar. For each schema: Domain (YAML). The domain of the schema (entities, properties, relations, keys, enums) in a read-only editor, with syntax highlighting, search and folding. It shows only the domain: never the sources, the connections nor the rest of the configuration. Entities. Each entity unfolds into: Properties , with their types (the primary key in bold); Relations , with the related entity and the cardinality ( customer → Customers · N — 1 ); the Open button of a relation opens the related entity. The Open button (↗) of an entity, a double click or Enter open its form . What is saved in the schema: folders, queries and diagrams ( below ).
docs.title: Explorer

docs.text: Like a table in a database IDE, in its own tab, with these sections: Section Shows Properties each property: type (or enum), length, required, primary key (and unique), auto increment, default, the entity and property a foreign key references (a link to it), and its read / write expressions Relations its relations (name, type, entity, from, to, cardinality, weak) and Referenced by : the relations of other entities that point to it; each entity is a link to its form Keys and indexes primary key, unique key, indexes with their fields, constraints with their message and condition Data its rows in a table, read only , 50 per page, with Previous / Next; they can be copied and exported like any result Diagram the entity and its neighbours The Query button opens a query tab with Entity.page(1, 10) .
docs.title: Entity form

docs.text: Each query is a tab, with its own schema, text, data, options and result; switching tabs loses nothing. A tab is opened with + , from an entity ( Query ) or from a saved query, and closed with its ×. Editor with the autocompletion of the schema's domain (entities, properties, relations and functions) and the errors of λORM marked in the text while typing. Mode: query or script (scripts only when the schema has them enabled and the credential has script ). Data and options (JSON), and for queued executions the topic and the chunk . Actions: plan , metadata , model , parameters (fills the data with the query's variables), constraints , execute (Ctrl+Enter), execute queued and, in script mode, execute script . An action the credential cannot use is disabled, and its tooltip says why. Result: status, operation, time, rows and size, and four views: tree , table (when the result is a list of rows), JSON and YAML . The tree and the table show up to 200 rows; the exports have all of them. The copy icon copies what is shown (the table as tab-separated text, ready to paste in a spreadsheet). Export downloads the whole result as JSON , YAML or TXT (tab-separated) . History of the last queries of each schema, to bring one back.

docs.text: The + of a schema or of a folder adds: New folder. Folders nest, to organise what is saved. New query. A query tab whose folder is that one. New diagram. See Diagrams . Each saved item has a name and a description (shown when the pointer is over it). Its row has Edit (name, description and folder) and Delete (with confirmation; a folder takes what it holds). Items are moved by dragging them onto a folder or onto the schema. Two items of the same kind cannot have the same name in a folder. A query tab has Save (Ctrl+S) and Save as… : the first save asks for the name, the description and the folder. A • in the tab marks changes that are not saved; once saved it says saved . Opening a saved query that is already open goes to its tab.

docs.text: WebSocket API The webSocket transport offers the operations of the REST API over one persistent JSON-RPC 2.0 connection , plus notifications that REST cannot give: the end of a queued execution and the changes of state of the schema. transports: webSocket: port: 8083 The connection is opened against the schema's route, ws://localhost:8083/iot/v1 ( ws://localhost:8083/ for a single schema at the root), and is authenticated in the upgrade with the same headers as REST. A connection to the root of a gateway with several schemas has only general.* and gateway.schemas . → { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "query.execute", "params": { "query": "Products.filter(p => p.price > minPrice)", "data": { "minPrice": 50 } } } ← { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": [ { "id": 29, "name": "Thüringer Rostbratwurst", "price": 123.79 } ] } → { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "query.script", "params": { "script": "1 + 1" } } ← { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "error": { "code": -32000, "message": "the credential \"reader\" does not have the \"script\" permission", "data": { "name": "ForbiddenError", "status": 403 } } } The params are the body (or the route parameters) of the equivalent REST method. An error carries in data the name and the HTTP status that REST would have answered. Methods Method Params REST equivalent general.version — GET /version general.health — GET /health general.ping — GET /ping gateway.schemas — (only at the root) GET /schemas query.execute query , data? , options? POST /execute query.script script , data? , options? POST /script query.executeQueued topic , query , data? , chunk? , options? , notify? POST /execute-queued query.plan query , options? POST /plan query.metadata query POST /metadata query.model query POST /model query.parameters query POST /parameters query.constraints query POST /constraints schema.schema — GET /schema schema.version — GET /schema/version schema.domain — GET /domain schema.entities / schema.entity — / entity GET /entities[/{entity}] schema.enums / schema.enum — / enum GET /enums[/{enum}] schema.sources / schema.source — / source GET /sources[/{source}] schema.mappings / schema.mapping / schema.entityMapping — / mapping / mapping , entity GET /mappings… schema.views — GET /views schema.stages / schema.stage — / stage GET /stages[/{stage}] schema.typings — GET /typings stage.exists stage GET /stages/{stage}/exists stage.export stage GET /stages/{stage}/export stage.import stage , data POST /stages/{stage}/import The permissions are the same as in REST. Notifications Messages from the server without an id : Notification When Params queue.completed an execution queued with query.executeQueued and notify: true on this connection ended queueId , ok: true , rows (sent to the topic) queue.failed that execution failed queueId , ok: false , error schema.statusChanged the schema of the connection went to error / restarting , or back to ready path , status , reason → { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "query.executeQueued", "params": { "topic": "countries", "query": "Countries.map(p => [p.iso3, p.name])", "chunk": 1000, "notify": true } } ← { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "result": { "queueId": "q-123" } } ← { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "queue.completed", "params": { "queueId": "q-123", "ok": true, "rows": 250 } } If the schema stops being ready , the requests answer an error with status: 503 ; the connection stays open and works again when the schema recovers. The AsyncAPI document of the transport is at GET /asyncapi (and /asyncapi.json ). From Node, the client uses this transport with a ws:// URL.

docs.text: Bulk Insert This page shows how to insert many records at once with bulkInsert . Use it instead of Insert when you have a list of records to load, such as an import or a large dataset. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL. bulkInsert receives an array of records and inserts them in chunks, with one statement per chunk instead of one statement per record. The size of the chunks depends on the connection, and you can lower it with the chunkSize option of orm.execute . This reduces the round trips between the application and the database, which makes inserting large volumes of data much faster and lightens the load on the database server. Bulk insert into one entity Inserts a list of categories. Lambda: Categories.bulkInsert() SQL Result: INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName,Description) VALUES ? Bulk insert with a related entity Inserts a list of orders, each one with its details. Lambda: Orders.bulkInsert().include(p => p.details) SQL Result: -- the orders INSERT INTO Orders(CustomerID,EmployeeID,OrderDate,RequiredDate,ShippedDate,ShipVia,Freight,ShipName,ShipAddress,ShipCity,ShipRegion,ShipPostalCode,ShipCountry) VALUES ? -- the details of all the orders INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES ? Code example Inserts two categories and prints the ids of the records inserted. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Categories } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const categories = [ { name: 'Beverages4', description: 'Soft drinks, coffees, teas, beers, and ales' }, { name: 'Condiments4', description: 'Sweet and savory sauces, relishes, spreads, and seasonings' } ] const query = () => Categories.bulkInsert() // returns the ids of the records inserted const result = await orm.execute(query, categories) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Delete This page shows how to delete records: with a filter, by primary key, all the records of an entity, and together with related entities. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL. delete returns the number of affected rows : 0 means that no row matched the filter. const count = await orm.execute('Categories.delete().filter(p => p.id == id)', { id: 9 }) // 1 Delete with a filter Deletes the details of an order. Lambda: Orders.details.delete().filter(p => p.orderId === id) SQL Result: DELETE o FROM `Order Details` AS o WHERE o.OrderID = ? Delete by primary key When delete() has no filter, it filters by the primary key, whose value is taken from the data passed. The primary key of the order details is made of orderId and productId : Lambda: Orders.details.delete() SQL Result: DELETE o FROM `Order Details` AS o WHERE (o.OrderID = ? AND o.ProductID = ?) Delete all the records To delete all the records of an entity, use deleteAll instead of delete . This prevents deleting all the records by mistake. Lambda: Orders.details.deleteAll() SQL Result: DELETE FROM `Order Details` Delete an entity and its related entities Deletes an order and its details. The order is filtered by its primary key, and each detail sent by its own primary key. The details are deleted first, and then the order. Lambda: Orders.delete().include(p => p.details) SQL Result: -- the order DELETE o FROM Orders AS o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- each detail sent DELETE o1 FROM `Order Details` AS o1 WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?) Code example Deletes an order with its details and prints the number of orders deleted. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const order = { id: 1, customerId: 'ALFKI', employeeId: 6, orderDate: '1997-08-24T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1997-09-21T22:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1997-09-01T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 1, freight: '29.4600', name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste', address: 'Obere Str. 57', city: 'Berlin', region: null, postalCode: '12209', country: 'Germany', details: [ { orderId: 1, productId: 28, unitPrice: '45.6000', quantity: '15.0000', discount: '0.0000' }, { orderId: 1, productId: 39, unitPrice: '18.0000', quantity: '21.0000', discount: '0.0000' } ] } const query = () => Orders.delete().include(p => p.details) // returns the number of orders deleted const count = await orm.execute(query, order) console.log(count) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Lambda expressions This page summarizes the building blocks of a λORM query: the methods you chain on an entity, and the operators and functions you can use inside the lambdas. Use it as a quick reference; each method links to the page with its examples. Queries are lambda expressions written in the programming language itself. They refer to the entities and properties of the domain, so they are independent of the database language and of how the data is stored. Example The following query reads the products whose name starts with "A", with the name of their category, sorted by category (ascending) and product (descending), and returns the first page of 10 records: Products .filter(p => upper(substr(p.name, 1, 1)) == "A") .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, product: p.name })) .sort(p => [p.category, desc(p.product)]) .page(1, 10) On Oracle, λORM translates it into: SELECT c.CategoryName AS "category", p.ProductName AS "product" FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID WHERE UPPER(SUBSTR(p.ProductName,1,1)) = 'A' ORDER BY "category" asc, "product" desc OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY The same query runs on any other engine: on MySQL, for example, the pagination becomes LIMIT 0,10 . Advantages Queries are written in the same programming language as the application. There is no new language to learn. Expressions are easy to write and to read. The IDE's IntelliSense helps you write the expressions. Syntax errors are caught while you write. Query methods Method Description SQL equivalent Examples filter Filters the records. WHERE Select having Filters the groups. HAVING Grouping map Specifies the properties to return. SELECT Select distinct Specifies the properties to return, removing duplicate records. SELECT DISTINCT Select first Returns the first record. SELECT + ORDER BY + LIMIT Select last Returns the last record. SELECT + ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT Select sort Specifies the order of the records. ORDER BY Select page Paginates the records. LIMIT / OFFSET (depends on the dialect) Select include Loads the records of related entities. Include insert Inserts a record. INSERT Insert upsert Inserts a record, or updates it if one with the same primary key exists. INSERT … ON CONFLICT / MERGE Insert bulkInsert Inserts many records at once. INSERT Bulk Insert update Updates records; it always has a filter. UPDATE with WHERE Update updateAll Updates all the records of an entity. UPDATE without WHERE Update delete Deletes records; it always has a filter. DELETE with WHERE Delete deleteAll Deletes all the records of an entity. DELETE without WHERE Delete There is no method for joins: an INNER JOIN is deduced when the query navigates a relation, as in p.category.name (see Join ). There is no method for GROUP BY: it is deduced when an aggregate function is used (see Grouping ). Operators The operators are the same as in JavaScript. docs.text: Grouping This page shows how to group records and compute aggregates (sums, counts, maximums…), and how to filter the groups with having . The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL. You do not declare the grouping: λORM deduces it when the query uses an aggregate function. The records are grouped by the properties returned that are not inside an aggregate function. Aggregate functions Function Description avg Calculates the average of the values in a group. count Counts the records in a group. first Returns the first value in a group. last Returns the last value in a group. max Calculates the maximum. min Calculates the minimum. sum Calculates the sum. Sum with filter and sort Reads, for the orders of a customer, the order date and the total (sum of quantity × unit price), sorted by total in descending order. The records are grouped by order , the only property returned that is not an aggregate. Lambda: Orders.details .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName) .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) })) .sort(p => desc(p.total)) SQL Result: SELECT o1.OrderDate AS `order`, SUM((o.Quantity * o.UnitPrice)) AS total FROM `Order Details` o INNER JOIN Orders o1 ON o1.OrderID = o.OrderID INNER JOIN Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o1.CustomerID WHERE c.CompanyName = ? GROUP BY o1.OrderDate ORDER BY total desc Grouping and having Reads the highest price of each category, considering the products with a price greater than 5 whose supplier is from a given country, or with fewer than 3 units in stock. Only the categories whose highest price is greater than 50 are returned, sorted by that price in descending order. filter is applied to the records before grouping (WHERE); having is applied to the groups (HAVING). Lambda: Products .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3)) .having(p => max(p.price) > 50) .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) })) .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice)) SQL Result: SELECT c.CategoryName AS category, MAX(p.UnitPrice) AS largestPrice FROM Products p INNER JOIN Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = p.SupplierID INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID WHERE ((p.UnitPrice > 5 AND s.Country = ?) OR p.UnitsInStock < 3) GROUP BY c.CategoryName HAVING MAX(p.UnitPrice) > 50 ORDER BY largestPrice desc Code example import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Products } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // highest price per category, for the categories whose highest price is greater than 50 const query = (country: string) => Products .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3)) .having(p => max(p.price) > 50) .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) })) .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice)) const result = await orm.execute(query, { country: 'USA' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Include This page shows how to load related entities together with the main entity, using the include method. Use it when the result must contain an object with its relations (an order with its customer and its details), or when the related entity is in another source. include works with every type of relation ( oneToMany , manyToOne and oneToOne , see relations ). In λORM terms, a oneToMany relation points to one record (each order has one customer ) and a manyToOne relation is a collection (each order has many details ). Inside an include you can also filter the related records and choose their properties. For each include, λORM runs one statement that reads all the related records needed, and then assembles the objects in memory. This avoids running one statement per record, which considerably improves performance. To link the records, λORM adds the keys it needs to the statements ( __customerId , LambdaOrmParentId …); they are removed from the result. Includes can be used in selects, inserts, upserts, updates, deletes and bulk inserts. The SQL shown on this page is the one generated for MySQL. Include a oneToMany relation Reads an order and its customer. Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.customer) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the customers of the orders read above SELECT c.CustomerID AS id, c.CompanyName AS name, c.ContactName AS contact, c.ContactTitle AS phone, c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "id": 10248, "customerId": "VINET", "employeeId": 5, "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "requiredDate": "1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z", "shippedDate": "1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z", "shipViaId": 3, "freight": 32.38, "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l-Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France", "customer": { "id": "VINET", "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "contact": "Paul Henriot", "phone": "Accounting Manager", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France" } } ] Include manyToOne and oneToMany relations Reads an order with its details and its customer. To include several relations, return them in an array. Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => [p.details, p.customer]) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the details of the orders read above SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.Discount AS discount, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the customers of the orders read above SELECT c.CustomerID AS id, c.CompanyName AS name, c.ContactName AS contact, c.ContactTitle AS phone, c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "id": 10248, "customerId": "VINET", "employeeId": 5, "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "requiredDate": "1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z", "shippedDate": "1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z", "shipViaId": 3, "freight": 32.38, "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l-Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France", "details": [ { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 11, "unitPrice": 14, "quantity": 12, "discount": 0 }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 42, "unitPrice": 9.8, "quantity": 10, "discount": 0 }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 72, "unitPrice": 34.8, "quantity": 5, "discount": 0 } ], "customer": { "id": "VINET", "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "contact": "Paul Henriot", "phone": "Accounting Manager", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France" } } ] Nested includes An included relation can include its own relations. This example reads an order with its customer and its details; for each detail it reads the product, and for each product its category. Lambda: Orders .filter(p => p.id == id) .include(p => [p.details.include(q => q.product.include(r => r.category)), p.customer]) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the details of the orders SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.Discount AS discount, o1.ProductID AS `__productId`, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the products of the details SELECT p.ProductID AS id, p.ProductName AS name, p.SupplierID AS supplierId, p.CategoryID AS categoryId, p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, p.UnitPrice AS price, p.UnitsInStock AS inStock, p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder, p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel, p.Discontinued AS discontinued, p.CategoryID AS `__categoryId`, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN (?) -- the categories of the products SELECT c.CategoryID AS id, c.CategoryName AS name, c.Description AS description, c.CategoryID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Categories c WHERE c.CategoryID IN (?) -- the customers of the orders SELECT c1.CustomerID AS id, c1.CompanyName AS name, c1.ContactName AS contact, c1.ContactTitle AS phone, c1.Address AS address, c1.City AS city, c1.Region AS region, c1.PostalCode AS postalCode, c1.Country AS country, c1.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c1 WHERE c1.CustomerID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "id": 10248, "customerId": "VINET", "employeeId": 5, "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "requiredDate": "1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z", "shippedDate": "1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z", "shipViaId": 3, "freight": 32.38, "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l-Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France", "details": [ { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 11, "unitPrice": 14, "quantity": 12, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 11, "name": "Queso Cabrales", "supplierId": 5, "categoryId": 4, "quantity": "1 kg pkg.", "price": 21, "inStock": 22, "onOrder": 30, "reorderLevel": 30, "discontinued": false, "category": { "id": 4, "name": "Dairy Products", "description": "Cheeses" } } }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 42, "unitPrice": 9.8, "quantity": 10, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 42, "name": "Singaporean Hokkien Fried Mee", "supplierId": 20, "categoryId": 5, "quantity": "32 - 1 kg pkgs.", "price": 14, "inStock": 26, "onOrder": 0, "reorderLevel": 0, "discontinued": true, "category": { "id": 5, "name": "Grains/Cereals", "description": "Breads, crackers, pasta, and cereal" } } }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 72, "unitPrice": 34.8, "quantity": 5, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 72, "name": "Mozzarella di Giovanni", "supplierId": 14, "categoryId": 4, "quantity": "24 - 200 g pkgs.", "price": 34.8, "inStock": 14, "onOrder": 0, "reorderLevel": 0, "discontinued": false, "category": { "id": 4, "name": "Dairy Products", "description": "Cheeses" } } } ], "customer": { "id": "VINET", "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "contact": "Paul Henriot", "phone": "Accounting Manager", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France" } } ] Include only some properties You can choose the properties to return both for the main entity and for each included entity, so that the query returns only the data you need. This example reads the date of an order; the name and full address of its customer; the quantity and unit price of its details; the name of each product and the name of its category. Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => [ // name of the customer and full address p.customer.map(p => ({ name: p.name, address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ') ', p.country) })), // quantity and unit price of the details, with the name of the product and of its category p.details.include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ]) // date of the order .map(p => p.orderDate) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`, o.OrderID AS `__id` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the customers of the orders SELECT c.CompanyName AS name, CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(c.Address,', '),c.City),' ('),c.PostalCode),') '),c.Country) AS address, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) -- the details of the orders SELECT o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.ProductID AS `__productId`, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the products of the details SELECT p.ProductName AS name, p.CategoryID AS `__categoryId`, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN (?) -- the categories of the products SELECT c1.CategoryName AS name, c1.CategoryID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Categories c1 WHERE c1.CategoryID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye, Reims (51100) France" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 12, "unitPrice": 14, "product": { "name": "Queso Cabrales", "category": { "name": "Dairy Products" } } }, { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 9.8, "product": { "name": "Singaporean Hokkien Fried Mee", "category": { "name": "Grains/Cereals" } } }, { "quantity": 5, "unitPrice": 34.8, "product": { "name": "Mozzarella di Giovanni", "category": { "name": "Dairy Products" } } } ] } ] Relations in another source The related entity can be in another source (another database or schema) of the stage. Since each include runs as a separate statement, include works across sources at any depth: // Orders and OrderLines in one source, Products and Categories in another Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines.include(l => l.product.include(q => q.category))) Filter by a field of a relation in another source A filter can also use a property of a relation whose entity is in another source. The other source is queried first, and the keys found are then used to filter with in : Lambda: // OrderLines (source "sales") filtered by the name of its product (source "catalog") OrderLines.filter(p => p.product.name == name && p.orderId == orderId) Executed as: // 1. on the source of Products Products.filter(p => p.name == name) // 2. on the source of OrderLines, with the ids found in 1 OrderLines.filter(p => in(p.productId, ids) && p.orderId == orderId) Each comparison is replaced on its own, so && , || and ! keep their meaning. It can be combined with other conditions, also with || : OrderLines.filter(p => p.orderId == orderId && (p.product.name == name || p.quantity > 100)) . When the other source has no match, the query returns no rows. Only one level of relation is supported ( p.product.name , not p.product.category.name ). The other side of each comparison must be a value (a literal or a variable). Comparing with a property, as in p.product.name == p.description , fails with an error saying that the relation is in another source. Code example The query of Include only some properties , run from Node with @lambdaorm/lib : import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const query = (id: number) => Orders .filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => [ p.customer.map(p => ({ name: p.name, address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ') ', p.country) })), p.details.include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ]) .map(p => p.orderDate) const result = await orm.execute(query, { id: 10248 }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()

Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.customer) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the customers of the orders read above SELECT c.CustomerID AS id, c.CompanyName AS name, c.ContactName AS contact, c.ContactTitle AS phone, c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) docs.text: Reads an order with its details and its customer. To include several relations, return them in an array. Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => [p.details, p.customer]) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the details of the orders read above SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.Discount AS discount, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the customers of the orders read above SELECT c.CustomerID AS id, c.CompanyName AS name, c.ContactName AS contact, c.ContactTitle AS phone, c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) docs.text: An included relation can include its own relations. This example reads an order with its customer and its details; for each detail it reads the product, and for each product its category. Lambda: Orders .filter(p => p.id == id) .include(p => [p.details.include(q => q.product.include(r => r.category)), p.customer]) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight, o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region, o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the details of the orders SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.Discount AS discount, o1.ProductID AS `__productId`, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the products of the details SELECT p.ProductID AS id, p.ProductName AS name, p.SupplierID AS supplierId, p.CategoryID AS categoryId, p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, p.UnitPrice AS price, p.UnitsInStock AS inStock, p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder, p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel, p.Discontinued AS discontinued, p.CategoryID AS `__categoryId`, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN (?) -- the categories of the products SELECT c.CategoryID AS id, c.CategoryName AS name, c.Description AS description, c.CategoryID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Categories c WHERE c.CategoryID IN (?) -- the customers of the orders SELECT c1.CustomerID AS id, c1.CompanyName AS name, c1.ContactName AS contact, c1.ContactTitle AS phone, c1.Address AS address, c1.City AS city, c1.Region AS region, c1.PostalCode AS postalCode, c1.Country AS country, c1.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c1 WHERE c1.CustomerID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "id": 10248, "customerId": "VINET", "employeeId": 5, "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "requiredDate": "1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z", "shippedDate": "1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z", "shipViaId": 3, "freight": 32.38, "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l-Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France", "details": [ { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 11, "unitPrice": 14, "quantity": 12, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 11, "name": "Queso Cabrales", "supplierId": 5, "categoryId": 4, "quantity": "1 kg pkg.", "price": 21, "inStock": 22, "onOrder": 30, "reorderLevel": 30, "discontinued": false, "category": { "id": 4, "name": "Dairy Products", "description": "Cheeses" } } }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 42, "unitPrice": 9.8, "quantity": 10, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 42, "name": "Singaporean Hokkien Fried Mee", "supplierId": 20, "categoryId": 5, "quantity": "32 - 1 kg pkgs.", "price": 14, "inStock": 26, "onOrder": 0, "reorderLevel": 0, "discontinued": true, "category": { "id": 5, "name": "Grains/Cereals", "description": "Breads, crackers, pasta, and cereal" } } }, { "orderId": 10248, "productId": 72, "unitPrice": 34.8, "quantity": 5, "discount": 0, "product": { "id": 72, "name": "Mozzarella di Giovanni", "supplierId": 14, "categoryId": 4, "quantity": "24 - 200 g pkgs.", "price": 34.8, "inStock": 14, "onOrder": 0, "reorderLevel": 0, "discontinued": false, "category": { "id": 4, "name": "Dairy Products", "description": "Cheeses" } } } ], "customer": { "id": "VINET", "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "contact": "Paul Henriot", "phone": "Accounting Manager", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye", "city": "Reims", "region": null, "postalCode": "51100", "country": "France" } } ]
docs.title: Nested includes

docs.text: You can choose the properties to return both for the main entity and for each included entity, so that the query returns only the data you need. This example reads the date of an order; the name and full address of its customer; the quantity and unit price of its details; the name of each product and the name of its category. Lambda: Orders.filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => [ // name of the customer and full address p.customer.map(p => ({ name: p.name, address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ') ', p.country) })), // quantity and unit price of the details, with the name of the product and of its category p.details.include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ]) // date of the order .map(p => p.orderDate) SQL Result: -- the order SELECT o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`, o.OrderID AS `__id` FROM Orders o WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- the customers of the orders SELECT c.CompanyName AS name, CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(c.Address,', '),c.City),' ('),c.PostalCode),') '),c.Country) AS address, c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?) -- the details of the orders SELECT o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.ProductID AS `__productId`, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) -- the products of the details SELECT p.ProductName AS name, p.CategoryID AS `__categoryId`, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN (?) -- the categories of the products SELECT c1.CategoryName AS name, c1.CategoryID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Categories c1 WHERE c1.CategoryID IN (?) Data Result: [ { "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Vins et alcools Chevalier", "address": "59 rue de l'Abbaye, Reims (51100) France" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 12, "unitPrice": 14, "product": { "name": "Queso Cabrales", "category": { "name": "Dairy Products" } } }, { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 9.8, "product": { "name": "Singaporean Hokkien Fried Mee", "category": { "name": "Grains/Cereals" } } }, { "quantity": 5, "unitPrice": 34.8, "product": { "name": "Mozzarella di Giovanni", "category": { "name": "Dairy Products" } } } ] } ]
docs.title: Include only some properties

docs.text: The related entity can be in another source (another database or schema) of the stage. Since each include runs as a separate statement, include works across sources at any depth: // Orders and OrderLines in one source, Products and Categories in another Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines.include(l => l.product.include(q => q.category)))
docs.title: Relations in another source

docs.text: The query of Include only some properties , run from Node with @lambdaorm/lib : import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const query = (id: number) => Orders .filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => [ p.customer.map(p => ({ name: p.name, address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ') ', p.country) })), p.details.include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ]) .map(p => p.orderDate) const result = await orm.execute(query, { id: 10248 }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Insert This page shows how to insert records: with all the properties of the entity or only some of them, together with related entities ( include ), and how to insert or update in one step ( upsert ). To insert many records at once, see Bulk Insert . The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL, unless stated otherwise. A query is based on both the expression and the schema. If you do not specify the properties to insert, all the properties of the entity are inserted. How each property is stored in each source (table and column names) is resolved by the mapping of that source in the schema. Insert all the properties When the properties are not specified, the data passed must be an object with the properties of the entity. Lambda: Categories.insert() SQL Result: INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName,Description) VALUES(?,?) The primary key id is not inserted because it is auto-increment: the database generates it. Insert some properties Only the properties specified are inserted. Here, name is a variable of the data passed to the query. Lambda: Categories.insert({ name: name }) SQL Result: INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName) VALUES(?) Insert with include To insert an object together with its related objects, include the relation. This example inserts an order and its details; the key of the new order is assigned to each detail. Lambda: Orders.insert().include(p => p.details) SQL Result: -- the order INSERT INTO Orders(CustomerID,EmployeeID,OrderDate,RequiredDate,ShippedDate,ShipVia,Freight,ShipName,ShipAddress,ShipCity,ShipRegion,ShipPostalCode,ShipCountry) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?) -- each detail of the order INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?) Upsert upsert() inserts the record or, if a record with the same primary key already exists, updates it. It is written like an insert: upsert() with all the properties, or with the properties specified. The entity needs a primary key, and the data must include it (so an auto-increment key is of little use here). Lambda: // inserts the country, or updates it when one with the same iso3 exists Countries.upsert() await orm.execute('Countries.upsert()', { iso3: 'ARG', name: 'Argentine' }) // inserted await orm.execute('Countries.upsert()', { iso3: 'ARG', name: 'Argentina' }) // updated: the same row SQL Result: -- MySQL / MariaDB INSERT INTO Countries(iso3,name) VALUES(?,?) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE name = VALUES(name) -- PostgreSQL INSERT INTO Countries(iso3,name) VALUES($1,$2) ON CONFLICT (iso3) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name -- SQL Server MERGE INTO Countries WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS t USING (SELECT 1 AS x) AS s ON t.iso3 = @iso3 WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = @name WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (iso3,name) VALUES (@iso3,@name); -- Oracle MERGE INTO Countries t USING (SELECT 1 FROM DUAL) s ON (t.iso3 = :iso3) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = :name WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (iso3,name) VALUES (:iso3,:name) Upsert is supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle (these two with MERGE , from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0). Warning On MongoDB, upsert fails with a "not supported yet" error. SQLite (SQL.js) does not support it either. When the key is generated (auto-increment) and not sent, the upsert inserts. On SQL Server the identity column is never inserted (the database generates it) and OUTPUT INSERTED returns it; Oracle's MERGE cannot return values, so it returns the key that was sent. Upsert is also what an update with include of a composite relation uses to save the children. Code example Inserts an order with two details and prints the id of the new order. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const order = { customerId: 'VINET', employeeId: 5, orderDate: '1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 3, freight: 32.38, name: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier', address: '59 rue de l-Abbaye', city: 'Reims', postalCode: '51100', country: 'France', // orderId is assigned from the new order details: [ { productId: 11, unitPrice: 14, quantity: 12, discount: 10 }, { productId: 42, unitPrice: 9.8, quantity: 10, discount: 10 } ] } const query = () => Orders.insert().include(p => p.details) // returns the id of the order created const result = await orm.execute(query, order) console.log(JSON.stringify(result)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()
