docs.text: Join This page shows how λORM reads properties of related entities. There is no join method: when a query uses a property through a relation, such as p.category.name , λORM adds the join that the relation defines in the schema. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL. Note A join needs both entities in the same source. To read related entities that are in another source, use Include ; to filter by a property of a relation in another source, see Filter by a field of a relation in another source . Simple join Reads the name of each product and the name of its category, through the category relation. Lambda: Products.map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name })) SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID Join with distinct and sort Reads the distinct combinations of quantity per unit and category name, sorted by category. Lambda: Products .distinct(p => ({ quantity: p.quantity, category: p.category.name })) .sort(p => p.category) SQL Result: SELECT DISTINCT p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID ORDER BY category asc Join with filter Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10. Lambda: Products .filter(p => p.price > 10) .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name })) SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10 Join and pagination Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10, sorted by category, and returns the first page of 10 records. Lambda: Products .filter(p => p.price > 10) .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name })) .sort(p => p.category) .page(1, 10) SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10 ORDER BY category asc LIMIT 0,10 Multiple joins and grouping Reads, for the orders of a customer, the order date and the total (sum of quantity × unit price of its details), sorted by total in descending order. The query starts from the order details ( Orders.details ) and goes through two relations: order , and from the order, customer . Because sum is an aggregate function, λORM also groups by the order date (see Grouping ). Lambda: Orders.details .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName) .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) })) .sort(p => desc(p.total)) SQL Result: SELECT o1.OrderDate AS `order`, SUM((o.Quantity * o.UnitPrice)) AS total FROM `Order Details` o INNER JOIN Orders o1 ON o1.OrderID = o.OrderID INNER JOIN Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o1.CustomerID WHERE c.CompanyName = ? GROUP BY o1.OrderDate ORDER BY total desc Code example import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const query = (customerName: string) => Orders.details .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName) .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) })) .sort(p => desc(p.total)) const result = await orm.execute(query, { customerName: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier' }, { stage: 'MySQL' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Metadata This page describes the methods that analyse a query without running it: the parameters it needs, the shape of its result, the constraints that apply, its analysed tree and the statements it would execute. Use them to validate a query, to build a form or a type for its data, or to see the SQL that λORM generates. These methods do not access the database, so the connections are not needed: you can call orm.init(schema, false) to load the schema without connecting. Method Description orm.parameters(query) The variables the query uses (which go in data ), with their types. orm.model(query) The properties of the result, with their types. orm.constraints(query) The constraints that apply to the entities of the query. orm.metadata(query) The analysed tree of the query: each statement with its entity, columns, parameters and constraints. orm.plan(query, options?) How the query is executed: the dialect, the source and the statement of each part. options.stage selects the stage. orm.normalize(query) The query in its complete form, for example with the properties of map made explicit. The query can be a lambda function or a string. The same information is available from the CLI ( lambdaorm parameters , model , constraints , metadata , plan ) and from the Data Gateway ( POST /parameters , /model , /constraints , /metadata , /plan ). Example import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { // load the schema without connecting to the databases await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml', false) const query = (id: number) => Orders .filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => p.details) .map(p => ({ name: p.orderDate, customer: p.customer.name })) console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.parameters(query), null, 2)) console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.model(query), null, 2)) console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.constraints(query), null, 2)) console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.metadata(query), null, 2)) console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.plan(query, { stage: 'MySQL' }), null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } finally { await orm.end() } })() Results The results include LambdaOrmParentId , the internal key that λORM uses to link the details to their order (see Include ). Parameters The query needs id , an integer: [ { "name": "id", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "details", "type": "Orders.details", "children": [ { "name": "LambdaOrmParentId", "type": "[integer]" } ] } ] Model Each order of the result has name , customer and the array details : [ { "name": "name", "type": "dateTime" }, { "name": "customer", "type": "string" }, { "name": "details", "type": "Orders.details[]", "children": [ { "name": "orderId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "productId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "unitPrice", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "quantity", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "discount", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "LambdaOrmParentId", "type": "integer" } ] } ] Constraints { "entity": "Orders", "constraints": [], "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "constraints": [] } ] } Metadata One statement for the orders and, as its child, one for the details ( pos fields omitted): { "classtype": "Sentence", "name": "select", "type": "any", "entity": "Orders", "alias": "o", "clause": "select", "columns": [ { "name": "name", "type": "dateTime" }, { "name": "customer", "type": "string" }, { "name": "__id", "type": "integer" } ], "parameters": [{ "name": "id", "type": "integer" }], "constraints": [], "values": [], "defaults": [], "children": [ { "classtype": "Sentence", "name": "select", "type": "any", "entity": "Orders.details", "alias": "o1", "clause": "select", "columns": [ { "name": "orderId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "productId", "type": "integer" }, { "name": "unitPrice", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "quantity", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "discount", "type": "decimal" }, { "name": "LambdaOrmParentId", "type": "integer" } ], "parameters": [{ "name": "LambdaOrmParentId", "type": "any" }], "constraints": [], "values": [], "defaults": [], "children": [] } ] } Plan { "entity": "Orders", "dialect": "MySQL", "source": "MySQL", "sentence": "SELECT o.OrderDate AS name, c.CompanyName AS ", "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "dialect": "MySQL", "source": "MySQL", "sentence": "SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.Discount AS discount, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM `Order Details` o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?) docs.text: Query Language This page introduces the λORM query language: what a query looks like, the kinds of queries there are and where each one is documented. λORM queries are written as JavaScript lambda expressions over the entities of the domain. You can write them as TypeScript/JavaScript code, navigating the entities of the model, or send them as a string (for example from the CLI or to the Data Gateway ). λORM translates each query into the language of the database engine of each source (SQL for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite, or MongoDB queries). Query types DQL DQL (Data Query Language) queries retrieve data. They can be as simple as reading all the records of an entity, or they can filter, sort, group and paginate the records, compute values from them and load related entities. See: Select , Join , Grouping , Include DML DML (Data Manipulation Language) queries change data. They include the following operations: insert : adds new records to an entity (also bulkInsert and upsert ). update : modifies existing records. delete : removes records. See: Insert , Bulk Insert , Update , Delete DDL DDL (Data Definition Language) statements create, modify and drop database structures and related objects: CREATE : creates new objects in the database, such as tables and indexes. ALTER : modifies the structure of existing objects, for example adding, changing or removing the columns of a table. DROP : deletes objects from the database. You do not write DDL queries: λORM generates and runs them when you use the schema synchronization commands. See: Push , Pull , Fetch , Introspect , Incorporate Example The following query reads the countries of a region, with their states whose name starts with "F". It returns the name, subregion and position of each country, 3 countries per page: Countries .filter(p => p.region == region) .map(p => [p.name, p.subregion, p.latitude, p.longitude]) // properties of the country .include(p => p.states.filter(p => substr(p.name, 1, 1) == "F") // states starting with 'F' .map(p => [p.name, p.latitude, p.longitude]) ) .page(1, 3) // first page, 3 countries per page In this schema, Countries is in a MySQL source and States in a PostgreSQL source (see Stage with multiple sources ). λORM runs one statement per source: -- MySQL: the countries of the region, first page of 3 records SELECT c.name AS name, c.subregion AS subregion, c.latitude AS latitude, c.longitude AS longitude, c.iso3 AS `__iso3` FROM Countries c WHERE c.region = ? ORDER BY c.name asc LIMIT 0,3 -- PostgreSQL: the states starting with 'F' of the countries read above SELECT s.NAME AS "name", s.LATITUDE AS "latitude", s.LONGITUDE AS "longitude", s.COUNTRY_CODE AS "LambdaOrmParentId" FROM TBL_STATES s WHERE SUBSTR(s.NAME,1,1) = 'F' AND s.COUNTRY_CODE IN (?) The states are then attached to their country in memory, so each country of the result has a states array. Advantages Queries are written in the same programming language as the application. There is no new language to learn. Queries are easy to write and to read. The IDE's IntelliSense helps you write the expressions. Syntax errors are caught while you write.

docs.text: Select This page shows how to read records: all the properties of an entity or only some of them, the first or last record, distinct values and pagination. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL. Every query is based on the schema, from which λORM knows the properties of each entity, its primary key, indexes, relations and constraints. That is why, to read all the properties of an entity, you do not need to list them. All the properties of an entity Reads all the properties of all the products. Lambda: Products SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductID AS id, p.ProductName AS name, p.SupplierID AS supplierId, p.CategoryID AS categoryId, p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, p.UnitPrice AS price, p.UnitsInStock AS inStock, p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder, p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel, p.Discontinued AS discontinued FROM Products p One property Reads only the name of each product. Lambda: Products.map(p => p.name) SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductName AS name FROM Products p First Reads the first product, ordered by its primary key. Lambda: Products.first() SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductID AS id, p.ProductName AS name, p.SupplierID AS supplierId, p.CategoryID AS categoryId, p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, p.UnitPrice AS price, p.UnitsInStock AS inStock, p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder, p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel, p.Discontinued AS discontinued FROM Products p ORDER BY p.ProductID asc LIMIT 0,1 first can also receive the properties to return, as map does: Products.first(p => ({ name: p.name, price: p.price })) . In that case the records are ordered by the first property returned. Last Reads the last product, ordered by its primary key. Lambda: Products.last() SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductID AS id, p.ProductName AS name, p.SupplierID AS supplierId, p.CategoryID AS categoryId, p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, p.UnitPrice AS price, p.UnitsInStock AS inStock, p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder, p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel, p.Discontinued AS discontinued FROM Products p ORDER BY p.ProductID desc LIMIT 0,1 Distinct Reads the distinct combinations of quantity per unit and category name, sorted by category. The category name comes from the category relation, so λORM adds the join (see Join ). Lambda: Products .distinct(p => ({ quantity: p.quantity, category: p.category.name })) .sort(p => p.category) SQL Result: SELECT DISTINCT p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID ORDER BY category asc Pagination Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10, sorted by category, and returns the first page of 10 records. Lambda: Products .filter(p => p.price > 10) .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name })) .sort(p => p.category) .page(1, 10) SQL Result: SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category FROM Products p INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10 ORDER BY category asc LIMIT 0,10 page(page, records) receives the page number (starting at 1) and the number of records per page. How the page is expressed depends on the dialect: LIMIT on MySQL, OFFSET … FETCH NEXT … ROWS ONLY on Oracle, and so on. Usage The same query, with the minimum price as a parameter ( minPrice ), run in three ways. Node With the library @lambdaorm/lib : import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Products } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // products with a price greater than minPrice, with their category, first page of 10 const query = (minPrice: number) => Products .filter(p => p.price > minPrice) .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name })) .sort(p => p.category) .page(1, 10) const result = await orm.execute(query, { minPrice: 10 }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })() CLI With the CLI @lambdaorm/cli : lambdaorm execute -q "Products.filter(p=>p.price>minPrice).map(p=>({name:p.name,category:p.category.name})).sort(p=>p.category).page(1,10)" -d "{\"minPrice\":10}" Data Gateway Through the REST API of the Data Gateway : curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/execute?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "Products.filter(p=>p.price>minPrice).map(p=>({name:p.name,category:p.category.name})).sort(p=>p.category).page(1,10)", "data": {"minPrice": 10}}'

docs.text: Update This page shows how to update records: all the properties or only some of them, with a filter or for all the records, together with related entities, and how to save a whole aggregate (a parent with its composite children). The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL, unless stated otherwise. A query is based on both the expression and the schema. If you do not specify the properties to update, all the properties of the entity are updated. How each property is stored in each source (table and column names) is resolved by the mapping of that source in the schema. Result: affected rows update returns the number of affected rows (as delete does). 0 means that no row matched the filter, which is useful to answer "not found" or to detect a conflict with an optimistic lock: const query = 'Orders.update(p => ({ status: status, version: version + 1 })).filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version)' const first = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'sent', version: 1 }) // 1 const second = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'accepted', version: 1 }) // 0: the version changed When the update has includes, the result is the number of rows affected in the main entity. Update all the properties of a record Without a filter, update filters by the primary key, whose value is taken from the data passed. Lambda: Orders.update() SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET CustomerID = ?, EmployeeID = ?, OrderDate = ?, RequiredDate = ?, ShippedDate = ?, ShipVia = ?, Freight = ?, ShipName = ?, ShipAddress = ?, ShipCity = ?, ShipRegion = ?, ShipPostalCode = ?, ShipCountry = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? Update one property in all the records To update all the records of an entity, use updateAll instead of update . This prevents updating all the records by mistake. Lambda: Orders.updateAll({ postalCode: postalCode }) SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET ShipPostalCode = ? Update one property with a filter Updates the name of the order whose id is entity.id . Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }).filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? Update with a related entity Updates the name of an order and, for each detail sent, all the properties of the detail. Each detail is filtered by its primary key. Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }) .include(p => p.details.update(p => p)) .filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: -- the order UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- each detail sent UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ?,Quantity = ?,Discount = ? WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?) Update fields of the related entity Updates the name of an order and only the unit price of each detail sent. In the update of the relation, unitPrice is the value sent for each detail. Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }) .include(p => p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: unitPrice }))) .filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: -- the order UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- each detail sent UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ? WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?) Note Inside the update of a relation, p.unitPrice refers to the current value of the column, not to the value sent: p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: p.unitPrice })) generates SET UnitPrice = o1.UnitPrice , which leaves the column as it is. Update an entity and several related entities Updates a customer, its orders and the details of each order. Lambda: Customers.update().include(p => p.orders.include(p => p.details)) SQL Result: -- the customer UPDATE Customers c SET CustomerID = ?,CompanyName = ?,ContactName = ?,ContactTitle = ?,Address = ?,City = ?,Region = ?,PostalCode = ?,Country = ? WHERE c.CustomerID = ? -- each order of the customer UPDATE Orders o SET CustomerID = ?,EmployeeID = ?,OrderDate = ?,RequiredDate = ?,ShippedDate = ?,ShipVia = ?,Freight = ?,ShipName = ?,ShipAddress = ?,ShipCity = ?,ShipRegion = ?,ShipPostalCode = ?,ShipCountry = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- details is a composite relation included as it is: each detail sent is inserted or updated (upsert), -- and the details of the order that were not sent are deleted (see "Update an aggregate" below) INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE UnitPrice = VALUES(UnitPrice),Quantity = VALUES(Quantity),Discount = VALUES(Discount) Update an aggregate (composite relation) When the included relation is composite ( composite: true ) and is included as it is ( include(p => p.lines) ), the update saves the whole aggregate: children sent that already exist are updated, children sent that do not exist are inserted (with the parent's key), children of the parent that were not sent are deleted, if the relation is absent from the data, the children are untouched. The child entity needs a primary key. In this example, Orders has a composite relation lines : domain: entities: - name: Orders primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, length: 36, required: true } - { name: status, length: 20, required: true } relations: - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId } - name: OrderLines primaryKey: [orderId, line] properties: - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true } - { name: line, type: integer, required: true } - { name: product, length: 40, required: true } - { name: quantity, type: integer } Lambda: const [order] = await orm.execute('Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines)', { id: orderId }) const kept = { ...order.lines.find(p => p.line === 1), quantity: 7 } // updated const added = { orderId, line: 3, product: 'c', quantity: 3 } // inserted // line 2 is not sent: deleted await orm.execute('Orders.update().include(p => p.lines)', { ...order, status: 'sent', lines: [kept, added] }) SQL Result (PostgreSQL): UPDATE orders o SET status = $1 WHERE o.id = $2 -- one per child sent INSERT INTO order_lines(order_id,line,product,quantity) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4) ON CONFLICT (order_id,line) DO UPDATE SET product = EXCLUDED.product, quantity = EXCLUDED.quantity -- the children not sent DELETE FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = $1 AND NOT ((order_id = $2 AND line = $3) OR (order_id = $4 AND line = $5)) It is supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle (these two from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0), which save the children with upsert . On MongoDB the composite children are embedded in the parent's document, so they are replaced there. To only update the children sent (without inserting or deleting), include the relation with an explicit update: Orders.update().include(p => p.lines.update(l => ({ quantity: quantity }))) . Inside it, quantity is the value sent for each child (see Update fields of the related entity ). Code example Updates a customer with its orders and their details, and prints the number of customers updated. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Customers } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build` (async () => { try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // customer with its orders and their details const customer = { id: 'ALFKI', name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste', contact: 'Maria Anders', phone: 'Sales Representative', address: 'Obere Str. 57', city: 'Berlin', region: null, postalCode: '12209', country: 'Germany', orders: [ { id: 1, customerId: 'ALFKI', employeeId: 6, orderDate: '1997-08-24T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1997-09-21T22:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1997-09-01T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 1, freight: '29.4600', name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste', address: 'Obere Str. 57', city: 'Berlin', region: null, postalCode: '12209', country: 'Germany', details: [ { orderId: 1, productId: 28, unitPrice: '45.6000', quantity: '15.0000', discount: '0.0000' }, { orderId: 1, productId: 39, unitPrice: '18.0000', quantity: '21.0000', discount: '0.0000' }, { orderId: 1, productId: 46, unitPrice: '12.0000', quantity: '2.0000', discount: '0.0000' } ] }, { id: 2, customerId: 'ALFKI', employeeId: 4, orderDate: '1997-10-02T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1997-10-30T23:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1997-10-12T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 2, freight: '61.0200', name: 'Alfred-s Futterkiste', address: 'Obere Str. 57', city: 'Berlin', region: null, postalCode: '12209', country: 'Germany', details: [ { orderId: 2, productId: 63, unitPrice: '43.9000', quantity: '20.0000', discount: '0.0000' } ] } ] } const query = () => Customers.update().include(p => p.orders.include(p => p.details)) // returns the number of customers updated const result = await orm.execute(query, customer) console.log(result) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // releases the connections await orm.end() } })()
docs.title: Update

docs.text: This page shows how to update records: all the properties or only some of them, with a filter or for all the records, together with related entities, and how to save a whole aggregate (a parent with its composite children). The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL, unless stated otherwise. A query is based on both the expression and the schema. If you do not specify the properties to update, all the properties of the entity are updated. How each property is stored in each source (table and column names) is resolved by the mapping of that source in the schema.
docs.title: Update

docs.text: update returns the number of affected rows (as delete does). 0 means that no row matched the filter, which is useful to answer "not found" or to detect a conflict with an optimistic lock: const query = 'Orders.update(p => ({ status: status, version: version + 1 })).filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version)' const first = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'sent', version: 1 }) // 1 const second = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'accepted', version: 1 }) // 0: the version changed When the update has includes, the result is the number of rows affected in the main entity.
docs.title: Result: affected rows

docs.text: Without a filter, update filters by the primary key, whose value is taken from the data passed. Lambda: Orders.update() SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET CustomerID = ?, EmployeeID = ?, OrderDate = ?, RequiredDate = ?, ShippedDate = ?, ShipVia = ?, Freight = ?, ShipName = ?, ShipAddress = ?, ShipCity = ?, ShipRegion = ?, ShipPostalCode = ?, ShipCountry = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ?
docs.title: Update all the properties of a record

docs.text: To update all the records of an entity, use updateAll instead of update . This prevents updating all the records by mistake. Lambda: Orders.updateAll({ postalCode: postalCode }) SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET ShipPostalCode = ?
docs.title: Update one property in all the records

docs.text: Updates the name of the order whose id is entity.id . Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }).filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ?
docs.title: Update one property with a filter

docs.text: Updates the name of an order and, for each detail sent, all the properties of the detail. Each detail is filtered by its primary key. Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }) .include(p => p.details.update(p => p)) .filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: -- the order UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- each detail sent UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ?,Quantity = ?,Discount = ? WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?)
docs.title: Update with a related entity

docs.text: Updates the name of an order and only the unit price of each detail sent. In the update of the relation, unitPrice is the value sent for each detail. Lambda: Orders.update({ name: entity.name }) .include(p => p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: unitPrice }))) .filter(p => p.id === entity.id) SQL Result: -- the order UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- each detail sent UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ? WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?) Note Inside the update of a relation, p.unitPrice refers to the current value of the column, not to the value sent: p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: p.unitPrice })) generates SET UnitPrice = o1.UnitPrice , which leaves the column as it is.
docs.title: Update fields of the related entity

docs.text: Updates a customer, its orders and the details of each order. Lambda: Customers.update().include(p => p.orders.include(p => p.details)) SQL Result: -- the customer UPDATE Customers c SET CustomerID = ?,CompanyName = ?,ContactName = ?,ContactTitle = ?,Address = ?,City = ?,Region = ?,PostalCode = ?,Country = ? WHERE c.CustomerID = ? -- each order of the customer UPDATE Orders o SET CustomerID = ?,EmployeeID = ?,OrderDate = ?,RequiredDate = ?,ShippedDate = ?,ShipVia = ?,Freight = ?,ShipName = ?,ShipAddress = ?,ShipCity = ?,ShipRegion = ?,ShipPostalCode = ?,ShipCountry = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ? -- details is a composite relation included as it is: each detail sent is inserted or updated (upsert), -- and the details of the order that were not sent are deleted (see "Update an aggregate" below) INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE UnitPrice = VALUES(UnitPrice),Quantity = VALUES(Quantity),Discount = VALUES(Discount)
docs.title: Update an entity and several related entities

docs.text: When the included relation is composite ( composite: true ) and is included as it is ( include(p => p.lines) ), the update saves the whole aggregate: children sent that already exist are updated, children sent that do not exist are inserted (with the parent's key), children of the parent that were not sent are deleted, if the relation is absent from the data, the children are untouched. The child entity needs a primary key. In this example, Orders has a composite relation lines : domain: entities: - name: Orders primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, length: 36, required: true } - { name: status, length: 20, required: true } relations: - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId } - name: OrderLines primaryKey: [orderId, line] properties: - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true } - { name: line, type: integer, required: true } - { name: product, length: 40, required: true } - { name: quantity, type: integer } Lambda: const [order] = await orm.execute('Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines)', { id: orderId }) const kept = { ...order.lines.find(p => p.line === 1), quantity: 7 } // updated const added = { orderId, line: 3, product: 'c', quantity: 3 } // inserted // line 2 is not sent: deleted await orm.execute('Orders.update().include(p => p.lines)', { ...order, status: 'sent', lines: [kept, added] }) SQL Result (PostgreSQL): UPDATE orders o SET status = $1 WHERE o.id = $2 -- one per child sent INSERT INTO order_lines(order_id,line,product,quantity) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4) ON CONFLICT (order_id,line) DO UPDATE SET product = EXCLUDED.product, quantity = EXCLUDED.quantity -- the children not sent DELETE FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = $1 AND NOT ((order_id = $2 AND line = $3) OR (order_id = $4 AND line = $5)) It is supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle (these two from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0), which save the children with upsert . On MongoDB the composite children are embedded in the parent's document, so they are replaced there. To only update the children sent (without inserting or deleting), include the relation with an explicit update: Orders.update().include(p => p.lines.update(l => ({ quantity: quantity }))) . Inside it, quantity is the value sent for each child (see Update fields of the related entity ).

docs.text: Bitwise Operators Bitwise operators work on the binary representation of integer values. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Results on MySQL MySQL evaluates bitwise operations as unsigned 64-bit integers. The longitude of Brazil is -55, so several of the results below are very large numbers. Summary Operator Description ~ Bitwise NOT & Bitwise AND | Bitwise OR ^ Bitwise XOR (exclusive OR); it is not exponentiation, use ** for that << Left shift >> Right shift Bitwise NOT ( ~ ) Inverts all the bits of a . Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: ~a Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: ~ p.longitude }) Result: [{"result":54}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ~ c.longitude AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Bitwise AND ( & ) Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bits of a and b are both 1. Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: a & b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude & 1 }) Result: [{"result":1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.longitude & 1 AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Bitwise OR ( | ) Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bit of a or of b is 1. Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: a | b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude | 1 }) Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.longitude | 1 AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Bitwise XOR ( ^ ) Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bits of a and b are different. Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: a ^ b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude ^ 1 }) Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.longitude ^ 1 AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Left shift ( << ) Shifts the bits of a to the left by b positions. Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: a << b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude << 1 }) Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.longitude << 1 AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Right shift ( >> ) Shifts the bits of a to the right by b positions. Operands and result are numbers. Syntax: a >> b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude >> 1 }) Result: [{"result":9223372036854776000}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.longitude >> 1 AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ORDER BY result asc LIMIT 0,1 Database support Engine differences Oracle : & , | and ^ are translated to BITAND , BITOR and BITXOR . PostgreSQL : ^ is translated to the # operator (XOR). MongoDB : bitwise operators cannot currently be translated to MongoDB queries.

docs.text: Comparison Operators and Functions Comparison operators and functions compare two or more values and return a boolean. They are mostly used in the predicate of filter (the WHERE clause of the generated SQL), but they can be used in any expression of a query. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Operator / function Description == , === Equal to != , !== , <> Not equal to > Greater than < Less than >= Greater than or equal to <= Less than or equal to between Checks whether a value is within a range in Checks whether a value is in a list of values includes Checks whether a list contains a value Equal ( == , === ) Returns true when both operands are equal. == and === are equivalent: both are translated to = in SQL. Syntax: a == b a === b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 === "BRA").map(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Not equal ( != , !== , <> ) Returns true when the operands are different. The three forms are equivalent and are translated to <> in SQL. Syntax: a != b a !== b a <> b See the Logical page for an example that uses != . Greater than, less than ( > , < , >= , <= ) Compare two values of the same type (numbers, strings or dates). a > b : a is greater than b . a < b : a is less than b . a >= b : a is greater than or equal to b . a <= b : a is less than or equal to b . Name of the first country (ordered by name) whose latitude is between -11 and -9 (exclusive) and whose longitude is -55: Countries.filter(p=> p.latitude < -9 && p.latitude > -11 && p.longitude == -55 ).first(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE (c.latitude < -9 AND (c.latitude > -11 AND c.longitude = -55)) ORDER BY c.name asc LIMIT 0,1 between Returns true when value is within the range from to to . In SQL it is translated to value BETWEEN from AND to , which includes both limits. Signature: between(value: T, from: T, to: T): boolean Countries.filter(p=> between(p.latitude,-11,-9) && p.longitude == -55 ).first(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE (c.latitude BETWEEN -11 AND -9 AND c.longitude = -55) ORDER BY c.name asc LIMIT 0,1 in Returns true when value is equal to one of the values of list . It replaces several conditions joined with || , and is translated to value IN (...) in SQL. Signature: in(value: T, list: T[]): boolean Countries.filter(p=> in(p.iso3,["BRA","ARG"])).map(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Argentina"},{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG') includes Returns true when list contains value . It is the same check as in , with the arguments in the opposite order: the list comes first. contains is an alias of includes . Signature: includes(list: T[], value: T): boolean For example, includes(["BRA","ARG"], p.iso3) generates the same WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG') condition as the in example above on MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite. Database support Engine differences MongoDB : between is translated to {"$gte": from, "$lt": to} , so the upper limit is excluded , unlike SQL BETWEEN . includes cannot currently be translated to a MongoDB query; use in instead. SQL Server : includes is translated to a LIKE (text search) instead of IN ; use in to check a value against a list.

docs.text: Returns true when value is equal to one of the values of list . It replaces several conditions joined with || , and is translated to value IN (...) in SQL. Signature: in(value: T, list: T[]): boolean Countries.filter(p=> in(p.iso3,["BRA","ARG"])).map(p=> p.name) Result: [{"name":"Argentina"},{"name":"Brazil"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.name AS name FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG')
docs.title: in

docs.text: Returns true when list contains value . It is the same check as in , with the arguments in the opposite order: the list comes first. contains is an alias of includes . Signature: includes(list: T[], value: T): boolean For example, includes(["BRA","ARG"], p.iso3) generates the same WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG') condition as the in example above on MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite.
docs.title: includes

docs.text: Engine differences MongoDB : between is translated to {"$gte": from, "$lt": to} , so the upper limit is excluded , unlike SQL BETWEEN . includes cannot currently be translated to a MongoDB query; use in instead. SQL Server : includes is translated to a LIKE (text search) instead of IN ; use in to check a value against a list.

docs.text: Date and Time Functions Date and time functions get the current date and time, convert strings to dates, extract parts of a date, add intervals to a date and calculate the difference between two dates. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Results depend on the engine and the time zone Date and time values are calculated by the database. The results below were obtained on MySQL in a session that was not in UTC, so some values (for example those of date , time or hour ) are shifted by the time zone. Expect different values on other engines or time zones. Summary Function Description now Current date and time today Current date curTime Current time dateTime Converts a string to a date and time date Converts a string to a date time Converts a string to a time dateToString Converts a date to an ISO 8601 string year Year of a date month Month of a date day Day of the month of a date weekday Day of the week of a date hour Hour of a date minute Minute of a date second Second of a date millisecond Millisecond of a date addYear Adds years to a date addMonth Adds months to a date addDay Adds days to a date addHour Adds hours to a date addMinute Adds minutes to a date addSecond Adds seconds to a date addMillisecond Adds milliseconds to a date addTime Adds a time to a date subtractTime Subtracts a time from a date dayDiff Difference between two dates in days hourDiff Difference between two dates in hours secondDiff Difference between two dates in seconds millisecondDiff Difference between two dates in milliseconds dayToDate Date for a number of days since 1970-01-01 hourToDate Date for a number of hours since 1970-01-01 secondToDate Date for a number of seconds since 1970-01-01 millisecondToDate Date for a number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01 Current date and time now Returns the current date and time. Signature: now(): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:now()}) Result: [{"result":"2022-08-15T09:54:22.000Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT NOW() AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' today Returns the current date. Signature: today(): date Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:today()}) Result: [{"result":"2022-08-14T22:00:00.000Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CURDATE() AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' curTime Returns the current time. Signature: curTime(): time Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:curTime()}) Result: [{"result":"11:54:22"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CURTIME() AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Conversions dateTime Converts value to a date and time. Signature: dateTime(value: string): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dateTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06T12:39:11.000Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATETIME) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' date Converts value to a date (without the time). Signature: date(value: string): date Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:date("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-05T22:00:00.000Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATE) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' time Converts value to a time (without the date). Signature: time(value: string): time Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:time("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":"00:20:21"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', TIME) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' dateToString Converts date to a string in ISO 8601 format. Signature: dateToString(date: dateTime): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dateToString(dateTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z"))}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06T14:39:11Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATETIME), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Date parts These functions return a part of a date as an integer. year Returns the year of value . Signature: year(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:year("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":2021}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' month Returns the month of value (1 to 12). Signature: month(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:month("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":9}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' day Returns the day of the month of value . Signature: day(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:day("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":6}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DAYOFMONTH('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' weekday Returns the day of the week of value . The numbering depends on the engine: on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite ( DAYOFWEEK ) 1 is Sunday and 7 is Saturday, so the example (a Monday) returns 2; on PostgreSQL ( extract(dow ...) ) 0 is Sunday. Signature: weekday(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:weekday("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":2}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DAYOFWEEK('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' hour Returns the hour of value . Signature: hour(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hour("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":0}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' minute Returns the minute of value . Signature: minute(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:minute("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":20}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' second Returns the second of value . Signature: second(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:second("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":21}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXTRACT(SECOND FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' millisecond Returns the millisecond of value . Signature: millisecond(value: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")}) Result: [{"result":0}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ROUND(EXTRACT(MICROSECOND FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z')/1000,0) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Adding intervals These functions add value units to date and return the new date. Use a negative value to subtract. addYear Adds value years to date . Signature: addYear(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addYear("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2023-09-06 14:39:11.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 YEAR) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addMonth Adds value months to date . Signature: addMonth(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMonth("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-11-06 14:39:11.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 MONTH) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addDay Adds value days to date . Signature: addDay(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addDay("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-08 14:39:11.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 DAY) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addHour Adds value hours to date . Signature: addHour(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addHour("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 16:39:11.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' HOUR AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addMinute Adds value minutes to date . Signature: addMinute(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMinute("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:41:11.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' MINUTE AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addSecond Adds value seconds to date . Signature: addSecond(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addSecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:39:13.444000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' SECOND AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addMillisecond Adds value milliseconds to date . Signature: addMillisecond(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMillisecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)}) Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:39:11.446000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL (2 * 1000) MICROSECOND) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' addTime Adds time to date . Signature: addTime(date: dateTime, time: time): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z","08:22:12")}) Result: [{"result":"08:42:33"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ADDTIME('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z','08:22:12') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' subtractTime Subtracts time from date . Signature: subtractTime(date: dateTime, time: time): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:subtractTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z","08:22:12")}) Result: [{"result":"-08:01:51"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SUBTIME('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z','08:22:12') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Differences between dates These functions return date1 - date2 in the given unit, as an integer. dayDiff Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in days. Signature: dayDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dayDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")}) Result: [{"result":4}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATEDIFF('2021-09-06T14:39:11','2021-09-02T12:30:10') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' hourDiff Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in hours. Signature: hourDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hourDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")}) Result: [{"result":98}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' secondDiff Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in seconds. Signature: secondDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:secondDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")}) Result: [{"result":353341}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' millisecondDiff Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in milliseconds. Signature: millisecondDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecondDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")}) Result: [{"result":353341000}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ROUND(TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11')/1000,0) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Numbers to dates These functions convert a number of time units elapsed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (the Unix epoch) to a date. dayToDate Returns the date that is value days after the Unix epoch. Signature: dayToDate(value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dayToDate(2000)}) Result: [{"result":"1975-06-24T00:00:00Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000*24*3600), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' hourToDate Returns the date that is value hours after the Unix epoch. Signature: hourToDate(value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hourToDate(2000)}) Result: [{"result":"1970-03-25T08:00:00Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000*3600), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' secondToDate Returns the date that is value seconds after the Unix epoch. Signature: secondToDate(value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:secondToDate(2000)}) Result: [{"result":"1970-01-01T00:33:20Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' millisecondToDate Returns the date that is value milliseconds after the Unix epoch. Signature: millisecondToDate(value: number): dateTime Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecondToDate(2000)}) Result: [{"result":"1970-01-01T00:00:02Z"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000/1000), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Database support MongoDB In the current version, only now , today , date , year , month , day and weekday can be translated to MongoDB queries. The other date and time functions on this page are not available on MongoDB.

docs.text: Aggregate Functions Aggregate (group) functions calculate a single value from a set of rows. When a query's map mixes aggregate functions with other fields, λORM groups the rows by those other fields ( GROUP BY in SQL). See Grouping for more examples, including having . About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Function Description avg Average of the values count Number of rows first First value of the set last Last value of the set max Maximum value min Minimum value sum Sum of the values count Returns the number of rows in the set. count(1) counts all the rows. Signature: count(value: any): integer Number of countries in the Americas region: Countries.filter(p=> p.region == "Americas").map(p=> {result:count(1)}) Result: [{"result":57}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT COUNT(1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.region = 'Americas' Number of countries in each region: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,countries:count(1)}) Result: [{"region":"","countries":2} ,{"region":"Africa","countries":60} ,{"region":"Americas","countries":57} ,{"region":"Asia","countries":50} ,{"region":"Europe","countries":53} ,{"region":"Oceania","countries":27} ,{"region":"Polar","countries":1} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, COUNT(1) AS countries FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region max Returns the maximum value of the set. Signature: max(value: T): T Maximum latitude of the countries of each region: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,max:max(p.latitude)}) Result: [{"region":"","max":-53.1} ,{"region":"Africa","max":34} ,{"region":"Americas","max":72} ,{"region":"Asia","max":48} ,{"region":"Europe","max":78} ,{"region":"Oceania","max":15.2} ,{"region":"Polar","max":-74.65} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, MAX(c.latitude) AS max FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region min Returns the minimum value of the set. Signature: min(value: T): T Minimum latitude of the countries of each region: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,min:min(p.latitude)}) Result: [{"region":"","min":-54.4333} ,{"region":"Africa","min":-49.25} ,{"region":"Americas","min":-54.5} ,{"region":"Asia","min":-8.8333} ,{"region":"Europe","min":35} ,{"region":"Oceania","min":-41} ,{"region":"Polar","min":-74.65} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, MIN(c.latitude) AS min FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region avg Returns the average of the values of the set. Signature: avg(value: number): number Average latitude of the countries of each region: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,avg:avg(p.latitude)}) Result: [{"region":"","avg":-53.76665} ,{"region":"Africa","avg":1.283335} ,{"region":"Americas","avg":10.42610526} ,{"region":"Asia","avg":25.822002} ,{"region":"Europe","avg":49.35021321} ,{"region":"Oceania","avg":-10.93023704} ,{"region":"Polar","avg":-74.65} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, AVG(c.latitude) AS avg FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region sum Returns the sum of the values of the set. It is translated to SUM(...) in SQL. Signature: sum(value: number): number first Returns the first value of the set. Signature: first(value: T): T last Returns the last value of the set. Signature: last(value: T): T first and last on SQL databases On SQL databases, first and last used as aggregates are translated to FIRST(...) and LAST(...) ; check that your database engine supports these aggregate functions. On MongoDB they are translated to $first and $last . Do not confuse them with the first and last query methods (for example Countries.first(p=> p.name) ), which return the first or last row of a query; see Select .

docs.text: Logical Operators Logical operators combine or negate boolean expressions, for example to join several conditions in the predicate of filter . About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Operator Description SQL ! Logical NOT NOT && Logical AND AND || Logical OR OR NOT ( ! ) Negates a boolean expression: returns true when value is false , and false when it is true . Syntax: !value For example, Countries.filter(p=> !(p.iso3 == "BRA")) generates the condition WHERE NOT c.iso3 = 'BRA' . AND ( && ) Returns true when both operands are true . Syntax: a && b Number of countries in South America whose longitude is less than -30: Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America" && p.longitude < -30 ).map(p=> {result:count(1)}) Result: [{"result":15}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT COUNT(1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE (c.subregion = 'South America' AND c.longitude < -30) OR ( || ) Returns true when at least one of the operands is true . Syntax: a || b Number of countries in South America or Central America: Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America" || p.subregion == "Central America" ).map(p=> {result:count(1)}) Result: [{"result":23}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT COUNT(1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE (c.subregion = 'South America' OR c.subregion = 'Central America') Combining conditions Operators can be combined with the comparison operators described in Comparison . Number of countries in the Americas region that are not in Northern America: Countries.filter(p=> p.region == "Americas" && p.subregion != "Northern America" ).map(p=> {result:count(1)}) Result: [{"result":51}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT COUNT(1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE (c.region = 'Americas' AND c.subregion <> 'Northern America')

docs.text: Nullable Functions Nullable functions check whether a value is null, or replace null values with another value. About the examples The examples run against the Countries and States entities of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated. In the test schema, Countries is stored in MySQL and States in PostgreSQL (mapped to the TBL_STATES table), so the SQL of each example is shown in the dialect of its data source. To see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Function Description nvl Returns a default value when the value is null nvl2 Returns one value when the value is not null and another when it is null isNull Checks whether a value is null isNotNull Checks whether a value is not null nvl Returns value when it is not null; otherwise returns default . Signature: nvl(value: T, default: T): T Number of states whose latitude is null (null is replaced with -100, so the condition matches it): States.filter(p=> nvl(p.latitude,-100)== -100).map(p=> count(1)) Result: [{"count":68}] Generated SQL (PostgreSQL): SELECT COUNT(1) FROM TBL_STATES s WHERE (CASE WHEN s.LATITUDE IS NOT NULL THEN s.LATITUDE ELSE -100 END) = -100 Native name of the country with ISO 3 code "CIV", or "???" when it is null: Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "CIV" ).map(p=> {native: nvl(p.native,"???")}) Result: [{"native":"???"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT IFNULL(c.native,'???') AS native FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'CIV' nvl2 Returns a when value is not null, and b when it is null. Signature: nvl2(value: any, a: T, b: T): T Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "CIV" ).map(p=> {native: nvl2(p.native,"is not null","is null")}) Result: [{"native":"is null"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (CASE WHEN c.native IS NOT NULL THEN 'is not null' ELSE 'is null' END) AS native FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'CIV' isNull Returns true when value is null. Signature: isNull(value: any): boolean Number of states whose latitude is null: States.filter(p=> isNull(p.latitude)).map(p=> count(1)) Result: [{"count":68}] Generated SQL (PostgreSQL): SELECT COUNT(1) FROM TBL_STATES s WHERE (s.LATITUDE IS NULL) isNotNull Returns true when value is not null. Signature: isNotNull(value: any): boolean Number of states whose latitude is not null: States.filter(p=> isNotNull(p.latitude)).map(p=> count(1)) Result: [{"count":4813}] Generated SQL (PostgreSQL): SELECT COUNT(1) FROM TBL_STATES s WHERE (s.LATITUDE IS NOT NULL) Database support MongoDB In the current version, nvl , nvl2 , isNull and isNotNull cannot be translated to MongoDB queries.

docs.text: Numeric Operators and Functions Numeric operators and functions perform arithmetic, rounding, trigonometric and logarithmic calculations. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Operators Operator Description - Negation ( -a ) or subtraction ( a - b ) + Addition * Multiplication / Division ** Exponentiation: a raised to the power of b // Root: the b -th root of a % Modulus: remainder of a / b Functions Function Description abs Absolute value acos Arc cosine asin Arc sine atan Arc tangent atan2 Arc tangent of y / x ceil Smallest integer greater than or equal to a number cos Cosine cosh Hyperbolic cosine exp e raised to a power floor Largest integer less than or equal to a number ln Natural logarithm log Logarithm in a given base log10 Base 10 logarithm remainder Remainder of a division round Rounds to a number of decimals sign Sign of a number sin Sine sinh Hyperbolic sine tan Tangent tanh Hyperbolic tangent trunc Truncates to a number of decimals toNumber Converts a value to a number Arithmetic operators The arithmetic operators take numbers and return a number. Precedence follows the usual arithmetic rules ( ** before * and / , which go before + and - ); use parentheses to change it. In SQL, ** is translated to POWER(a,b) , // to POWER(a,(1/b)) and % to MOD(a,b) . Syntax: -a , a - b a + b a * b a / b a ** b a // b a % b Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 3+2-1 }) Result: [{"result":4}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((3 + 2) - 1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 3*4-1}) Result: [{"result":11}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((3 * 4) - 1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1-2-5}) Result: [{"result":-6}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((1 - 2) - 5) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: (2+3)*2}) Result: [{"result":10}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((2 + 3) * 2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 2*(3+2)}) Result: [{"result":10}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (2 * (3 + 2)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1+2*3*4}) Result: [{"result":25}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (1 + ((2 * 3) * 4)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: (1+(2**3)*4)}) Result: [{"result":33}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (1 + (POWER(2,3) * 4)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1+2**(3*4)}) Result: [{"result":4097}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (1 + POWER(2,(3 * 4))) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' abs Returns the absolute value of value . Signature: abs(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: abs(-9)}) Result: [{"result":9}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ABS(-9) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' acos Returns the arc cosine of value , in radians. Signature: acos(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: acos(0.434)}) Result: [{"result":1.121868332427735}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ACOS(0.434) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' asin Returns the arc sine of value , in radians. Signature: asin(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: asin(0.434)}) Result: [{"result":0.44892799436716174}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ASIN(0.434) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' atan Returns the arc tangent of value , in radians. Signature: atan(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: atan(2)}) Result: [{"result":1.1071487177940904}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ATAN(2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' atan2 Returns the arc tangent of y / x , in radians, using the signs of both arguments to choose the quadrant. Signature: atan2(y: number, x: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: atan2(90, 15)}) Result: [{"result":1.4056476493802699}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ATAN(90,15) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ceil Returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to value . Signature: ceil(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ceil(2)}) Result: [{"result":2}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CEIL(2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' cos Returns the cosine of value (in radians). Signature: cos(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: cos(2)}) Result: [{"result":-0.4161468365471424}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT COS(2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' cosh Returns the hyperbolic cosine of value . Signature: cosh(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: cosh(2)}) Result: [{"result":3.7621956910836314}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((EXP(2) + EXP(-2)) / 2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' exp Returns e raised to the power of value . Signature: exp(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: exp(7)}) Result: [{"result":1096.6331584284585}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT EXP(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' floor Returns the largest integer less than or equal to value . Signature: floor(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: floor(7)}) Result: [{"result":7}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT FLOOR(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ln Returns the natural logarithm (base e ) of value . Signature: ln(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ln(7)}) Result: [{"result":1.9459101490553132}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' log Returns the logarithm of value in base base . For example, log(7,10) is the base 7 logarithm of 10. Signature: log(base: number, value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log(7,10)}) Result: [{"result":1.1832946624549385}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LOG(7,10) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' log10 Returns the base 10 logarithm of value . Signature: log10(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log10(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.8450980400142568}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LOG10(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' remainder Returns the remainder of dividing n1 by n2 . On MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite it is calculated as n1 - n2 * ROUND(n1 / n2) , so the result can be negative (see the example); on PostgreSQL it is translated to MOD(n1,n2) , which returns 1 for the same example. Signature: remainder(n1: number, n2: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: remainder(7,2)}) Result: [{"result":-1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (7 - 2*ROUND(7/2)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' round Rounds value to decimals decimal places. Signature: round(value: number, decimals: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: round(7.984938,2)}) Result: [{"result":7.98}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ROUND(7.984938,2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' sign Returns the sign of value : -1 if it is negative, 0 if it is zero and 1 if it is positive. Signature: sign(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sign(-7)}) Result: [{"result":-1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SIGN(-7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' sin Returns the sine of value (in radians). Signature: sin(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sin(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.6569865987187891}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SIN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' sinh Returns the hyperbolic sine of value . Signature: sinh(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sinh(7)}) Result: [{"result":548.3161232732465}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((EXP(7) - EXP(-7)) / 2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' tan Returns the tangent of value (in radians). Signature: tan(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tan(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.8714479827243188}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TAN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' tanh Returns the hyperbolic tangent of value . Signature: tanh(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tanh(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.9999983369439447}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (EXP(2*7) - 1)/(EXP(2*7) + 1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' trunc Truncates value to decimals decimal places, without rounding. Signature: trunc(value: number, decimals: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: trunc(7.984938,2)}) Result: [{"result":7.98}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TRUNCATE(7.984938,2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' toNumber Converts value to a number. On MySQL it is translated to CONVERT(value, DECIMAL) , which has no decimal places, so the example returns 3; on PostgreSQL it is translated to CAST(value AS INTEGER) . Signature: toNumber(value: any): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: toNumber("3.141516")}) Result: [{"result":3}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT('3.141516', DECIMAL) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Database support Some functions have no direct equivalent in every engine, so λORM translates them to an equivalent expression. For example, on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite cosh , sinh and tanh are calculated with EXP , and trunc is translated to TRUNCATE ; on SQL Server trunc is translated to ROUND(value,decimals,1) , ceil to CEILING and atan2 to ATN2 . MongoDB remainder and toNumber cannot currently be translated to MongoDB queries. trunc is translated to $trunc without the number of decimals, so the value is truncated to an integer.

docs.text: Returns the natural logarithm (base e ) of value . Signature: ln(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ln(7)}) Result: [{"result":1.9459101490553132}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: ln

docs.text: Returns the logarithm of value in base base . For example, log(7,10) is the base 7 logarithm of 10. Signature: log(base: number, value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log(7,10)}) Result: [{"result":1.1832946624549385}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LOG(7,10) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: log

docs.text: Returns the base 10 logarithm of value . Signature: log10(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log10(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.8450980400142568}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LOG10(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: log10

docs.text: Returns the remainder of dividing n1 by n2 . On MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite it is calculated as n1 - n2 * ROUND(n1 / n2) , so the result can be negative (see the example); on PostgreSQL it is translated to MOD(n1,n2) , which returns 1 for the same example. Signature: remainder(n1: number, n2: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: remainder(7,2)}) Result: [{"result":-1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (7 - 2*ROUND(7/2)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: remainder

docs.text: Rounds value to decimals decimal places. Signature: round(value: number, decimals: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: round(7.984938,2)}) Result: [{"result":7.98}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ROUND(7.984938,2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: round

docs.text: Returns the sign of value : -1 if it is negative, 0 if it is zero and 1 if it is positive. Signature: sign(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sign(-7)}) Result: [{"result":-1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SIGN(-7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: sign

docs.text: Returns the sine of value (in radians). Signature: sin(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sin(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.6569865987187891}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SIN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: sin

docs.text: Returns the hyperbolic sine of value . Signature: sinh(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sinh(7)}) Result: [{"result":548.3161232732465}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT ((EXP(7) - EXP(-7)) / 2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: sinh

docs.text: Returns the tangent of value (in radians). Signature: tan(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tan(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.8714479827243188}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TAN(7) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: tan

docs.text: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of value . Signature: tanh(value: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tanh(7)}) Result: [{"result":0.9999983369439447}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (EXP(2*7) - 1)/(EXP(2*7) + 1) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: tanh

docs.text: Truncates value to decimals decimal places, without rounding. Signature: trunc(value: number, decimals: number): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: trunc(7.984938,2)}) Result: [{"result":7.98}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT TRUNCATE(7.984938,2) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: trunc

docs.text: Converts value to a number. On MySQL it is translated to CONVERT(value, DECIMAL) , which has no decimal places, so the example returns 3; on PostgreSQL it is translated to CAST(value AS INTEGER) . Signature: toNumber(value: any): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: toNumber("3.141516")}) Result: [{"result":3}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT('3.141516', DECIMAL) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
docs.title: toNumber

docs.text: Some functions have no direct equivalent in every engine, so λORM translates them to an equivalent expression. For example, on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite cosh , sinh and tanh are calculated with EXP , and trunc is translated to TRUNCATE ; on SQL Server trunc is translated to ROUND(value,decimals,1) , ceil to CEILING and atan2 to ATN2 . MongoDB remainder and toNumber cannot currently be translated to MongoDB queries. trunc is translated to $trunc without the number of decimals, so the value is truncated to an integer.

See Query Language for an introduction to queries. Each page describes the operators and functions of one category, with their signature, an example query, its result and the SQL generated for it.
