docs.text: Sort Functions The sort method orders the rows of a query ( ORDER BY in SQL). Its predicate returns the field to sort by, optionally wrapped in asc or desc to set the direction. Without asc or desc , rows are sorted in ascending order. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Function Description asc Sorts in ascending order (the default) desc Sorts in descending order Default order When the predicate returns a field without asc or desc , rows are sorted in ascending order. Number of countries in each region, from the smallest to the largest: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,countries:count(1)}).sort(p=> p.countries) Result: [{"region":"Polar","countries":1} ,{"region":"","countries":2} ,{"region":"Oceania","countries":27} ,{"region":"Asia","countries":50} ,{"region":"Europe","countries":53} ,{"region":"Americas","countries":57} ,{"region":"Africa","countries":60} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, COUNT(1) AS countries FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region ORDER BY countries asc asc Sorts the rows by value in ascending order. Signature: asc(value: any): void Maximum latitude of each region, sorted by that maximum: Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,max:max(p.latitude)}).sort(p=> asc(p.max)) Result: [{"region":"Polar","max":-74.65} ,{"region":"","max":-53.1} ,{"region":"Oceania","max":15.2} ,{"region":"Africa","max":34} ,{"region":"Asia","max":48} ,{"region":"Americas","max":72} ,{"region":"Europe","max":78} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.region AS region, MAX(c.latitude) AS max FROM Countries c GROUP BY c.region ORDER BY max asc desc Sorts the rows by value in descending order. Signature: desc(value: any): void ISO 3 codes of the countries of South America in descending order: Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America").map(p=> p.iso3).sort(p=> desc(p.iso3)) Result: [{"iso3":"VEN"} ,{"iso3":"URY"} ,{"iso3":"SUR"} ,{"iso3":"SGS"} ,{"iso3":"PRY"} ,{"iso3":"PER"} ,{"iso3":"GUY"} ,{"iso3":"GUF"} ,{"iso3":"FLK"} ,{"iso3":"ECU"} ,{"iso3":"COL"} ,{"iso3":"CHL"} ,{"iso3":"BRA"} ,{"iso3":"BOL"} ,{"iso3":"ARG"} ] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT c.iso3 AS iso3 FROM Countries c WHERE c.subregion = 'South America' ORDER BY c.iso3 desc Reference fields through the lambda parameter Write desc(p.iso3) , not desc(iso3) . A name that is not reached through the lambda parameter ( p ) is read as a query parameter: sort(p=> desc(iso3)) generates ORDER BY ? desc , and the rows are not sorted by the field.

docs.text: String Functions String functions transform text values: change the case, pad, trim, replace or extract part of a string, and convert values to strings. About the examples The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan . Summary Function Description chr Character for an ASCII code concat Concatenates strings lower Converts to lowercase upper Converts to uppercase lpad Pads the left side of a string rpad Pads the right side of a string ltrim Removes leading spaces rtrim Removes trailing spaces trim Removes leading and trailing spaces replace Replaces every occurrence of a value mask Hides the middle of a string substr , substring Extracts part of a string strCount Counts the occurrences of a value toString Converts a value to a string chr Returns the character whose ASCII code is ascii . Signature: chr(ascii: number): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: chr(68)}) Result: [{"result":"D"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CHAR(68 USING ASCII) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' concat Concatenates all its arguments into one string. Signature: concat(...values: any): string Region and subregion of Brazil, separated by a space: Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: concat(p.region," ",p.subregion) }) Result: [{"result":"Americas South America"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONCAT(CONCAT(c.region,' '),c.subregion) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' lower Converts value to lowercase. Signature: lower(value: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: lower(p.subregion) }) Result: [{"result":"south america"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LOWER(c.subregion) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' upper Converts value to uppercase. Signature: upper(value: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: upper(p.subregion) }) Result: [{"result":"SOUTH AMERICA"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT UPPER(c.subregion) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' lpad Pads the left side of value with pad until it is len characters long. Signature: lpad(value: string, len: number, pad: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: lpad(p.region,12,"_") }) Result: [{"result":"____Americas"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LPAD(c.region,12,'_') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' rpad Pads the right side of value with pad until it is len characters long. Signature: rpad(value: string, len: number, pad: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: rpad(p.region,12,"_") }) Result: [{"result":"Americas____"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT RPAD(c.region,12,'_') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' ltrim Removes the leading spaces of value . Signature: ltrim(value: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ltrim(" a ")}) Result: [{"result":"a "}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT LTRIM(' a ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' rtrim Removes the trailing spaces of value . Signature: rtrim(value: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: rtrim(" a ")}) Result: [{"result":" a"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT RTRIM(' a ') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' trim Removes the leading and trailing spaces of value . It is translated to TRIM(value) in SQL. Signature: trim(value: string): string replace Returns value with every occurrence of source replaced by target . Signature: replace(value: string, source: string, target: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: replace(p.region,"a","*")}) Result: [{"result":"Americ*s"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT REPLACE(c.region,'a','*') AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' mask Masks a sensitive value: keeps its first three and last three characters and replaces the rest with *** . Signature: mask(value: string): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: mask(p.subregion)}) Result: [{"result":"Sou***ica"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT Concat(LEFT(c.subregion,3),'***',RIGHT(c.subregion,3)) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' substr, substring Returns the part of value that starts at position from (the first character is position 1 in SQL) and is count characters long. substr and substring are equivalent. Signature: substr(value: string, from: number, count: number): string substring(value: string, from: number, count: number): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: substr(p.subregion,1,3)}) Result: [{"result":"Sou"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SUBSTR(c.subregion,1,3) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: substring(p.subregion,1,3)}) Result: [{"result":"Sou"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT SUBSTR(c.subregion,1,3) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' strCount Returns the number of times value appears in source . The search is case-sensitive. Signature: strCount(source: string, value: string): number Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: strCount(p.subregion,"a")}) Result: [{"result":1}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT (LENGTH(c.subregion)-LENGTH(REPLACE(c.subregion,'a',''))) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' toString Converts value to a string. Signature: toString(value: any): string Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: toString(p.latitude)}) Result: [{"result":"-10.0000"}] Generated SQL (MySQL): SELECT CONVERT(c.latitude, CHAR) AS result FROM Countries c WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA' Database support MongoDB In the current version, chr , lpad , rpad , ltrim , rtrim , trim , replace , mask , substr , substring and strCount cannot be translated to MongoDB queries. concat , lower , upper and toString are supported.

docs.text: Engines This page lists the differences between the database engines supported by λORM. λORM runs the same queries and stage commands on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB and SQLite (dialect SQLjs ). The same model gives the same results on every engine, except for the differences below. These differences are checked by the engines lab , which runs the same tests on PostgreSQL 17, MySQL 8.4, MariaDB 11.4, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 23 Free and MongoDB 7. Summary PostgreSQL MySQL / MariaDB SQL Server Oracle MongoDB string without length TEXT VARCHAR(80) VARCHAR(80) VARCHAR2(80) — json JSONB JSON NVARCHAR(MAX) CLOB native '' (empty string) '' '' '' NULL '' upsert() yes yes yes ( MERGE ) yes ( MERGE ) not yet (clear error) update().include() of a composite relation yes yes yes yes yes (children are embedded) composite children own table own table own table own table embedded in the parent's document push / fetch of columns yes yes yes yes schemaless: only whether the collection exists column rename ( previousMapping ) RENAME COLUMN RENAME COLUMN sp_rename RENAME COLUMN — Types String without length : unbounded ( TEXT ) only on PostgreSQL; on the other engines it is VARCHAR(80) . Set length for longer values, or dbType in the property mapping. json : objects and lists are written and read as such on every engine; the column type changes (see the table). dateTime : PostgreSQL writes it with milliseconds and offset, so a timestamptz(3) column ( dbType ) keeps the exact instant. On the other engines the precision depends on the column type ( DATETIME keeps at least the seconds). Empty string : '' , 0 and false are values, never NULL. Oracle is the exception: it has no empty string and stores '' as NULL, so a value written as '' comes back as null and a filter p.email == "" finds nothing. See Property types . Writes update and delete return the number of affected rows on every engine. upsert() uses ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE on PostgreSQL, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL and MariaDB, and MERGE on SQL Server and Oracle (from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0). On MongoDB it fails with a "not supported yet" error. update().include() of a composite relation inserts, updates and deletes the children with upsert, so it has the same support. On MongoDB the composite children are embedded in the parent's document, so the update replaces them there. Stage commands push and fetch compare tables and columns on every SQL engine. MongoDB is schemaless: fetch only says whether each collection exists, and its fields are whatever its documents have. See Push and Fetch . Transactions On every SQL engine a transaction uses one connection per source and commits or rolls back source by source (there is no two-phase commit). MongoDB transactions need a replica set.

docs.text: Schema Use This page shows how to write a simple schema in YAML or JSON, how to generate the model and repositories from it with the CLI, and how to load it in an application. Simple configuration example The same schema, with one entity mapped to the table TBL_COUNTRIES of a MySQL database, written in YAML and in JSON. Configuration in YAML: domain: entities: - name: Countries primaryKey: ["iso3"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: name required: true - name: iso3 length: 3 required: true infrastructure: mappings: - name: mapping1 entities: - name: Countries mapping: TBL_COUNTRIES properties: - name: iso3 mapping: ISO3 - name: name mapping: NAME sources: - name: source1 dialect: MySQL mapping: mapping1 connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} Configuration in JSON: { "domain": { "entities": [ { "name": "Countries", "primaryKey": ["iso3"], "uniqueKey": ["name"], "properties": [ { "name": "iso3", "required": true, "type": "string", "length": 3 }, { "name": "name", "required": true, "type": "string" } ] } ] }, "infrastructure": { "mappings": [ { "name": "mapping1", "entities": [ { "name": "Countries", "mapping": "TBL_COUNTRIES", "properties": [ { "name": "iso3", "mapping": "ISO3" }, { "name": "name", "mapping": "NAME" } ] } ] } ], "sources": [ { "name": "source1", "mapping": "mapping1", "dialect": "MySQL", "connection": "${CNN_MYSQL}" } ] } } Build source code When the schema is created or changed, the model and the repositories are generated with the build command of the CLI ( @lambdaorm/cli ): lambdaorm build -l node -m generates only the model and -r only the repositories; by default both are generated. The files are written in the domain folder inside the src folder (see Paths ). See also Build . The model file, model.ts , has a class, a query interface and a queryable for each entity: export class Country { iso3?: string name?: string } export interface QryCountry { iso3: string name: string } export let Countries: Queryable<QryCountry> A repository file is generated for each entity, for example repositoryCountry.ts . It is created only once, so you can add your own code to it: import { Repository, IOrm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Country, QryCountry } from './model' export class CountryRepository extends Repository<Country, QryCountry> { constructor (stage?: string, orm?:IOrm) { super('Countries', stage, orm) } // Add your code here } Set schema orm.init() initializes the ORM with the schema. The schema can be given in three ways: Without arguments: the schema file is looked for in the current folder. A .yaml , .yml or .json file whose name contains lambdaorm (for example lambdaORM.yaml ) is used; if there is none, one whose name contains orm , schema or lambda . With the path of the schema file, including its extension ( .yaml , .yml or .json ), which tells how to read it. A folder can also be given. With the schema as an object. In this example the path of the schema file is given, and a query is executed: import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { await orm.init('/home/my/app1/lambdaORM.yaml') try { const countries = await orm.execute(`Countries.map(p=>{name:p.name,code:p.iso3}) .sort(p=> desc(p.name)) .page(1,10)`) console.log(countries) } catch (error) { console.log(error) } finally { await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Schema This section explains the schema of λORM: what it contains, how it is defined and used, and how it is synchronized with the databases. The schema holds all the configuration the ORM needs. It separates the business model ( domain ) from the persistence of the data ( infrastructure ): In the domain, the entities and enums that represent the business model are completely clean, without any attribute that couples them to persistence. All queries are written against the business model, so they are decoupled from the physical model of the data. In the infrastructure, everything needed to store and read the data in the different sources (databases) is defined. The schema can be written in a YAML or JSON file (usually lambdaORM.yaml ), or passed as an object when the ORM is initialized. All the expressions used to define conditions and actions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr . Example This example shows a stage that uses two sources: source 1 is MySQL and holds the Countries table, and source 2 is PostgreSQL and holds the States table. For the Countries entity, the names of the table and its columns are the same as the names of the entity and its properties, so no mapping needs to be written. For the States entity, the names of the table and its columns are different, so the mapping defines them. In this section Definition : every key of the schema. Expressions , Environment variables and Composite entities . Schema Use : how to load the schema and generate the model. Examples: Basic , Extend , Multiple stages , Stage with multiple sources , Composite and Listener . Synchronization : push, pull, fetch, introspect and incorporate. Engines : differences between database engines. The Data Gateway publishes a schema over the network; its own settings are in a separate configuration file .

docs.text: Composite Entity This page explains composite entities: entities whose records are part of the records of another entity, as the lines of an order are part of the order. When a relation is composite , its records are treated as part of a document: In non-relational databases (MongoDB), the records of the relation are stored inside the document of the parent, in the same collection. In relational databases, the records are stored in their own table, but queries, import and export treat them as an object that contains the records of the relation. Define a composite entity An entity is composite when its name starts with the name of its parent followed by a period, for example Devices.Components . When the composite entity defines a relation to its parent with target , the inverse relation created in the parent ( components in the example) is composite. ... domain: entities: ... - name: Devices primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: id length: 32 required: true default: 'concat(type,"-",switch(type){case"phone":imei;default:mac;})' - name: type length: 16 required: true enum: DeviceType - name: name length: 32 required: true ... - name: Devices.Components extends: Products primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["deviceId", "name"] properties: - name: id length: 50 required: true default: concat(deviceId,"-",lower(substring(replace(name," ","-"),0,16))) - name: deviceId length: 32 required: true - name: name length: 16 required: true ... relations: - name: device from: deviceId entity: Devices to: id target: components ... A relation can also be declared composite with composite: true (see Relation ). See a complete example, with the same entity stored in MongoDB and in PostgreSQL, in Composite example .

docs.text: Environment Variables on Schema This page shows how to use environment variables in the schema, to keep connections and secrets out of the schema file. Any value of the schema can be taken from an environment variable, with the notation $VARIABLE or ${VARIABLE} . The variables are replaced when the schema is loaded. With the CLI, the -e option reads them from a file (for example -e .env ). Examples Connection to the database The connection of each source is read from an environment variable: infrastructure: sources: - name: source1 dialect: MySQL mapping: mapping1 connection: $CNN_MYSQL - name: source2 dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: mapping2 connection: $CNN_POSTGRES The variable holds the connection as JSON: CNN_MYSQL={"host":"localhost","port":3306,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"} CNN_POSTGRES={"host":"localhost","port":5433,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"} Key of the encryption functions The key used by encrypt and decrypt is read from an environment variable, inside an expression: domain: entities: ... - name: Users extends: Basics primaryKey: ["username"] uniqueKey: ["email"] properties: - name: username length: 32 required: true - name: firstname required: true - name: lastname required: true - name: email required: true length: 255 writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") ...

docs.text: Expressions on Schema This page lists the functions that λORM adds to the expressions used in the schema (defaults, read and write values, constraints, conditions, tasks and listeners). All these expressions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr . Besides the operators and functions of 3xpr, λORM adds the following functions. General functions Function Description toBase64(value:string):string Encodes a string to base64. getBase64(value:string):string Decodes a base64 string. encrypt(value:string,key:string):string Encrypts a string with a key. decrypt(value:string,key:string):string Decrypts a string with a key. Example In this example encrypt stores the email encrypted in the database, and decrypt returns it decrypted in the results. domain: entities: ... - name: Users extends: Basics primaryKey: ["username"] uniqueKey: ["email"] properties: - name: username length: 32 required: true - name: firstname required: true - name: lastname required: true - name: email required: true length: 255 writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") ... Orm functions These functions call the methods of the Orm class, so an expression can run or inspect another query. Function Description orm.execute(query:string,data:any,options:any):any Executes a query and returns the result. orm.plan(query:string,options:any):any Returns the execution plan of a query. orm.metadata(query:string):any Returns the metadata of a query. orm.model(query:string):any Returns the model of a query. orm.parameters(query:string):any Returns the parameters of a query. orm.constraints(query:string):any Returns the constraints of a query. Example In this example a listener uses orm.execute to run, on the insights stage, the same query that was just executed on the default or cqrs stage. This is a way to implement the CQRS pattern. See Listener . application: listeners: - name: syncInsights on: [insert, update, delete] condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs") after: orm.execute(query,data,{stage:"insights"}) See the CLI - northwind CQRS lab .

docs.text: Definition This page is the reference of the schema file ( lambdaORM.yaml ): its structure and every key of its domain , application and infrastructure sections, with an example for each. The schema holds all the configuration the ORM needs. It separates the business model ( domain ) from the persistence of the data ( infrastructure ): In the domain, the entities and enums that represent the business model are completely clean, without any attribute that couples them to persistence. All queries are written against the business model, so they are decoupled from the physical model of the data. In the infrastructure, everything needed to store and read the data in the different sources is defined. The schema can be written in a YAML or JSON file, or passed as an object when the ORM is initialized (see Schema Use ). All the expressions used to define conditions and actions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr (see Expressions on Schema ), and any value can come from an environment variable (see Environment Variables ). Structure domain: enums: - name: string extends: string abstract: boolean values: - name: string value: any entities: - name: string abstract: boolean extends: string singular: string view: boolean primaryKey: string[] uniqueKey: string[] required: string[] properties: - name: string type: string | integer | decimal | boolean | dateTime | date | time | json length: number required: boolean autoIncrement: boolean view: boolean enum: string key: string default: expression readExp: expression readValue: expression writeValue: expression indexes: - name: string fields: string[] relations: - name: string type: oneToMany | manyToOne | oneToOne from: string entity: string to: string composite: boolean weak: boolean target: string constraints: - message: string condition: expression application: start: - name: string condition: expression expression: expression end: - name: string condition: expression expression: expression listeners: - name: string on: [select | insert | upsert | update | delete] condition: expression before: expression after: expression error: expression transactional: boolean infrastructure: mappings: - name: string extends: string entities: - name: string mapping: string abstract: boolean extends: string sequence: string filter: expression properties: - name: string mapping: string readMappingExp: expression dbType: string previousMapping: string sources: - name: string dialect: MySQL | MariaDB | PostgreSQL | Oracle | SqlServer | MongoDB | SQLjs mapping: string connection: object | environment variable stages: - name: string sources: - name: string condition: expression views: - name: string entities: - name: string exclude: boolean properties: - name: string exclude: boolean readExp: expression paths: src: string state: string domain: string queue: config: object consumers: - name: string config: object subscribe: object execute: expression Main sections Key Description domain The business model: enums and entities. application Tasks run when the ORM starts and ends, and listeners. infrastructure How and where the data is stored: mappings, sources, stages, views. Domain Key Description enums The enums of the model. entities The entities of the model. An enum can be used as the type of a property. An entity is defined with its properties, relations, keys, indexes and constraints. Enum An enum defines a set of values that can then be used as the type of a property. Key Description Required name Name of the enum. yes values Values of the enum ( name and value ). yes extends Name of another enum whose values this enum inherits. abstract The enum is only used as a base for other enums. When a value has no value , its name is used. Enum example In this example the DeviceType enum is defined and used as the type of the type property of the Devices entity. domain: enums: - name: DeviceType values: - name: phone value: phone - name: computer value: computer - name: robot value: robot entities: ... - name: Devices extends: Products primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: id length: 32 required: true default: 'concat(type,"-",switch(type){case"phone":imei;default:mac;})' - name: type length: 16 required: true enum: DeviceType - name: name length: 32 required: true ... Entity An entity is defined with its properties, relations and constraints. Key Description Required name Name of the entity. A name with a period ( Orders.details ) defines a composite entity . yes properties Properties of the entity. yes abstract The entity is only used as a base for other entities (no table is created for it). extends Name of the entity whose properties, primary key and relations this entity inherits. singular Singular name, used for the classes generated by lambdaorm build (by default it is deduced from the name). view The entity is a view: push creates no table for it (see below). primaryKey Properties of the primary key. uniqueKey Properties of the unique key. required Properties that are required (the same as required: true on each of them). indexes Indexes ( name and fields ). relations Relations with other entities. constraints Constraints validated when a record is written. The properties of the primary key and the unique key are required unless they say otherwise. Abstract and extends in Entity In this example the abstract entity Positions is defined, and the entity Countries extends it: Countries gets the properties latitude and longitude . domain: entities: - name: Positions abstract: true properties: - name: latitude length: 16 - name: longitude length: 16 - name: Countries extends: Positions primaryKey: ["iso3"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: name required: true - name: iso3 length: 3 required: true An entity does not need to be abstract to be extended. See Extend . Set Entity as view This example defines the Users entity as a view, because its table is managed by an external system. Push creates no table for a view entity, and the stage commands do not change it. domain: entities: ... - name: Users view: true extends: Basics primaryKey: ["username"] uniqueKey: ["email"] properties: - name: username length: 32 required: true - name: firstname required: true - name: lastname ... Property Key Description Required Default name Name of the property. yes type Type of the property (see Property types ). string length Length of a string property. see below required The property cannot be null. false autoIncrement The value is generated by the database. false enum Name of the enum the value must belong to. view The property is not stored: its value comes from readExp . false default Expression evaluated by λORM to set the value when a record is inserted. readExp Read expression, resolved in the source (database). readValue Expression evaluated by λORM on the value read from the source. writeValue Expression evaluated by λORM on the value before it is written. key Fixed value used to filter reads and updates, and set on insert. Property types Type Value in Node Column created by push (by default) string string VARCHAR(length) ; without length : TEXT on PostgreSQL, VARCHAR(80) on other engines integer number INTEGER (Oracle NUMBER(10) ) decimal number DECIMAL(10,4) (Oracle NUMBER(19,4) ) boolean boolean BOOLEAN (SqlServer BIT , Oracle CHAR(1) ) dateTime Date TIMESTAMP (PostgreSQL), DATETIME (MySQL, MariaDB, SqlServer), DATE (Oracle) date Date DATE (SqlServer SMALLDATETIME ) time Date TIME (Oracle DATE ) json object or list JSONB (PostgreSQL), JSON (MySQL, MariaDB), NVARCHAR(MAX) (SqlServer), CLOB (Oracle), TEXT (others) json : objects and lists are written and read as such (there is no need to call JSON.stringify or JSON.parse ). dateTime : on PostgreSQL the value is written with milliseconds and its offset, so a timestamptz column (see dbType in Property Mapping ) keeps the exact instant. string without length : on PostgreSQL it is unbounded ( TEXT ); on the other engines it is VARCHAR(80) , so set length when a value can be longer. '' , 0 and false are values, never NULL (Oracle is the exception: it stores '' as NULL). See also Engines for the differences between engines. In this example name has no length, settings is a JSON object and createdAt a date and time: domain: entities: - name: Products primaryKey: ["id"] properties: - name: id length: 36 required: true - name: name # TEXT on PostgreSQL, VARCHAR(80) elsewhere required: true - name: settings type: json # { "color": "red", "tags": ["a", "b"] } in and out as an object - name: createdAt type: dateTime Set Property as view and readExp A view property is not stored in the database (push creates no column for it): its value is computed when reading, with the expression in readExp . In this example fullName is built from lastname and firstname . domain: entities: ... - name: Users extends: Basics primaryKey: ["username"] uniqueKey: ["email"] properties: - name: username length: 32 required: true - name: firstname required: true - name: lastname required: true - name: fullName view: true readExp: concat(lastname,", ",firstname) ... readExp can also be set on a stored property: the expression is applied when reading, and nothing changes when writing. Default value in Property When a record is inserted without a value for the property, the expression in default is evaluated by λORM (not by the database) and its result is written. In this example the id of a group is built from its name. domain: entities: - name: Groups extends: Basics primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: id length: 32 default: lower(substring(replace(name," ","-"),0,32)) required: true - name: name length: 32 required: true Read and write value in Property readValue and writeValue are evaluated by λORM: writeValue transforms the value before it is written, and readValue transforms the value read from the database. In this example the email is stored encrypted and returned decrypted; the key comes from an environment variable. domain: entities: ... - name: Users extends: Basics primaryKey: ["username"] uniqueKey: ["email"] properties: - name: username length: 32 required: true - name: email required: true length: 255 writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") ... Key value in Property The value set in key is used as a filter in read, update and delete queries, and it is assigned to the property when a record is inserted. This is useful to define several entities on the same table or collection. In this example a Locations table stores countries, states and cities, and each one is worked with as a separate entity: domain: entities: - name: Locations abstract: true primaryKey: ["type","code"] uniqueKey: ["type","name"] properties: - name: code required: true length: 16 - name: type required: true length: 16 - name: name required: true - name: Countries extends: Locations properties: - name: type key: 'country' - name: States extends: Locations properties: - name: type key: 'state' - name: Cities extends: Locations properties: - name: type key: 'city' infrastructure: mappings: - name: default entities: - name: Locations abstract: true mapping: TBL_LOCATIONS properties: - name: code mapping: CODE - name: type mapping: TYPE - name: name mapping: NAME - name: Countries extends: Locations - name: States extends: Locations - name: Cities extends: Locations Relation Key Description Required Default name Name of the relation. yes from Property of this entity. yes entity Related entity. yes to Property of the related entity. yes type Type of the relation (see below). oneToMany composite The related records are part of this entity (see Composite Entity ). false weak Push creates no foreign key for the relation (for example between entities in different sources). false target Name of the inverse relation created in the related entity. The type of the relation determines what it returns: Type Meaning Returns oneToMany Many records of this entity reference one record of entity . one object manyToOne Many records of entity reference this record. a list oneToOne One record of this entity relates to one record of entity . one object manyToOne relations are always weak. Target relation With target , the inverse relation is created in the related entity. For example, if the entity DeviceStatuses has a relation with Devices with target: statuses , a relation called statuses is created in Devices . The type of the target relation depends on the type of the source relation: Source Target oneToMany manyToOne oneToOne oneToOne domain: entities: - name: DeviceStatuses extends: Basics primaryKey: ["id"] indexes: - name: time fields: ["time"] properties: - name: id type: integer required: true autoIncrement: true - name: deviceId length: 32 required: true - name: time type: dateTime relations: - name: device from: deviceId entity: Devices to: id target: statuses Constraint Key Description Required message Message returned when it fails. yes condition Boolean expression to evaluate. yes Constraints are expressions evaluated by λORM when a record is inserted or updated. The ORM also creates constraints from other definitions, for example: A required property gets a constraint that checks that it is not null. A property whose type is an enum gets a constraint that checks that the value belongs to the enum. You can add your own constraints with a message and a condition : when the condition is not met, the write fails with the message. In this example the format of the email and the order of two dates are validated: domain: entities: - name: Users properties: ... - name: email required: true length: 255 writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}") constraints: - message: invalid email condition: test(email,"^\w+([\.-]?\w+)*@\w+([\.-]?\w+)*(\.\w{2,3})+$") - name: Files properties: - name: id length: 255 required: true - name: type length: 16 required: true enum: FileType - name: deviceId length: 32 required: true - name: startDate type: dateTime required: true - name: endDate type: dateTime required: true constraints: - message: endDate cannot be less than startDate condition: startDate<=endDate Application Key Description start Tasks run when the ORM is initialized ( orm.init() ). end Tasks run when the ORM is closed ( orm.end() ). listeners Expressions run before or after a query, or when it fails. Task Each task of start and end has: Key Description Required name Name of the task. yes expression Expression to run. yes condition The task only runs when this expression is true. Listener Key Description Required Default name Name of the listener. yes on Categories of query that trigger it: select , insert , upsert , update , delete . yes condition The listener only runs when this expression is true. before Expression run before the query. after Expression run after the query. error Expression run when the query fails. transactional false runs the listener outside the query's transaction. true See Listener for how listeners run and the arguments they receive. Infrastructure Key Description mappings How the entities are mapped to the tables or collections of the databases. sources The databases and their connections. stages Scenarios that decide which source each entity is read from and written to. views Views that restrict or modify the results of the queries. paths Folders where generated files and the ORM state are written. queue Kafka queue, used by the Data Gateway . When some of them are omitted, λORM completes them: Without mappings , an empty mapping is created (named after the source when there is only one source). A source without mapping uses the first mapping. Without stages , a stage called default with the first source is created. Without views , a view called default with no restrictions is created. Mapping A mapping defines how the entities are stored in the tables or collections of a database. Entities and properties that are not listed are mapped to a table or column with the same name. Key Description Required name Name of the mapping. yes entities Entity mappings. extends Name of a mapping whose entity mappings this one inherits. Entity Mapping Key Description Required Default name Name of the entity. yes mapping Name of the table or collection in the database. the entity name abstract The entity mapping is only used as a base for others. extends Name of the entity mapping this one inherits from. sequence Name of the sequence used to generate the values. filter Expression that filters the records of the table. properties Property mappings. Abstract and extends in Entity Mapping Abstract entity mappings are useful as a base for other entity mappings. This example defines the abstract entity mapping Locations , and the concrete entities extend it, so the three of them are stored in the table TBL_LOCATIONS . ... infrastructure: mappings: - name: default entities: - name: Locations abstract: true mapping: TBL_LOCATIONS properties: - name: code mapping: CODE - name: type mapping: TYPE - name: name mapping: NAME - name: Countries extends: Locations - name: States extends: Locations - name: Cities extends: Locations ... Filter in Entity Mapping The filter of an entity mapping is applied to every query of the entity. This example reads the users of the user_entity table that belong to a given realmId . ... infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: keycloak entities: - name: Users mapping: user_entity filter: realmId == "${REALM_ID}" properties: - name: username mapping: username - name: firstname mapping: first_name - name: lastname mapping: last_name - name: email mapping: email - name: created mapping: created_timestamp readMappingExp: millisecondToDate(created/1000) - name: realmId length: 255 mapping: realm_id ... Property Mapping Key Description Required Default name Name of the property. yes mapping Name of the column in the database. the property name readMappingExp Read expression, resolved in the source. dbType Column type used by push (DDL), instead of the one deduced from the property type. previousMapping Previous name of the column: push renames the column instead of adding a new one. Column type in Property Mapping dbType sets the column type used by every DDL that creates or alters the column ( push , push -o ). Use it to choose a type that the property type alone does not give, for example an instant with milliseconds or a binary JSON on PostgreSQL: infrastructure: mappings: - name: catalog entities: - name: Products mapping: products properties: - name: settings mapping: settings dbType: jsonb - name: createdAt mapping: created_at dbType: timestamptz(3) Rename a column with previousMapping To rename a column without losing its data, set the new name in mapping and the current one in previousMapping . Push then generates ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN icon TO icon_name (SqlServer sp_rename ) instead of adding a new column. infrastructure: mappings: - name: catalog entities: - name: Categories mapping: categories properties: - name: icon mapping: icon_name previousMapping: icon Remove previousMapping once the rename has been applied in every database. Renaming a table is not supported. Read expression in Property Mapping The expression in readMappingExp is resolved in the source, and its result is returned in read queries. In this example the column created_timestamp , stored in milliseconds, is returned as a date: infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: keycloak entities: - name: Users mapping: user_entity filter: realmId == "${REALM_ID}" properties: ... - name: created mapping: created_timestamp readMappingExp: millisecondToDate(created/1000) - name: realmId length: 255 mapping: realm_id ... Source A source is a database and its connection. Key Description Required Default name Name of the source. yes dialect Dialect: MySQL , MariaDB , PostgreSQL , Oracle , SqlServer , MongoDB or SQLjs . yes mapping Name of the mapping used by the source. the first mapping connection Connection: an object or an environment variable that holds it. yes Set connection in Source The connection can be defined with an environment variable or directly in the schema. Writing it in the schema is not recommended, because of security and because the connection usually changes from one environment to another; use it only for a temporary local test. Using an environment variable: ... infrastructure: sources: - name: test dialect: MySQL mapping: test connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} ... In the schema: ... infrastructure: sources: - name: test dialect: MySQL mapping: test connection: host: localhost port: 3306 user: test password: test database: test ... Stage A stage is a scenario: its rules decide which source each entity uses. A query runs on the stage given in its options; without one, it runs on the first stage. Key Description Required name Name of the stage. yes sources Source rules. yes Source Rule Key Description Required Default name Name of the source. yes condition Boolean expression that selects the source. true Condition on Source Rule condition decides on which source a query or a DDL sentence runs. The variables available in the expression are: Variable Description Value entity Entity of the sentence name of the entity action Action of the sentence select , insert , bulkInsert , update , upsert , delete , createEntity , … category Category of the sentence select , insert , upsert , update , delete , create , alter , drop , … type Type of the sentence dql , dml , ddl read The sentence reads boolean write The sentence writes boolean dml The sentence is a query (DQL or DML) boolean ddl The sentence is DDL boolean The rules are evaluated in the order they are defined, and the first source whose condition is true is used. In the following example, the entity Users uses the source keycloak , and all the other entities use the source main . ... infrastructure: stages: - name: default sources: - name: main condition: entity != "Users" - name: keycloak condition: entity == "Users" Catch-all source A source rule without condition is a catch-all: since the first matching source wins, it only receives the entities that no previous source took. This applies to queries (DML) as well as to push and the other stage commands (DDL), so the catch-all source does not get the tables of the entities assigned to other sources. Put it last. infrastructure: stages: - name: default sources: - name: keycloak condition: entity == "Users" - name: main View A view restricts or modifies the results of the queries. A query uses the view given in the view option; entities not listed in a view have no restrictions. Key Description Required name Name of the view. yes entities Entity views. In the following example, the default view masks apiKey and hides email , the collector view cannot access users and groups, and the admin view can access everything. infrastructure: views: - name: default entities: - name: Devices properties: - name: apiKey readExp: '"***"' - name: Users properties: - name: created readExp: date(created) - name: email exclude: true - name: collector entities: - name: Users exclude: true - name: Groups exclude: true - name: GroupUsers exclude: true - name: admin entities: [] Entity View Key Description Required name Name of the entity. yes exclude The entity cannot be accessed with this view. properties Property views. Exclude in Entity View An entity with exclude cannot be accessed when this view is used. infrastructure: views: ... - name: collector entities: - name: Users exclude: true - name: Groups exclude: true - name: GroupUsers exclude: true ... Property View Key Description Required name Name of the property. yes exclude The property cannot be accessed with this view. readExp Read expression, resolved in the source. Exclude in Property View A property with exclude cannot be accessed when this view is used. infrastructure: views: - name: default entities: ... - name: Users properties: - name: created readExp: date(created) - name: email exclude: true ... Read expression in Property View With readExp , the result of the expression is returned in read queries instead of the stored value. In this example created is returned as a date, without the time: infrastructure: views: - name: default entities: ... - name: Users properties: - name: created readExp: date(created) ... Paths Folders, relative to the folder of the schema, where generated files and the ORM state are written. Key Description Default src Source code folder. src domain Folder, inside src , where lambdaorm build writes the model and repositories. domain state Folder of the ORM state (model of each stage, DDL scripts applied by push). orm_state infrastructure: paths: src: src domain: domain state: orm_state Queue infrastructure.queue configures a Kafka queue. It is not used by @lambdaorm/lib itself: it is read by the Data Gateway for queued executions, and it adds the function queue.send(topic, messages) to the expressions. Key Description config Kafka client configuration ( kafkajs ). consumers Consumers: each one has a name , a consumer config , a subscribe (topic) and an execute expression run for every message, with the variables message , topic and partition . In this example every message of the topic insights-sync is executed on the insights stage: infrastructure: queue: config: $QUEUE_CONFIG consumers: - name: syncInsights config: groupId: group1 subscribe: topic: insights-sync fromBeginning: true execute: orm.execute(message.query, message.data, {stage:"insights"})

docs.text: This page is the reference of the schema file ( lambdaORM.yaml ): its structure and every key of its domain , application and infrastructure sections, with an example for each. The schema holds all the configuration the ORM needs. It separates the business model ( domain ) from the persistence of the data ( infrastructure ): In the domain, the entities and enums that represent the business model are completely clean, without any attribute that couples them to persistence. All queries are written against the business model, so they are decoupled from the physical model of the data. In the infrastructure, everything needed to store and read the data in the different sources is defined. The schema can be written in a YAML or JSON file, or passed as an object when the ORM is initialized (see Schema Use ). All the expressions used to define conditions and actions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr (see Expressions on Schema ), and any value can come from an environment variable (see Environment Variables ).

docs.text: Basic Schema Example This page shows a basic schema: two related entities stored in one MySQL database. A basic schema defines the entities, the mapping and the sources: The entities define the properties, relations and keys. The mapping defines how the entities are mapped to the tables of the database. The sources define the dialect and the connection of each database. Many keys can be omitted, because they have a default value. For example: A property without type is a string. A property without required is not required (unless it is part of the primary or unique key). A string property without length is TEXT on PostgreSQL and VARCHAR(80) on the other engines. Without mapping information, the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties. Schema Example In this schema, Countries has many States : the relation states of Countries returns the list of its states, and the relation country of States returns its country. The mapping test is empty, so the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties. domain: entities: - name: Countries primaryKey: ["iso3"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: name required: true - name: iso3 length: 3 required: true relations: - name: states type: manyToOne composite: true from: iso3 entity: States to: countryCode - name: States primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"] properties: - name: id type: integer required: true - name: name required: true - name: countryCode required: true length: 3 relations: - name: country from: countryCode entity: Countries to: iso3 infrastructure: mappings: - name: test sources: - name: test dialect: MySQL mapping: test connection: host: localhost port: 3306 user: test password: test database: test stages: - name: default sources: - name: test Labs CLI - simple

docs.text: Composite Example This page shows a composite entity, Orders.details , stored in MongoDB on one stage and in PostgreSQL on another, and how the same query returns the same result on both. A period in the name of an entity defines a composite entity : Orders.details is a composite entity of Orders . If the source is NoSQL, the details are stored inside the order, in a single collection; if the source is relational, they are stored in separate tables. In the domain they are treated the same way whatever the type of source, so the model does not depend on the persistence technology. Composite entity In this example Orders.details is a composite entity of Orders . Its relation order , with target: details , creates the composite relation details in Orders . Part of the schema where the composite entity is defined: domain: entities: ... - name: Orders primaryKey: [id] indexes: - name: orderDate fields: [orderDate] properties: - name: id type: integer required: true autoIncrement: true - name: customerId required: true length: 5 - name: orderDate type: dateTime - name: Orders.details primaryKey: [orderId, productId] properties: - name: orderId required: true type: integer - name: productId required: true type: integer - name: unitPrice type: decimal - name: quantity type: decimal relations: - name: order from: orderId entity: Orders to: id target: details ... docs.text: This page shows a composite entity, Orders.details , stored in MongoDB on one stage and in PostgreSQL on another, and how the same query returns the same result on both. A period in the name of an entity defines a composite entity : Orders.details is a composite entity of Orders . If the source is NoSQL, the details are stored inside the order, in a single collection; if the source is relational, they are stored in separate tables. In the domain they are treated the same way whatever the type of source, so the model does not depend on the persistence technology.

docs.text: Listener on Schema This page explains listeners: expressions that λORM runs before or after a query, or when it fails. They are defined in application.listeners (see Listener ). on : the categories of query that trigger the listener: select , insert , upsert , update and delete . A bulk insert belongs to the insert category, and a merge to the upsert category. condition : an expression that decides whether the listener runs. before , after and error : the expressions to run before the query, after it, or when it fails. transactional : whether the listener runs inside the query's transaction (default true ). How listeners run before , after and error run one after the other and are awaited : orm.execute returns when they have finished. An error in before prevents the sentence; an error in after fails it (the error listeners run first). They run in the sentence's transaction : the orm.execute calls of a listener use the same connections, and a rollback undoes what they wrote. A sentence with listeners that runs on its own opens a transaction for the sentence and its listeners, so both are all or nothing. A listener's orm.execute can name another stage ( { stage: "insights" } ): it joins the same transaction (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0). transactional: false runs a listener outside the transaction: what it writes is kept even if the transaction rolls back (for example, an audit log). In this example, touchInstallation updates the installation of each inserted file in the same transaction, and audit writes an audit log that is kept even if the transaction rolls back: application: listeners: - name: touchInstallation on: [insert] condition: entity == "InstallationFiles" after: >- orm.execute("Installations.update(p => ({ lastEventAt: at })).filter(p => p.id == id)", { id: data.installationId, at: data.uploadedAt }) - name: audit on: [insert, update, delete] transactional: false after: orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entity: entity, action: action }) Arguments The arguments available in condition , before , after and error : Parameter Description query The query expression that was executed data The data that was sent when the expression was executed options The options that were sent when the expression was executed result It is only available in the after event and contains the result of the expression execution action The action that was executed (select, insert, bulkInsert, update, upsert, merge, bulkMerge, delete, bulkDelete) type The type of sentence that was executed (dql, dml) category The category of the sentence that was executed (select, insert, update, delete, upsert) sentence The sentence that was executed dialect The dialect of the source where the sentence was executed source The source where the sentence was executed entity The entity that was affected by the sentence error It is only available in the error event and contains the error that occurred Listener Example This example declares a listener that copies the data to the insights stage (CQRS pattern). When records are inserted, updated or deleted on the default or cqrs stage, the listener runs. Its after expression executes the same query, with the same data, on the insights stage, in the same transaction as the original query: if the write in insights fails, the original one is rolled back too. docs.text: Multiple Stages This page shows a schema with two stages: the same model stored in two different databases. A stage is a usage scenario. Several stages can be defined for different reasons, for example: To run the same business model on Oracle and on SQL Server and compare their performance. To use one stage as the origin and another as the destination of a data migration. To use one stage for reads and another for writes. To use one stage for the development environment and another for the QA environment. docs.text: Stage with Multiple Sources This page shows a stage whose entities are stored in different databases, first with the same mapping and then with a different mapping for each source. When the entities are in different databases, the stage says which source each entity uses. This is done with the condition of each source rule: an expression evaluated for each entity; when it is true, that source is used. The conditions are evaluated in the order of the stage, so when an entity meets the conditions of two sources, the first one is used. A source without condition takes the entities that no previous source took. Multiple sources sharing the mapping In this schema, States is stored in a PostgreSQL database ( dataSource2 ) and every other entity in a MySQL database ( dataSource1 ). Both sources use the same mapping (the default one, since none is defined), so the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties. domain: entities: - name: Countries primaryKey: ["iso3"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: name required: true - name: iso3 length: 3 required: true relations: - name: states type: manyToOne composite: true from: iso3 entity: States to: countryCode - name: States primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"] properties: - name: id type: integer required: true - name: name required: true - name: countryCode required: true length: 3 relations: - name: country from: countryCode entity: Countries to: iso3 infrastructure: sources: - name: dataSource1 dialect: MySQL connection: host: localhost port: 3306 user: test password: test database: test - name: dataSource2 dialect: PostgreSQL connection: host: localhost port: 5432 user: test password: test database: test stages: - name: stage1 sources: - name: dataSource2 condition: entity == "States" - name: dataSource1 Multiple sources with different mappings In this schema, dataSource1 is a MySQL database that holds the Countries table, and dataSource2 is a PostgreSQL database that holds the States table. For Countries , the names of the table and its columns are the same as the names of the entity and its properties, so its mapping ( mapping1 ) is empty. For States , the names of the table and its columns are different, so mapping2 defines them. domain: entities: - name: Positions abstract: true properties: - name: latitude length: 16 - name: longitude length: 16 - name: Countries extends: Positions primaryKey: ["iso3"] uniqueKey: ["name"] properties: - name: name required: true - name: iso3 length: 3 required: true - name: region - name: subregion relations: - name: states type: manyToOne composite: true from: iso3 entity: States to: countryCode - name: States extends: Positions primaryKey: ["id"] uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"] properties: - name: id type: integer required: true - name: name required: true - name: countryCode required: true length: 3 relations: - name: country from: countryCode entity: Countries to: iso3 infrastructure: mappings: - name: mapping1 - name: mapping2 entities: - name: States mapping: TBL_STATES properties: - name: id mapping: ID - name: name mapping: NAME - name: countryCode mapping: COUNTRY_CODE - name: latitude mapping: LATITUDE - name: longitude mapping: LONGITUDE sources: - name: dataSource1 dialect: MySQL mapping: mapping1 connection: $CNN_MYSQL - name: dataSource2 dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: mapping2 connection: $CNN_POSTGRES stages: - name: stage1 sources: - name: dataSource2 condition: entity == "States" - name: dataSource1 Environment variables: CNN_MYSQL={"host":"localhost","port":3306,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"} CNN_POSTGRES={"host":"localhost","port":5433,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"} Labs CLI - two datasource same query

docs.text: Fetch This page explains fetch, which shows the differences between the sources (databases) of a stage and the schema without applying any change: what it compares, the CLI command lambdaorm fetch and the orm.stage.fetch() method. What fetch compares Fetch reads the databases of the stage and compares them with the model (drift). The result has one entry per mapping, with the entities that differ: tables missing in the database or missing in the model, columns missing on one side, columns with another type, length or nullability, a different primary key. Each entity has its differences , in readable text. When the databases are in step with the model, every mapping has no entities. Relations (foreign keys) and indexes are not compared. On MongoDB, which is schemaless, fetch only checks that each collection exists. Example of a result, after adding the property phone to Customers in the model: - name: default entities: - name: Customers mapping: customers differences: - column phone missing in the database Result when the database is in step with the model: - name: default entities: [] CLI lambdaorm fetch -s default -o yaml Option Description -w , --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s , --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e , --envfile File of environment variables to read. -o , --output Output format: json , beautiful , light or yaml . The command exits with code 1 when there are differences (and 0 when the databases are in step), so it can be used in CI to detect drift: lambdaorm fetch -s default || echo "the database differs from the model" See the CLI lab . Node orm.stage.fetch() returns the differences. To read the mappings of the databases as they are (every table and column), use orm.stage.read() . import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { const orm = new Orm() try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') const mappings = await orm.stage.fetch({ stage: 'default' }) const differing: any[] = mappings.flatMap(p => p.entities || []) for (const entity of differing) { console.log(entity.name, entity.differences) } // the databases' own mappings const database = await orm.stage.read({ stage: 'default' }) await orm.helper.fs.write('./mappings.yaml', orm.helper.yaml.dump(database)) } finally { await orm.end() } })() See the Node lab .

docs.text: Incorporate This page explains incorporate, which updates the schema from a JSON data file, pushes the changes to the sources (databases) and imports the data: the CLI command lambdaorm incorporate and the orm.stage.incorporate() method. Incorporate: Deduces the entities, properties and relations from the data and adds them to the schema file, as introspect does. Runs a push , so the databases of the stage get the new tables and columns. Imports the data into the databases. CLI lambdaorm incorporate -d countries.json -n countries Option Description -d , --data JSON data file (or the data as inline JSON). Required. -n , --name Name of the root entity (default: the name of the file). -w , --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s , --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e , --envfile File of environment variables to read. Files generated in the orm_state folder: ├── orm_state │ ├── default-data.json │ ├── default-model.json │ └── <source> │ └── V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql <stage>-model.json : the model of the stage. <stage>-data.json : the state of the import. <source>/V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql : the DDL applied to the source. DDL applied (MySQL): CREATE TABLE CountriesLanguages (id INTEGER AUTO_INCREMENT,languageCode VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL ,countryName VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_PK PRIMARY KEY (id)); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_UK UNIQUE (countryName,languageCode); CREATE TABLE Languages (code VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Languages_PK PRIMARY KEY (code)); CREATE TABLE Regions (code VARCHAR(2) NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Regions_PK PRIMARY KEY (code)); CREATE TABLE Positions (lat DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,`long` DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Positions_PK PRIMARY KEY (lat)); ALTER TABLE Positions ADD CONSTRAINT Positions_UK UNIQUE (`long`); CREATE TABLE Timezones (GmtOffset INTEGER ,name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,positionLat DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,countryName VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Timezones_PK PRIMARY KEY (name)); CREATE TABLE Countries (name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,phoneCode INTEGER NOT NULL ,priority INTEGER NOT NULL ,regionCode VARCHAR(2) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Countries_PK PRIMARY KEY (name)); ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_UK UNIQUE (phoneCode); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_countries_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryName) REFERENCES Countries (name); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_languages_FK FOREIGN KEY (languageCode) REFERENCES Languages (code); ALTER TABLE Timezones ADD CONSTRAINT Timezones_position_FK FOREIGN KEY (positionLat) REFERENCES Positions (lat); ALTER TABLE Timezones ADD CONSTRAINT Timezones_countries_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryName) REFERENCES Countries (name); ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_region_FK FOREIGN KEY (regionCode) REFERENCES Regions (code); See the CLI lab . Node orm.stage.incorporate(data, name, options) receives the data, the name of the root entity and, optionally, the query options (for example the stage): import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { const workspace = process.cwd() const orm = new Orm() try { const data = JSON.parse(await orm.helper.fs.read(workspace + '/countries.json') || '{}') await orm.init(workspace + '/lambdaORM.yaml') await orm.stage.incorporate(data, 'countries', { stage: 'default' }) } catch (e) { console.log(e) } finally { await orm.end() } })() As a result: The lambdaORM.yaml file is updated with the structure deduced from the data. The databases of the stage are updated with the new schema. The data is imported into the databases. See the Node lab .

docs.text: Introspect This page explains introspect, which updates the schema from the structure of a JSON data file and then pushes the changes to the sources (databases): the CLI command lambdaorm introspect and the orm.stage.introspect() method. Introspect: Deduces the entities, properties and relations from the data and adds them to the schema file. Runs a push , so the databases of the stage get the new tables and columns. The data is not imported; to import it too, use incorporate . CLI lambdaorm introspect -d countries.json -n countries Option Description -d , --data JSON data file (or the data as inline JSON). Required. -n , --name Name of the root entity (default: the name of the file). -w , --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s , --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e , --envfile File of environment variables to read. This command updates lambdaORM.yaml with the structure of the data in countries.json , with Countries as the root entity, and pushes the changes. Like push, it writes the model of the stage and the DDL applied to each source in the orm_state folder: ├── countries.json ├── lambdaORM.yaml └── orm_state ├── default-model.json └── <source> └── V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql DDL applied (MySQL): CREATE TABLE CountriesLanguages (id INTEGER AUTO_INCREMENT,languageCode VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL ,countryName VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_PK PRIMARY KEY (id)); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_UK UNIQUE (countryName,languageCode); CREATE TABLE Languages (code VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Languages_PK PRIMARY KEY (code)); CREATE TABLE Regions (code VARCHAR(2) NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Regions_PK PRIMARY KEY (code)); CREATE TABLE Positions (lat DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,`long` DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Positions_PK PRIMARY KEY (lat)); ALTER TABLE Positions ADD CONSTRAINT Positions_UK UNIQUE (`long`); CREATE TABLE Timezones (GmtOffset INTEGER ,name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,positionLat DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL ,countryName VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Timezones_PK PRIMARY KEY (name)); CREATE TABLE Countries (name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL ,phoneCode INTEGER NOT NULL ,priority INTEGER NOT NULL ,regionCode VARCHAR(2) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Countries_PK PRIMARY KEY (name)); ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_UK UNIQUE (phoneCode); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_countries_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryName) REFERENCES Countries (name); ALTER TABLE CountriesLanguages ADD CONSTRAINT CountriesLanguages_languages_FK FOREIGN KEY (languageCode) REFERENCES Languages (code); ALTER TABLE Timezones ADD CONSTRAINT Timezones_position_FK FOREIGN KEY (positionLat) REFERENCES Positions (lat); ALTER TABLE Timezones ADD CONSTRAINT Timezones_countries_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryName) REFERENCES Countries (name); ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_region_FK FOREIGN KEY (regionCode) REFERENCES Regions (code); See the CLI lab . Node orm.stage.introspect(data, name, options) receives the data, the name of the root entity and, optionally, the query options (for example the stage): import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { const workspace = process.cwd() const orm = new Orm() try { const data = JSON.parse(await orm.helper.fs.read(workspace + '/countries.json') || '{}') await orm.init(workspace + '/lambdaORM.yaml') await orm.stage.introspect(data, 'countries', { stage: 'default' }) } catch (e) { console.log(e) } finally { await orm.end() } })() As a result: The lambdaORM.yaml file is updated with the structure deduced from the data. docs.text: Pull This page explains pull, which updates the schema file with the structure of the sources (databases) of a stage: what it keeps, the CLI command lambdaorm pull and the orm.stage.pull() method. What pull keeps Pull reads the tables and columns of the databases and merges them into the schema: new tables become entities, new columns become properties, and the mappings are updated. Pull does not change the databases. By default it also removes from the schema the entities, properties and relations that are no longer in the database ( orm.stage.pull({ stage, removeEntities: false, removeProperties: false, removeRelations: false }) keeps them). It can be run on an existing schema: what was written by hand is kept, for example relation names chosen by hand and weak relations between sources (which have no foreign key in the database), application.listeners , infrastructure.stages . Columns named with reserved words (for example order ) are supported. docs.text: Push This page explains push, which updates the sources (databases) of a stage with the schema: how it works, the CLI command lambdaorm push and the orm.stage.push() method. How push works Push reads the databases of the stage (as fetch does) and generates the DDL that takes them to the model: Tables that do not exist are created with their primary key, unique key, foreign keys and indexes. In existing tables, missing columns are added ( ALTER TABLE … ADD ) and columns with another type, length or nullability are altered. A column declared with previousMapping in its property mapping is renamed ( ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN , SqlServer sp_rename ) instead of being added. See Rename a column . Push never drops anything that exists only in the database (tables, columns). fetch reports it, so it can be removed by hand if needed. The column types follow the property types and the dbType of the property mapping. See Property types . Each entity goes to the source chosen by the stage rules; a source without condition only gets the entities no other source took. Since the comparison is made against the databases, push works the same on any host or CI job: it does not need the orm_state folder of a previous push. The orm_state folder is still written, as a record of what was applied. Renaming a table is not supported. CLI Apply the changes: lambdaorm push Option Description -w , --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s , --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e , --envfile File of environment variables to read. -o , --output Generate the DDL without applying it (see below). -f , --force When a sentence fails, continue with the next ones. Example of the generated DDL on an empty database: CREATE TABLE Countries (name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL ,iso3 VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Countries_PK PRIMARY KEY (iso3)); ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_UK UNIQUE (name); CREATE TABLE States (id INTEGER NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL ,countryCode VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT States_PK PRIMARY KEY (id)); ALTER TABLE States ADD CONSTRAINT States_UK UNIQUE (countryCode,name); ALTER TABLE States ADD CONSTRAINT States_country_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryCode) REFERENCES Countries (iso3); After adding a property phone to Customers and renaming the column icon to icon_name (with previousMapping: icon ), a push generates only those changes: ALTER TABLE customers ADD phone VARCHAR(32); ALTER TABLE categories RENAME COLUMN icon TO icon_name; Generate the DDL without applying it With -o , push generates the DDL but does not apply it. -o alone prints the sentences of each source. -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, named <stage>.<source>.sql . Sources without changes get no file, and a database in step with the model gives no files at all. lambdaorm push -s default -o migrations migrations ├── default.catalog.sql └── default.accounts.sql The names are deterministic, so the scripts can be renamed into versioned migrations and applied by your own deploy process. Files in orm_state When push applies the changes, it records them in the orm_state folder: ├── orm_state │ ├── default-model.json │ └── main │ └── V231122154351__push.sql <stage>-model.json : the model of the stage at the last push. <source>/V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql : the sentences executed on that source. Labs: Simple Two stages Northwind Northwind multiple datasources Northwind CQRS Node orm.stage.push() returns an action that can give the sentences without applying them, or apply them: import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { const orm = new Orm() try { await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // the sentences, without applying them const sentences = await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).sentence() // the sentences grouped by source: [{ source: 'accounts', sentences: ['ALTER TABLE accounts ADD phone VARCHAR(32)'] }] const bySource = await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).sentencesBySource() // apply them await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).execute() } finally { await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Synchronization This page summarizes the commands that keep the schema and the databases of a stage in step. Synchronization works in both directions: from the schema to the sources (databases), and from the sources to the schema file. Each operation is available as a command of the CLI ( @lambdaorm/cli ) and as a method of orm.stage in @lambdaorm/lib . Operation Direction Changes the schema Changes the databases push schema → databases no yes pull databases → schema yes no fetch compares both no no introspect data file → schema → databases yes yes incorporate data file → schema → databases, then imports the data yes yes Push Push updates the sources (databases) with the schema, with the command lambdaorm push . Push compares the model with the databases themselves: it creates missing tables, adds and alters columns, renames the columns declared with previousMapping , and never drops what exists only in the database. lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes the DDL as one script per source ( <stage>.<source>.sql ) without applying it. More information Pull Pull updates the schema with the structure of the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm pull . What was written by hand in the schema (relations, listeners, stages) is kept. More information Fetch Fetch shows the differences between the sources and the schema, without applying any change, with the command lambdaorm fetch . The result is empty when the databases are in step with the model, and the command exits with code 1 when there are differences (useful in CI). More information Introspect Introspect updates the schema from the structure of a JSON data file and then pushes the changes to the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm introspect . More information Incorporate Incorporate does the same as introspect and then imports the data of the file into the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm incorporate . More information
