docs.text: Changelog All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. @lambdaorm/lib 3.2.2 Patch Changes e4ce3af: 3xpr 5.2.0 in every package (one copy of it). lib builds each Orm's 3xpr instance with the ExpressionsBuilder 3xpr now exports, instead of importing it from one of its files. Updated dependencies [e4ce3af] @lambdaorm/base@3.2.1 3.2.1 Patch Changes 2dc1ac1: Fixes found running the same checks on every engine (engines lab, docs/PLAN.md B7): stage.fetch / push compare a column the way the dialect creates it: no false drift (and no needless ALTER ) for MySQL/MariaDB booleans, Oracle numbers and nullability, SQL Server and MariaDB json; MariaDB LONGTEXT is read. MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle: in(p.x, list) with the list in a variable. json columns are read as objects also where the driver answers text (MariaDB, Oracle CLOB ); SQL Server writes them. SQL Server: delete with a filter ( DELETE c FROM t c ). Oracle: autoIncrement columns are identity columns; booleans are written as Y / N . MongoDB: transactions commit and roll back (the session was not used), update/delete answer the matched/deleted documents, autoIncrement keys, string literals and '' in filters, json values, in with a list, include of a composite relation, and update().include() of a composite saves the embedded children. upsert on SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB says it is not supported yet. 68faedb: Each Orm has its own 3xpr instance. With the shared one, every new Orm() replaced orm.execute (and the other orm.* functions): the listeners and scripts of an earlier Orm ran their queries on the last one created, outside their own transaction. 3.2.0 Minor Changes 7c18bef: - A filter by a field of a relation whose entity lives in another source works (L15): QuoteLines.filter(p => p.deviceModel.name == name) first queries DeviceModels on its source and then filters QuoteLines with in(p.deviceModelId, …) . Each comparison is solved on its own ( && , || , ! keep their meaning); the other side must be a value (a clear error otherwise) and only one level of relation is supported. PostgreSQL: in(p.x, list) / p.x.in(list) with the list in a variable works — the parameter was typed as its elements and the array was sent as a Postgres array literal (L33). 38e7d3b: New orm.executeScript(script, data, options) : evaluates a 3xpr script whose orm.execute(query, data, options) calls all run in one transaction, also across sources. The script can use variables, if , for , for … in , throw , try / catch and return ; it commits when it ends and rolls back and rejects when anything fails (a query, a function or a throw ). It works on a copy of data , cannot read environment variables, and its orm.execute calls without a stage run on the script's stage. Returns the value of the last statement (or of return ). js const quoteId = await orm.executeScript( ` orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" }); for (line in lines) { orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, deviceModelId: line.modelId, quantity: line.qty }); } orm.execute("Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: now() })).filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId }); quoteId `, { quoteId, accountId, lines } ); 3f3e1cc: Listeners ( application.listeners ) are awaited one after the other and run in the sentence's transaction: their orm.execute calls use the same connections, an error in before prevents the sentence, an error in after fails it, and a rollback undoes what they wrote. A sentence with listeners that runs on its own opens a transaction for itself and its listeners. They used to run detached ( forEach(async …) ): execute could return before them, their errors escaped as uncaught exceptions and they wrote outside the transaction — L10. New listener option transactional: false (base ListenerConfig ): the listener runs outside the transaction, and what it writes is kept even if the sentence's transaction rolls back. c2be59f: push compares the model with the databases (as fetch reads them), not with orm_state — L19: a new environment or a CI runner without the last push's orm_state no longer gets CREATE TABLE for tables that exist. Tables missing in the database are created with their keys, FKs and indexes; in existing tables, missing columns are added ( ADD COLUMN , L27), columns with another type, length or nullability are altered, and a property mapping with previousMapping: <old column> renames the column ( ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN , L20; SqlServer sp_rename ). Nothing that exists only in the database is dropped ( stage.fetch() reports it). orm_state is still written by push as a record. d16b60a: stage.push().sentencesBySource() : the DDL grouped per source (one script per database). cli: lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, <stage>.<source>.sql (deterministic names, to rename into a versioned migration); -o without a folder prints the DDL grouped by source — L19. e961817: update().include(p => p.children) on a composite relation saves the aggregate: the children sent are inserted or updated (upsert by primary key, with the parent's key), and the parent's children that were not sent are deleted. Children absent from the data are not touched. It used to update only the existing children that were sent — L17. Supported where upsert is (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB); SqlServer, Oracle and SQLjs report it as not supported yet (MongoDB keeps composite children embedded). An explicit include(p => p.children.update(…)) keeps updating only. 8b8f470: Stage commands: push/DDL: a stage's last source without condition is a catch-all, as in DML: it gets only the entities no other source took (it used to receive every entity) — L25. fetch/pull on PostgreSQL work with reserved words as column names ( order ): the metadata query quoted the column twice — L6, L21. stage.fetch() reports the drift: per mapping, the entities that differ from the model (present in one side only, different columns, types, lengths, required, primary key), each with its differences ; no entities when in step. stage.read() returns the databases' mappings as fetch did (pull uses it) — L22. cli: lambdaorm fetch exits with code 1 when there are differences (for CI). fetch , pull , schema , introspect and incorporate load the --envfile they declared (it was ignored). 907074b: Transactions: orm.transaction now waits for the transaction: it resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback (the error used to escape as an uncaught exception and the promise resolved undefined ) — L26. If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported. Everything executed inside orm.transaction joins it, also when it doesn't go through tr : orm.execute , repositories, the orm.execute function of an expression. It runs on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes it — L31. A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one, a query with include no longer opens a second transaction, and an execution on another stage inside a transaction fails with a clear error. Each Orm instance keeps its own transaction context. 7c8edd7: Types and values: New property type json (L1): objects and lists are written as JSON and come back as objects and lists. Column type: PostgreSQL JSONB , MySQL/MariaDB JSON , SqlServer NVARCHAR(MAX) , Oracle CLOB , others TEXT . A list is no longer sent as a Postgres array literal. The mapping's dbType reaches the DDL when a table or column is created or altered (it was used in one place only) — e.g. dbType: timestamptz(3) (L1, L2). PostgreSQL writes dateTime with milliseconds and the offset ( yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSSZZ ): milliseconds are kept and a timestamptz column stores the exact instant; timestamp columns keep storing the local time (L2). '' , 0 and false parameters are values: only undefined becomes NULL (an empty string used to be written as NULL, and so were 0 and false ) — L3. (The "" literal needs 3xpr 5.1.1.) A string property without length is no longer given length 80 in the model: PostgreSQL creates TEXT , the other dialects keep VARCHAR(80) — L24. On PostgreSQL, the next push of an existing model widens those columns to TEXT. de140f3: update answers the number of affected rows (as delete does, and as the repositories' update(): Promise<number> always declared); it answered { data: <parameters> } . Lets callers detect "not found" (0) and optimistic-lock conflicts ( filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version) → 0) — L4. SQLjs update / delete now return the modified rows too. 6319468: Entity.upsert() : insert, or update the row with the same primary key, in one sentence — PostgreSQL INSERT … ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c , MySQL/MariaDB ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE c = VALUES(c) (other dialects: a clear "not supported" error). Written like an insert ( upsert() , upsert(entity) , upsert({ … }) ); answers the data like insert — L18. It used to fail with function: upsert not found . Patch Changes 2ee8930: Upgrade the data7expressions dependencies to their latest major: 3xpr from 1.x to ^5.1.1 , h3lp and typ3s to ^5.0.0 (and json-light to ^5.0.0 in the CLI). No API changes were needed. Behaviour inherited from 3xpr: <= now has the same precedence as the other comparison operators ( a <= b == true used to evaluate as a <= (b == true) ). 3xpr 5.1.0 evaluates async expressions statement by statement (listeners, orm.execute inside expressions), never runs an async function while building an expression, and adds throw , try / catch , return , break and continue ; 3xpr 5.1.1 parses the empty string literal "" (it used to swallow the rest of the expression). ee1e7ac: Packaging: The published exports pointed to ./build/lib/index.js , a path the package doesn't have: require('@lambdaorm/lib') (and base, client) failed for everyone installing from npm. dist now rewrites exports (and bin ) like main — L7. cli: declares bin: lambdaorm , so npm i -g @lambdaorm/cli installs the lambdaorm command — L29. Every package's dist is smoke-tested before it can be released: required by its name (so exports applies) and, for the CLI, lambdaorm --help . b1dcd8b: - orm.executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout }) : when the timeout passes the script's transaction rolls back and the promise rejects. A finished transaction (committed or rolled back) refuses any later execution, so work that outlives it (a script that timed out, a kept tr ) never reaches the database. ExecutionError keeps the database's error code ( error.code , e.g. Postgres 23505 ); it used to be lost. Repositories A repository is associated with an entity and has methods to query and modify it, without writing the whole query. Generating repositories The lambdaorm build command generates the model ( model.ts ) and one repository per entity ( repository<Entity>.ts ) in the domain path of the project: lambdaorm build -w lab/northwind -r A repository file is generated only if it does not exist yet, so it is safe to add custom methods to it. import { Repository, IOrm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Product, QryProduct } from './model' export class ProductRepository extends Repository<Product, QryProduct> { constructor (stage?: string, orm?: IOrm) { super('Products', stage, orm) } // Add your code here } The constructor receives the stage (optional: the default stage when omitted) and, optionally, the orm instance. Example import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { ProductRepository } from './northwind/domain/repositoryProduct' (async () => { await orm.init() const productRepository = new ProductRepository('default') const country = 'USA' const result = await productRepository.query() .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3)) .having(p => max(p.price) > 50) .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) })) .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice)) .execute({ country }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) await orm.end() })() Methods Method Description insert(entity, include?) Inserts a record (and, with include , its related records). bulkInsert(entities, include?) Inserts several records. update(entity, include?) Updates a record. updateAll(data, map, filter?, include?) Updates all the records that match the filter (or all the records of the entity). upsert(entity, include?) Inserts a record, or updates it if one with the same primary key exists ( upsert ). bulkMerge(entities, include?) Inserts or updates several records. delete(entity, include?) Deletes a record. bulkDelete(entities, include?) Deletes several records. deleteAll(data, filter?, include?) Deletes all the records that match the filter (or all the records of the entity). list(data, filter?, include?) Returns the records that match the filter. distinct(data, filter?, include?) Returns the distinct records that match the filter. first(data, filter?, include?) Returns the first record, or null . last(data, filter?, include?) Returns the last record, or null . query() Starts a custom query on the entity ( filter , include , having , map , sort , page , …), run with execute(data) . execute(query, data?) Runs a query string appended to the entity, for example .filter(p => p.id == id) . data holds the values of the parameters used by filter and map .

docs.text: Script A script is a small program, written in 3xpr (a JavaScript-like expression language), that λORM runs with orm.executeScript(script, data, options) . Inside it, orm.execute(query, data, options) runs λORM queries, and variables, conditions and loops decide which ones and with what data. What it is for Many use cases are more than one query: place an order (the order, its lines, the customer's balance), move stock between warehouses, register a payment and its audit. Their writes must happen completely or not at all : an order without its lines, or a balance discounted for an order that was not saved, is a corrupt state. orm.transaction(options, callback) solves it in Node.js code. A script solves it in a single call that carries the whole use case , wherever the call comes from: Node.js ( orm.executeScript ), the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the Node.js client ( @lambdaorm/client ) or the CLI ( lambdaorm script ). A client in any language can run a use case with several reads and writes in one transaction, which it could not do by sending one query per request. Features All or nothing : everything the script executes is one transaction — committed when it ends, rolled back if anything fails (a query, a throw , the timeout). See below . Across sources and stages : queries on several databases, and on another stage with orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) , are part of the same transaction. Listeners included : what the schema's listeners write is committed or undone with the script. A language, not only queries : variables, if , for , while , switch , try/catch , throw , return , list functions ( filter , map , sum , …) and every function of 3xpr and λORM. Read your writes : a statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit. A result : the value of the last statement (or of return ) — a value, a row, an object built by the script. Safe for scripts sent by clients : no access to environment variables, works on a copy of data , timeout and maxIterations stop it (also a loop that never ends), and the Data Gateway runs scripts only when its configuration enables them ( scripts.enabled ) and the credential has the script permission. A first look — the examples go step by step, from a single query to a complete use case: const total = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines }, { stage: 'default' } ) The main feature: all or nothing Everything a script executes is one transaction. Every orm.execute of the script — on one source or on several, on the script's stage or on another one, and what the listeners write — runs on the same connections: when the script ends, everything is committed ; if anything fails — a query, a function, a rule that throw s, the timeout — everything the script did is rolled back , in every source and stage, and the promise rejects with that error. That is what a script is for: a use case with several reads and writes (an order with its lines, a stock movement, a transfer) that must happen completely or not at all , in a single call — also from the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client or the CLI , where a client could otherwise only send one query per request and could not undo the previous ones. When the script… Result ends normally commit of everything; resolves with the last value (or return ) throws ( throw ) rollback of everything; rejects with that error runs a query that fails (e.g. a duplicate key) rollback of everything; rejects with the database's error catches an error with try/catch it goes on; the error does not undo anything by itself passes timeout or maxIterations it stops, rollback of everything; rejects Arguments Argument Description script The 3xpr script data The variables of the script. The script works on a copy: data is never changed options The query options plus the script's limits ( ScriptOptions ), see below Option Description stage The stage of the transaction and of every orm.execute without a stage timeout Max time in ms: when it passes, the loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects maxIterations Max loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back Up to @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 the limits were a fourth argument ( executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout, maxIterations }) ); since 3.4.0 everything goes in options . Examples Each example says what it does and what happens when it fails. The model of the examples domain: entities: - name: Customers primaryKey: [id] uniqueKey: [code] properties: - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true } - { name: code, length: 20, required: true } - { name: name, required: true } - { name: notes } - { name: balance, type: decimal } - name: Orders primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, length: 36, required: true } - { name: customerId, type: integer } - { name: status, length: 20, required: true } - { name: version, type: integer, required: true } relations: - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId } - name: OrderLines primaryKey: [orderId, line] properties: - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true } - { name: line, type: integer, required: true } - { name: product, length: 40, required: true } - { name: quantity, type: integer } - name: AuditLogs primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true } - { name: entityName, length: 40 } - { name: refId, length: 36 } The examples run on the stage default ; examples 11 and 13 also write on a stage insights . They are the engines lab model, where the same scripts are tested on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB. 1. A single query The simplest script is one orm.execute . The script returns the value of its last statement — here the rows of the query. Even this runs in a transaction (it opens, the query runs, it commits). const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code }) `, { code }, { stage: 'default' } ) 2. Several statements, in order Statements run one after the other, each orm.execute awaited before the next. A statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit (they share the connection). const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name }); orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code).map(p => p.name)", { code: code }) `, { code, name: 'Ana' }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: [{ name: "Ana" }]. 3. Using the result of a statement Assign a result to a variable and use it below. An insert answers { data } with the values written, generated ones included: customer.data.id is the id the database generated. const result = await orm.executeScript(` customer = orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name }); orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.data.id, status: "new", version: 1 }); customer.data.id `, { code, name: 'Ana', orderId }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: the id generated for the customer. 4. Affected rows: "not found" as an error update and delete answer the number of affected rows. A script can turn 0 into an error; throw with a status is answered with that HTTP status by the Data Gateway. const result = await orm.executeScript(` updated = orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ name: name })).filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code, name: name }); if (updated == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + code + " not found" }; } updated `, { code: 'missing', name: 'Bob' }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: customer missing not found (404). 5. Conditions: create only what is missing if with a query in the condition. Run it twice with the same data: the second time it creates nothing. const result = await orm.executeScript(` created = 0; for (c in customers) { if (orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: c.code }).length() == 0) { orm.execute("Customers.insert()", c); created += 1; } } created `, { customers: [{ code: 'c1', name: 'Ana' }, { code: 'c2', name: 'Bob' }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 2 the first time, 0 the second. 6. Loops: one row per item for (item in list) over the data. Every insert of the loop is in the same transaction: all the lines are written, or none. Lists also have filter , map , sum , count … const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 25. 7. Aggregates with include A composite relation can be written with include , as in orm.execute outside a script. Here the order and its lines in one sentence, then read back with its lines. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert().include(p => p.lines)", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1, lines: lines.map(l => ({ orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty })) }); orders = orm.execute("Orders.filter(p => p.id == orderId).include(p => p.lines)", { orderId: orderId }); orders[0].lines.length() `, { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1 }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 2. 8. A business rule: throw, and everything is undone The rule is checked after writing: the order and its lines are already in the database (inside the transaction). throw stops the script and rolls back everything it wrote : no order and no line is left. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); if (total > maxTotal) { throw { status: 400, message: "the order exceeds " + maxTotal }; } total `, { orderId, maxTotal: 20, lines: [ …total 25… ] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: the order exceeds 20 (400); the order and its lines are not in the database. 9. Handling an error: try / catch An error caught with try/catch does not abort the script: it goes on and commits. Use it for optional steps; any error not caught rolls everything back. const result = await orm.executeScript(` try { if (vip) { throw "vip customers are reviewed by hand"; } note = "ok"; } catch (e) { note = e.message; } orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name, notes: note }); note `, { code, name: 'Ana', vip: true }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: "vip customers are reviewed by hand" (and the customer is written). 10. Listeners run inside the script's transaction A schema listener (here, one that writes an AuditLogs row after each order insert) runs in the script's transaction: committed with it, and undone with it if the script fails. application: listeners: - name: auditOrders on: [insert] condition: entity == "Orders" after: orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "Orders", refId: data.id }) const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); throw "cancel"; `, { orderId }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: cancel; neither the order nor its audit row are in the database. 11. Another stage in the same transaction orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) runs on another stage — other sources, even another database engine — in the same transaction : if anything fails afterwards, the write on the other stage is undone too. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "new order", refId: orderId }, { stage: insights }); if (fail) { throw "something failed after both writes"; } "done" `, { orderId, insights: 'insights', fail: true }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects; the order (default stage) and the audit row (insights stage) are both undone. 12. Limits: timeout and maxIterations Options of the script, with the stage: timeout (ms) stops it — also a loop that never ends — and rolls back; maxIterations caps the loop iterations of the whole script. Both are worth setting when scripts come from clients. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: "never kept" }); while (true) { x = 1; } `, { code }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 2000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) Result: rejects (maxIterations, or the timeout first); the customer is not written. 13. A complete use case: place an order Everything together: validate, write an aggregate, apply a rule, write on another stage and answer a summary. One call, one transaction — if any step fails, nothing of the order exists anywhere . const result = await orm.executeScript(` customers = orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == customerCode)", { customerCode: customerCode }); if (customers.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + customerCode + " not found" }; } customer = customers[0]; orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.id, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); if (total > customer.balance) { throw { status: 409, message: "insufficient balance" }; } orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ balance: balance })).filter(p => p.id == id)", { id: customer.id, balance: customer.balance - total }); orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "order total " + total, refId: orderId }, { stage: insights }); { orderId: orderId, total: total, balance: customer.balance - total } `, { customerCode: 'c1', orderId, insights: 'insights', lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) Result: { orderId, total: 25, balance: 75 } with a balance of 100; with a balance of 20 it rejects (409) and the order, its lines, the balance and the audit row are left as they were. 14. Another use case: a quote with its total on insights A quote with its lines on the main stage and its total on the insights stage (other sources, possibly another database), in one transaction. The account must exist; if any step fails, neither the quote, nor its lines, nor the total are left anywhere. (A model with Accounts , Quotes , QuoteLines and QuoteTotals .) const quoteId = await orm.executeScript(` account = orm.execute("Accounts.filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId }); if (account.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "account not found" }; } orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" }); for (line in lines) { orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, productId: line.productId, quantity: line.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); orm.execute("QuoteTotals.insert()", { quoteId: quoteId, total: total }, { stage: "insights" }); quoteId `, { quoteId, accountId, lines }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) The same script from a client The script and its data are the same everywhere; only the call changes. The URL of the Data Gateway includes the route of the schema, unless the gateway serves a single schema at the root, as in these examples. // @lambdaorm/client, against a Data Gateway import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/client' await orm.init('http://localhost:8080', { headers: { 'X-Api-Key': process.env.BACKEND_KEY } }) const result = await orm.executeScript(script, data, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000 }) # REST: a Data Gateway with scripts.enabled and a credential with the script permission curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/script -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "X-Api-Key: $BACKEND_KEY" \ -d '{ "script": "orm.execute(\"Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)\", { code: code })", "data": { "code": "c1" }, "options": { "stage": "default" } }' # CLI: a script file, data as JSON lambdaorm script -f place-order.3xpr -d '{ "customerCode": "c1", "orderId": "o-1", "lines": [] }' -s default The language Everything 3xpr has: Variables: total = 0; , objects { id: id, name: "x" } , lists [1, 2] , items[0].name . if / else if / else , while , for (i = 0; i < n; i += 1) , for (item in items) , switch / case , break , continue , return . throw "message" ; try { … } catch (e) { e.message } . throw { status: 404, message: "…" } makes the Data Gateway answer with that status; in Node the error's message is that object as JSON. Arrow functions as arguments: items.filter(p => p.qty > 1).map(p => p.name) , items.sum(p => p.qty) , items.each(p => …) . 3xpr's functions: strings ( upper , concat , …), numbers, dates ( now() , …), lists, nvl , iif , … (see Operators & Functions ). Not available: the ? : operator ( iif(c, a, b) evaluates both sides), ++ / -- (use i += 1 ) and declaring functions. Statements run in order, and each orm.execute is awaited before the next statement. Plus the functions λORM adds: Function Description orm.execute(query, data, options) Executes a query in the script's transaction; options.stage may name another stage (same transaction) orm.plan(query, options) The plan of a query ( .sentence , …) orm.parameters(query) The parameters of a query orm.metadata(query) The metadata of a query orm.model(query) The model (fields) a query returns orm.constraints(query) The constraints a query checks toBase64(value) / getBase64(value) "abc" → "YWJj" and back encrypt(value, key) / decrypt(value, key) AES Writing scripts: a few rules Statements end with ; ; the last one (without ; ) is the result. return value; ends the script early. Variables need no declaration: total = 0; . data is copied: the script never changes the caller's object. Count with i += 1 (there is no ++ ); use iif(condition, a, b) (there is no ? : ). A query's result can be indexed directly: orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code })[0].name ; an empty list is [] (both need 3xpr 5.3.1, from @lambdaorm/lib 3.4.1). A script can't read environment variables ( $VAR ). Transaction and stages One transaction for the whole script, also across sources and stages: commit at the end; rollback and reject on any error. orm.execute(query, data) without stage runs on the stage of options ; with { stage: "insights" } it runs on that stage, in the same transaction (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0). A statement sees what the previous ones wrote (same connection), before the commit. There is no two-phase commit: with several databases the commit goes source by source. Security and limits The script cannot read environment variables ( $VAR fails), so it can't read connection strings. timeout : when it passes, the script's loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects; whatever it still executes afterwards fails without reaching the database. maxIterations : the loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back. The Data Gateway uses scripts.maxIterations (default 100000). Since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 (3xpr 5.3.0) a while (true) {} no longer blocks the process: the timeout and maxIterations stop it. In the Data Gateway scripts are off by default ( scripts.enabled ) and need the script permission.
docs.title: Script

docs.text: A script is a small program, written in 3xpr (a JavaScript-like expression language), that λORM runs with orm.executeScript(script, data, options) . Inside it, orm.execute(query, data, options) runs λORM queries, and variables, conditions and loops decide which ones and with what data.
docs.title: Script

docs.text: Many use cases are more than one query: place an order (the order, its lines, the customer's balance), move stock between warehouses, register a payment and its audit. Their writes must happen completely or not at all : an order without its lines, or a balance discounted for an order that was not saved, is a corrupt state. orm.transaction(options, callback) solves it in Node.js code. A script solves it in a single call that carries the whole use case , wherever the call comes from: Node.js ( orm.executeScript ), the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the Node.js client ( @lambdaorm/client ) or the CLI ( lambdaorm script ). A client in any language can run a use case with several reads and writes in one transaction, which it could not do by sending one query per request.
docs.title: What it is for

docs.text: All or nothing : everything the script executes is one transaction — committed when it ends, rolled back if anything fails (a query, a throw , the timeout). See below . Across sources and stages : queries on several databases, and on another stage with orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) , are part of the same transaction. Listeners included : what the schema's listeners write is committed or undone with the script. A language, not only queries : variables, if , for , while , switch , try/catch , throw , return , list functions ( filter , map , sum , …) and every function of 3xpr and λORM. Read your writes : a statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit. A result : the value of the last statement (or of return ) — a value, a row, an object built by the script. Safe for scripts sent by clients : no access to environment variables, works on a copy of data , timeout and maxIterations stop it (also a loop that never ends), and the Data Gateway runs scripts only when its configuration enables them ( scripts.enabled ) and the credential has the script permission. A first look — the examples go step by step, from a single query to a complete use case: const total = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines }, { stage: 'default' } )
docs.title: Features

docs.text: Everything a script executes is one transaction. Every orm.execute of the script — on one source or on several, on the script's stage or on another one, and what the listeners write — runs on the same connections: when the script ends, everything is committed ; if anything fails — a query, a function, a rule that throw s, the timeout — everything the script did is rolled back , in every source and stage, and the promise rejects with that error. That is what a script is for: a use case with several reads and writes (an order with its lines, a stock movement, a transfer) that must happen completely or not at all , in a single call — also from the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client or the CLI , where a client could otherwise only send one query per request and could not undo the previous ones. When the script… Result ends normally commit of everything; resolves with the last value (or return ) throws ( throw ) rollback of everything; rejects with that error runs a query that fails (e.g. a duplicate key) rollback of everything; rejects with the database's error catches an error with try/catch it goes on; the error does not undo anything by itself passes timeout or maxIterations it stops, rollback of everything; rejects
docs.title: The main feature: all or nothing

docs.text: Argument Description script The 3xpr script data The variables of the script. The script works on a copy: data is never changed options The query options plus the script's limits ( ScriptOptions ), see below Option Description stage The stage of the transaction and of every orm.execute without a stage timeout Max time in ms: when it passes, the loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects maxIterations Max loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back Up to @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 the limits were a fourth argument ( executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout, maxIterations }) ); since 3.4.0 everything goes in options .

docs.text: Transaction A transaction groups several executions so that they are all committed together or all rolled back. In λORM a transaction is opened with orm.transaction(options, callback) . Usage orm.transaction receives: options : the query options, for example the stage ( { stage: 'default' } ); callback : an async function that receives a transaction object (named tr in the examples) and executes the queries with tr.execute(query, data, options) . When the callback ends, λORM commits; if it throws, λORM rolls back. await orm.transaction({ stage: 'default' }, async tr => { await tr.execute('Quotes.insert()', quote) // orm.execute inside the callback also joins the transaction await orm.execute('Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: at })).filter(p => p.id == id)', { id: quote.accountId, at: new Date() }) // another stage: same transaction await tr.execute('QuoteSummaries.insert()', summary, { stage: 'insights' }) }) Behavior The promise resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback . If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported. Everything executed inside the callback joins the transaction : tr.execute , orm.execute , repositories, and the orm.execute of a listener or of an expression. They run on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes them in every source. A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one: there is a single commit, done by the outer transaction. An execution without a stage runs on the transaction's stage. An execution with another stage joins the transaction too (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0): every stage shares the transaction's connections, and they commit or roll back together. A finished transaction rejects later executions. Warning There is no two-phase commit: with several databases, the commit is done source by source. If a later commit fails, the earlier ones are kept. To run several queries in one transaction from a single call — also over the Data Gateway or the CLI — see Script . Example The order and its details are inserted, read, updated and deleted in the same transaction: import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model' (async () => { try { await orm.init('./config/northwind.yaml') const order = { customerId: 'VINET', employeeId: 5, orderDate: '1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 3, freight: 32.38, name: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier', address: '59 rue de l-Abbaye', city: 'Reims', region: null, postalCode: '51100', country: 'France', details: [ { productId: 11, unitPrice: 14, quantity: 12, discount: false }, { productId: 42, unitPrice: 9.8, quantity: 10, discount: false }, { productId: 72, unitPrice: 34.8, quantity: 5, discount: false } ] } await orm.transaction({ stage: 'default' }, async (tr) => { // create the order const orderId = await tr.execute(() => Orders.insert().include(p => p.details), order) // get the order const result = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) const order2 = result[0] // update the order order2.address = 'changed 59 rue de l-Abbaye' order2.details[0].discount = true order2.details[1].unitPrice = 10 order2.details[2].quantity = 7 const updateCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.update().include(p => p.details), order2) console.log(updateCount) // get the order again const order3 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) console.log(JSON.stringify(order3)) // delete the order const deleteCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.delete().include(p => p.details), order3[0]) console.log(deleteCount) // the order no longer exists const order4 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) console.log(JSON.stringify(order4)) }) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // close the connections await orm.end() } })()

docs.text: Usage This page shows different ways of using λORM with the same example domain (Northwind) on different infrastructures: a single source, several sources, CQRS with several stages, and a Node.js client connected to a Data Gateway . To keep the schemas short, the properties, keys, indexes and relations of the entities, as well as the mappings, are omitted. The complete schemas are in the labs . Single source Schema The domain has five entities: Categories , Customers , Products and Orders , where Orders is a composite entity made of the orders and their details ( Orders.details ). The infrastructure has a single stage with a single source, Ordering , a MySQL database that uses the default mapping. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering mapping: default dialect: MySQL connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering Query The query gets an order of a customer, with its details. It is written as a lambda expression and run with the @lambdaorm/lib library. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model' (async () => { try { // initialize the ORM with the schema file await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // query const query = (customerId: string) => Orders .filter(p => p.customerId == customerId) .include(p => [ p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details .include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ]) .page(1, 1) // execute the query const result = await orm.execute(query, { customerId: 'CENTC' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } finally { await orm.end() } })() Result [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ] Multiple sources Schema In this case the entities of the domain are stored in different sources: Categories and Products are stored in the Catalog source, a MySQL database that uses the default mapping. Customers is stored in the Crm source, a PostgreSQL database that uses the default mapping. Orders is stored in the Ordering source, a MongoDB database that uses the mongoDb mapping. The condition of each source in the stage decides which entities it stores. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: mongoDb extends: default sources: - name: Catalog dialect: MySQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} - name: Crm dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES} - name: Ordering dialect: MongoDB mapping: mongoDb connection: ${CNN_MONGODB} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) Query This time the query is run from the CLI . The code does not change with the infrastructure, and the result is the same as in the previous case, although the data now comes from three databases. lambdaorm execute -e ".env" -q "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => [p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details.include(p => p.product.include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)).map(p => p.name)).map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])]).page(1,1)" -d "{\"customerId\": \"CENTC\"}" Result [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ] View the complete lab CQRS CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the model used to write data from the model used to read it. With λORM it is a matter of configuration. Schema This schema defines three stages for the same domain: default : data is read from and written to the Catalog , Crm and Ordering sources. insights : data is read from and written to the Insights source. cqrs : data is read from the Insights source but written to the Catalog , Crm and Ordering sources. To keep Insights in step with Catalog , Crm and Ordering , a listener runs after each insert, bulk insert, update or delete on the default and cqrs stages, and applies the same operation on the insights stage. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: mongoDb extends: default sources: - name: Catalog dialect: MySQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} - name: Crm dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES} - name: Ordering dialect: MongoDB mapping: mongoDb connection: ${CNN_MONGODB} - name: Insights dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_INSIGHTS} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) - name: insights sources: - name: Insights - name: cqrs sources: - name: Insights condition: action == "select" - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) application: listeners: - name: syncInsights on: [insert, bulkInsert, update, delete ] condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs") after: orm.execute(query,data,{stage:"insights"}) Query This time the query is run on a Data Gateway that serves this schema, through its REST API : curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/execute?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "Orders.filter(p=>p.customerId==customerId).include(p=>[p.details.include(p=>p.product.map(p=>p.name)).map(p=>{subTotal:p.quantity*p.unitPrice}),p.customer.map(p=>p.name)]).sort(p=>p.orderDate).page(1,1)", "data": {"customerId": "CENTC"}, "options": {"stage": "default"}}' Result [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000+02:00", "details": [ { "subTotal": 80, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones" } }, { "subTotal": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax" } } ], "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" } } ] Query plan on the default stage On the default stage, the data comes from different sources, according to the configuration of the stage: curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/plan?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "Orders.filter(p=>p.customerId==customerId).include(p=>[p.details.include(p=>p.product.map(p=>p.name)).map(p=>{subTotal:p.quantity*p.unitPrice}),p.customer.map(p=>p.name)]).sort(p=>p.orderDate).page(1,1)", "options": {"stage": "default"}}' Result: { "entity": "Orders", "dialect": "MongoDB", "source": "Ordering", "sentence": "[{ \"$match\" : { \"CustomerID\":{{customerId}} } }, { \"$project\" :{ \"_id\": 0 , \"id\":\"$_id\", \"customerId\":\"$CustomerID\", \"orderDate\":\"$OrderDate\", \"__id\":\"$_id\", \"__customerId\":\"$CustomerID\" ,\"details\": { \"$map\":{ \"input\": \"$\\\"Order Details\\\"\", \"in\": { \"subTotal\":{ \"$multiply\" :[\"$$this.Quantity\",\"$$this.UnitPrice\"] }, \"__productId\":\"$$this.ProductID\", \"LambdaOrmParentId\":\"$$this.OrderID\" } }} }} , { \"$sort\" :{ \"OrderDate\":1 } } , { \"$skip\" : 0 }, { \"$limit\" : 1 } , { \"$project\": { \"_id\": 0 } }]", "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "dialect": "MongoDB", "source": "Ordering", "children": [ { "entity": "Products", "dialect": "MySQL", "source": "Catalog", "sentence": "SELECT p.ProductName AS name, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN (?) " } ] }, { "entity": "Customers", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "Crm", "sentence": "SELECT c.CompanyName AS \"name\", c.CustomerID AS \"LambdaOrmParentId\" FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN ($1) " } ] } Query plan on the cqrs stage On the cqrs stage, a select reads all the data from a single source, Insights , according to the configuration of the stage. An insert, update or delete is executed on the corresponding source ( Catalog , Crm or Ordering ). curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/plan?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "Orders.filter(p=>p.customerId==customerId).include(p=>[p.details.include(p=>p.product.map(p=>p.name)).map(p=>{subTotal:p.quantity*p.unitPrice}),p.customer.map(p=>p.name)]).sort(p=>p.orderDate).page(1,1)", "options": {"stage": "cqrs"}}' Result: { "entity": "Orders", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "Insights", "sentence": "SELECT o.OrderID AS \"id\", o.CustomerID AS \"customerId\", o.OrderDate AS \"orderDate\", o.OrderID AS \"__id\", o.CustomerID AS \"__customerId\" FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = $1 ORDER BY o.OrderDate asc OFFSET 0 LIMIT 1 ", "children": [ { "entity": "Orders.details", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "Insights", "sentence": "SELECT (o1.Quantity * o1.UnitPrice) AS \"subTotal\", o1.ProductID AS \"__productId\", o1.OrderID AS \"LambdaOrmParentId\" FROM \"Order Details\" o1 WHERE o1.OrderID IN ($1) ", "children": [ { "entity": "Products", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "Insights", "sentence": "SELECT p.ProductName AS \"name\", p.ProductID AS \"LambdaOrmParentId\" FROM Products p WHERE p.ProductID IN ($1) " } ] }, { "entity": "Customers", "dialect": "PostgreSQL", "source": "Insights", "sentence": "SELECT c.CompanyName AS \"name\", c.CustomerID AS \"LambdaOrmParentId\" FROM Customers c WHERE c.CustomerID IN ($1) " } ] } CQRS with Kafka When the schema is served by a Data Gateway , the synchronization can go through Kafka instead: the listener publishes the inserts, updates and deletes of the default and cqrs stages to a topic with queue.send , and a consumer applies them on the insights stage. The queue is configured in infrastructure.queue ( config is the kafkajs configuration); see execute-queued . Schema ... infrastructure: ... queue: config: $QUEUE_CONFIG consumers: - name: syncInsights config: groupId: group1 subscribe: topic: insights-sync fromBeginning: true execute: orm.execute(message.query,message.data, {stage:"insights"}) application: listeners: - name: syncInsights on: [insert, bulkInsert, update, delete ] condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs") after: queue.send("insights-sync",[{query,data}]) Node.js client Schema With a client, the local schema only defines the domain, the URL of the Data Gateway and the paths where lambdaorm build -l client-node generates the model; the sources and their connections belong to the schema served by the Data Gateway . lambdaorm init -u <url> creates this schema with the domain read from the gateway. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: service: url: http://localhost:8080 paths: src: src domain: northwind/domain Query This time the query runs through the Node.js client ( @lambdaorm/client ), which connects to a Data Gateway, and it is written as a string. Here the gateway serves a single schema at the root, so the URL is the gateway's; otherwise it includes the route of the schema (for example http://localhost:8080/northwind ). import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/client' import fs from 'fs' import path from 'path' (async () => { try { await orm.init('http://localhost:8080', { headers: { 'X-Api-Key': process.env.BACKEND_KEY } }) // test the connection console.log(await orm.general.ping()) // import the data of the data.json file const content = fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, '../data.json'), 'utf-8') await orm.stage.import('default', JSON.parse(content)) // query as a string const query = `Orders .filter(p => p.customerId == customerId) .include(p => [ p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details .include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ])` // get the execution plan const plan = await orm.plan(query, { stage: 'default' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(plan, null, 2)) // execute the query const result = await orm.execute(query, { customerId: 'CENTC' }, { stage: 'default' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } finally { await orm.end() } })() Considerations With both @lambdaorm/lib and @lambdaorm/client , queries can be written as lambda expressions or as strings. Queries are written against the domain model and do not depend on the infrastructure. A project can start with a simple infrastructure and change it later without touching the code. Development, test and production environments can have different infrastructures (stages) with the same code. Many other use cases can be solved by configuring the schema and writing queries. Explore the labs and the rest of this documentation.

docs.text: λORM λORM (LambdaORM) ist ein TypeScript-ORM, das verteilte Abfragen über verschiedene Datenbank-Engines hinweg ausführt: MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB und SQLite. Abfragen werden als Lambda-Ausdrücke über ein Domänenmodell geschrieben, das von der Infrastruktur unabhängig ist. Eine einzige Abfrage kann Entitäten lesen oder schreiben, die in verschiedenen Datenbanken gespeichert sind – zum Beispiel einige in MySQL, andere in PostgreSQL und wieder andere in MongoDB –, und λORM zerlegt sie in eine Anweisung pro Quelle und führt die Ergebnisse zusammen. Dieselbe Domäne kann mehrere Stages (Infrastruktur-Szenarien) haben. In einem Stage können die Daten auf SQL Server, MongoDB und Oracle verteilt sein; in einem anderen kann alles in einer einzigen PostgreSQL-Datenbank liegen. So lassen sich Muster wie CQRS per Konfiguration umsetzen, ohne den Code zu ändern. Eine vollständige Liste finden Sie unter Funktionen . Verwendung Weg Paket Wann verwenden Node.js-Bibliothek @lambdaorm/lib Abfragen aus einer Node.js-/TypeScript-Anwendung ausführen. Siehe Verwendung . Kommandozeile @lambdaorm/cli (Befehl lambdaorm ) Ein Projekt erstellen, die Datenbanken synchronisieren, Daten importieren und exportieren und Abfragen aus einem Terminal oder in CI ausführen. Siehe CLI . Data Gateway Docker-Image flaviorita/data-gateway λORM-Schemas über das Netzwerk bereitstellen: eine REST API, MCP für KI-Agenten, eine WebSocket API und eine Web-UI. Siehe Data Gateway . Node.js-Client @lambdaorm/client Dieselben Abfragen aus Node.js gegen ein Data Gateway ausführen. Siehe Clients . npm install @lambdaorm/lib # the library npm install -g @lambdaorm/cli # the lambdaorm command Hinweis Die Pakete ohne Scope lambdaorm , lambdaorm-cli und lambdaorm-client-node werden nicht mehr gepflegt: Verwenden Sie die Pakete @lambdaorm/* . Abfragesprache Die folgende Abfrage liefert den höchsten Preis jeder Produktkategorie, wobei nur die Produkte berücksichtigt werden, die dem Filter entsprechen, und nur die Kategorien, deren höchster Preis über 50 liegt: import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' import { Products } from './northwind/domain/model' const query = (country: string) => Products .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3)) .having(p => max(p.price) > 50) .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) })) .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice)) await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // run the query, passing the value of the country parameter const result = await orm.execute(query, { country: 'ARG' }) await orm.end() In dieser Abfrage: filter behält die Produkte, deren Preis größer als 5 ist und deren Lieferant im angegebenen Land ansässig ist, sowie diejenigen mit weniger als 3 Einheiten auf Lager. map liefert den Kategorienamen und den höchsten Preis. Die Gruppierung ist implizit: Die Produkte werden nach Kategorie gruppiert, weil max eine Aggregatfunktion ist. having behält nur die Kategorien, deren höchster Preis größer als 50 ist. sort sortiert das Ergebnis absteigend nach dem höchsten Preis. supplier und category sind Beziehungen: Die Joins sind implizit. Siehe auch: Abfragesprache | Select | Join | Gruppierung | include | Insert | Bulk Insert | Update | Delete | Metadaten | Repository | Verwendung Include include liefert eine Entität zusammen mit ihren Beziehungen in derselben Abfrage, auch wenn diese in verschiedenen Datenbanken gespeichert sind. In diesem Beispiel wird die Abfrage als String geschrieben, eine Alternative zum Lambda-Ausdruck: import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib' (async () => { try { await orm.init('./config/northwind.yaml') const query = `Orders .filter(p => p.id === id) .include(p => [ p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details .include(p => p.product .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)) .map(p => p.name)) .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice]) ])` const result = await orm.execute(query, { id: 102 }, { stage: 'PostgreSQL' }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error.message) } finally { await orm.end() } })() Ergebnis: [ { "id": 102, "customerId": "SPLIR", "employeeId": 7, "orderDate": "1996-11-07T23:00:00.000Z", "requiredDate": "1996-12-05T23:00:00.000Z", "shippedDate": "1996-11-14T23:00:00.000Z", "shipViaId": 1, "freight": 8.63, "name": "Split Rail Beer & Ale", "address": "P.O. Box 555", "city": "Lander", "region": "WY", "postalCode": "82520", "country": "USA", "customer": { "name": "Split Rail Beer & Ale" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 24, "unitPrice": 5.9, "product": { "name": "Tourtire", "category": { "name": "Meat/Poultry" } } } ] } ] Weitere Informationen: include Schema Das Schema definiert Entitäten, Enumerationen, Indizes, eindeutige Schlüssel, Standardwerte, Constraints, Mappings, Quellen, Stages, Listener und mehr. Es wird in YAML oder JSON geschrieben. Bedingungen und Aktionen verwenden dieselbe Ausdruckssprache wie Abfragen. Siehe auch: Schema | Definition | Verwendung | Ausdrücke | Umgebungsvariablen | Composite | Listener | mehrere Stages | mehrere Quellen | Datenbank-Engines Synchronisierung λORM hält die Datenbanken und das Schema in beide Richtungen synchron: Synchronisierung | push | pull | fetch | introspect | incorporate Transaktionen und Skripte Transaktionen : orm.transaction führt mehrere Abfragen in einer Transaktion aus, auch über Quellen und Stages hinweg. Skripte : ein ganzer Anwendungsfall (Variablen, Bedingungen, Schleifen und mehrere Abfragen) in einer Transaktion und in einem einzigen Aufruf – aus Node.js, der CLI oder dem Data Gateway. Labs Vollständige Beispiele finden Sie in den λORM Labs . Verwandte Projekte λORM CLI : Kommandozeilenschnittstelle für λORM. Data Gateway : λORM-Schemas über REST, MCP und WebSocket, mit einer Web-UI. λORM-Client : Node.js-Client für das Data Gateway. 3xpr : erweiterbare Ausdrucks-Engine, die mathematische und logische Ausdrücke auswertet; λORM-Abfragen und -Skripte bauen darauf auf.

docs.text: Funktionen Ein Überblick über das, was λORM bietet, mit Links zu den Seiten, die jede Funktion beschreiben. Datenbank-Engines MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB und SQLite (SQLjs). Eine einzige Abfrage kann mehrere Datenbanken einbeziehen, auch unterschiedlicher Datenbank-Engines. Datenbank-Engines : die Unterschiede zwischen den Datenbank-Engines (Typen, leere Strings, upsert , …). Abfragesprache Abfragesprache auf Basis von JavaScript-Lambda-Ausdrücken. Abfragen können als JavaScript-/TypeScript-Code oder als String geschrieben werden. Klauseln für Select , Insert , Bulk Insert , Update und Delete . Implizite Joins und Gruppierung . Eager Loading von Beziehungen mit include , auch über Datenbanken hinweg. Operatoren und Funktionen . Abfrage-Metadaten : die Parameter, das Modell, die Constraints und der Ausführungsplan einer Abfrage. Verwendung Repositories und benutzerdefinierte Repositories . Transaktionen und verteilte Transaktionen , über Quellen und Stages hinweg. Skripte : ein ganzer Anwendungsfall (Variablen, Bedingungen, Schleifen und mehrere Abfragen) in einer Transaktion, auch über das Data Gateway. Verwendungsbeispiele : eine einzelne Quelle, mehrere Quellen, CQRS und der Node.js-Client. Schema Schema -Konfiguration, die das Domänenmodell von der Infrastruktur entkoppelt. Konfiguration in JSON oder YAML. Mappings zwischen der Domäne und der Infrastruktur. Vererbung von Entitäten ( extends ). Umgebungsvariablen . Indizes, eindeutige Schlüssel und Constraints. docs.text: λORM CLI Die λORM CLI ( @lambdaorm/cli ) ist eine Kommandozeilenanwendung zur Verwendung von λORM : Sie erstellt Projekte, synchronisiert die Datenbanken mit dem Schema, importiert und exportiert Daten und führt Abfragen und Skripte aus. Ihre Befehle laufen lokal mit einem Workspace ( -w ), und die meisten von ihnen können auch auf einem Data Gateway ausgeführt werden ( -u <url> ). Installation Installieren Sie das Paket global; es stellt den Befehl lambdaorm bereit: npm i -g @lambdaorm/cli lambdaorm --version Es erfordert Node.js 20 oder höher. Das Docker-Image des Data Gateway ( flaviorita/data-gateway ) enthält die CLI bereits. Hinweis Das Paket lambdaorm-cli ohne Scope ist das alte Paket und wird nicht mehr gepflegt. Befehle Befehl Beschreibung version Gibt die Version der CLI und die vom Projekt verwendete Version von @lambdaorm/lib aus. init Erzeugt die Struktur eines λORM-Projekts. build Erzeugt das Modell und die Repositories für die Sprache. schema Gibt Informationen über das Schema zurück. push Synchronisiert die Datenbanken mit dem Modell ( -o schreibt stattdessen die Skripte). pull Aktualisiert das Schema mit der Struktur der Datenbanken eines Stages. fetch Zeigt die Unterschiede zwischen den Datenbanken und dem Modell; endet mit Exit-Code 1, wenn es welche gibt. introspect Liest und analysiert eine Datendatei und aktualisiert das Schema. incorporate Aktualisiert das Schema anhand einer Datendatei, überträgt die Änderungen in die Datenbanken und importiert die Daten. drop Entfernt alle Datenbankobjekte, nicht jedoch die Datenbank selbst. import Importiert Daten aus einer Datei in die Datenbanken. export Exportiert Daten aus den Datenbanken. execute Führt eine Abfrage aus. script Führt ein Skript aus: mehrere Abfragen in einer Transaktion. plan Gibt den Ausführungsplan einer Abfrage zurück. metadata Gibt die Metadaten einer Abfrage zurück. parameters Gibt die Parameter einer Abfrage zurück. model Gibt das Modell des Ergebnisses einer Abfrage zurück. constraints Gibt die Constraints einer Abfrage zurück. lambdaorm <command> -h listet die Optionen eines Befehls auf; lambdaorm -h listet die Befehle auf. Den Befehl sync gibt es nicht mehr: Er wurde durch push ersetzt. Gemeinsame Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Pfad des Projekts (der Ordner mit lambdaORM.yaml ). Standard: das aktuelle Verzeichnis. stage -s Name des Stages. Standard: der erste Stage des Schemas. envfile -e Liest eine Datei mit Umgebungsvariablen (zum Beispiel die Verbindungszeichenfolgen). output -o Ausgabeformat des Ergebnisses: json , beautiful , light oder yaml . url -u URL des Schemas auf einem Data Gateway, um den Befehl dort statt lokal auszuführen. Jede Befehlsseite listet die Optionen auf, die der jeweilige Befehl akzeptiert. Exit-Code und Data Gateway Jeder Befehl endet mit Exit-Code 1, wenn er fehlschlägt (ab @lambdaorm/cli 1.6.3). Befehle laufen auf einem Data Gateway mit -u und der URL des Schemas, zum Beispiel http://gateway:8080/iot/v1 . Ist die Umgebungsvariable SERVICE_TOKEN gesetzt, wird sie als Authorization: Bearer <token> gesendet (für ein Gateway mit Bearer-Authentifizierung ). Siehe auch Clients . docs.text: Changelog All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. @lambdaorm/cli 1.6.2 Patch Changes e4ce3af: 3xpr 5.2.0 in every package (one copy of it). lib builds each Orm's 3xpr instance with the ExpressionsBuilder 3xpr now exports, instead of importing it from one of its files. b22e580: lambdaorm --version and lambdaorm version print this CLI's version (they printed the version of the project's package.json in the current directory, or looked for the old lambdaorm-cli package). Updated dependencies [e4ce3af] @lambdaorm/base@3.2.1 @lambdaorm/lib@3.2.2 @lambdaorm/client@0.9.1 1.6.1 Patch Changes Updated dependencies [2dc1ac1] Updated dependencies [68faedb] @lambdaorm/lib@3.2.1 1.6.0 Minor Changes 0e683c6: Scripts: several queries in one transaction. client: orm.executeScript(script, data, options) calls the service's POST /script (the service must run with SCRIPT_ENABLED=true ). cli: new lambdaorm script command, with the script inline ( -x ) or in a file ( -f ), its variables in -d ; local with the workspace or on a service with -u . d16b60a: stage.push().sentencesBySource() : the DDL grouped per source (one script per database). cli: lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, <stage>.<source>.sql (deterministic names, to rename into a versioned migration); -o without a folder prints the DDL grouped by source — L19. Patch Changes 2ee8930: Upgrade the data7expressions dependencies to their latest major: 3xpr from 1.x to ^5.1.1 , h3lp and typ3s to ^5.0.0 (and json-light to ^5.0.0 in the CLI). No API changes were needed. Behaviour inherited from 3xpr: <= now has the same precedence as the other comparison operators ( a <= b == true used to evaluate as a <= (b == true) ). 3xpr 5.1.0 evaluates async expressions statement by statement (listeners, orm.execute inside expressions), never runs an async function while building an expression, and adds throw , try / catch , return , break and continue ; 3xpr 5.1.1 parses the empty string literal "" (it used to swallow the rest of the expression). ee1e7ac: Packaging: The published exports pointed to ./build/lib/index.js , a path the package doesn't have: require('@lambdaorm/lib') (and base, client) failed for everyone installing from npm. dist now rewrites exports (and bin ) like main — L7. cli: declares bin: lambdaorm , so npm i -g @lambdaorm/cli installs the lambdaorm command — L29. Every package's dist is smoke-tested before it can be released: required by its name (so exports applies) and, for the CLI, lambdaorm --help . 8b8f470: Stage commands: push/DDL: a stage's last source without condition is a catch-all, as in DML: it gets only the entities no other source took (it used to receive every entity) — L25. fetch/pull on PostgreSQL work with reserved words as column names ( order ): the metadata query quoted the column twice — L6, L21. stage.fetch() reports the drift: per mapping, the entities that differ from the model (present in one side only, different columns, types, lengths, required, primary key), each with its differences ; no entities when in step. stage.read() returns the databases' mappings as fetch did (pull uses it) — L22. cli: lambdaorm fetch exits with code 1 when there are differences (for CI). fetch , pull , schema , introspect and incorporate load the --envfile they declared (it was ignored). docs.text: Build Erzeugt den Quellcode der Domäne für die Entwicklungssprache: das Modell ( model.ts , mit den Entitäten und Enumerationen) und ein Repository pro Entität ( repository<Entity>.ts ). Siehe Repositories . Eine Repository-Datei wird nur erzeugt, wenn sie noch nicht existiert, sodass darin hinzugefügter eigener Code erhalten bleibt; das Modell wird jedes Mal neu erzeugt. Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Projektpfad. language -l Entwicklungssprache: node (Standard, verwendet @lambdaorm/lib ) oder client-node (verwendet @lambdaorm/client ; die Domäne wird vom Data Gateway unter infrastructure.service.url des Schemas gelesen, wie von init -u geschrieben). model -m Erzeugt das Modell. repositories -r Erzeugt die Repositories. all -a Erzeugt das Modell und die Repositories (Standard, wenn weder -m , -r noch -a angegeben ist). src-path Relativer Pfad des Quellcodes im Workspace ( --src-path ). data-path Relativer Pfad des Datenordners im Workspace ( --data-path ). domain-path Relativer Pfad der Domäne im Quellcodepfad ( --domain-path ). url -u URL des Schemas auf einem Data Gateway. Beispiel lambdaorm build -w lab/countries

docs.text: Execute Führt einen Abfrageausdruck aus und gibt sein Ergebnis aus. Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Projektpfad (Standard: das aktuelle Verzeichnis). stage -s Name des Stages (Standard: der erste Stage des Schemas). query -q Abfrageausdruck. data -d Daten (Parameter) der Abfrage: JSON oder der Pfad einer JSON-Datei. envfile -e Liest eine Datei mit Umgebungsvariablen. output -o Ausgabeformat: json , beautiful , light oder yaml . url -u URL des Schemas auf einem Data Gateway , um den Befehl dort auszuführen. Beispiele Masseneinfügung Fügt die Länder aus einer JSON-Datei zusammen mit ihren Bundesstaaten ein: lambdaorm execute -w lab/countries -e lab/countries/.env -q "Countries.bulkInsert().include(p => p.states)" -d ./lab/countries/countries.json Abfrage lambdaorm execute -e ".env" -o beautiful -q "Products.distinct(p => ({ quantity: p.quantity, category: p.category.name })).sort(p => p.category).page(1,3)" Ergebnis: [ { "quantity": "10 boxes x 20 bags", "category": "Beverages" }, { "quantity": "24 - 12 oz bottles", "category": "Beverages" }, { "quantity": "12 - 355 ml cans", "category": "Beverages" } ] Auf einem Data Gateway lambdaorm execute -u http://gateway:8080/iot/v1 -o beautiful -q "Devices.filter(p => p.status == status)" -d '{"status": "active"}' Bei Bearer-Authentifizierung setzen Sie das Token in der Umgebungsvariablen SERVICE_TOKEN (siehe CLI ).

docs.text: Fetch Zeigt die Abweichungen zwischen den Datenbanken eines Stages und dem Modell: pro Mapping die Entitäten, die sich unterscheiden (auf einer Seite fehlend, abweichende Spalten, Typen, Längen, Nullbarkeit oder Primärschlüssel), jeweils mit ihren differences . Die Liste der Entitäten ist leer, wenn die Datenbanken mit dem Modell übereinstimmen. Beziehungen und Indizes werden nicht verglichen. Der Befehl endet mit Exit-Code 1, wenn es Unterschiede gibt , und kann daher in CI eingesetzt werden. Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Projektpfad (Standard: das aktuelle Verzeichnis). stage -s Name des Stages (Standard: der erste Stage des Schemas). envfile -e Liest eine Datei mit Umgebungsvariablen. output -o Ausgabeformat: json , beautiful , light oder yaml . url -u URL des Schemas auf einem Data Gateway , um den Befehl dort auszuführen. Beispiel lambdaorm fetch -w lab/countries -e lab/countries/.env -o beautiful || echo "the database differs from the model" Ergebnis: [ { "name": "default", "entities": [ { "name": "Countries", "mapping": "Countries", "differences": ["column phone missing in the database"], "properties": [ ... ] } ] } ] Bei Übereinstimmung: [ { "name": "default", "entities": [] } ]

docs.text: Push Synchronisiert die Datenbanken eines Stages mit dem Modell. Verglichen wird das Modell mit den Datenbanken (dem, was fetch liest), nicht mit der Datei orm_state : Neue Tabellen werden mit Schlüsseln, Fremdschlüsseln und Indizes erstellt; in bestehenden Tabellen werden fehlende Spalten hinzugefügt und Spalten mit abweichendem Typ, abweichender Länge oder Nullbarkeit geändert. Der Befehl löscht niemals , was nur in der Datenbank existiert ( fetch meldet es). orm_state wird weiterhin als Protokoll geschrieben. Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Projektpfad (Standard: das aktuelle Verzeichnis). stage -s Name des Stages (Standard: der erste Stage des Schemas). envfile -e Liest eine Datei mit Umgebungsvariablen. output -o Erzeugt die Anweisungen, wendet sie aber nicht an. Ohne Wert werden sie pro Quelle ausgegeben; mit einem Ordner wird für jede Quelle, die sich ändert, ein Skript geschrieben, <stage>.<source>.sql . force -f Schlägt eine Anweisung fehl, wird mit den nächsten Anweisungen fortgefahren. Hinweis push läuft nur lokal: Es hat keine Option -u . Beispiele Änderungen anwenden: lambdaorm push -w lab/countries -e lab/countries/.env Stattdessen die Skripte schreiben (zum Beispiel, um sie als versionierte Migrationen aufzubewahren): lambdaorm push -w lab/countries -e lab/countries/.env -s default -o migrations /home/user/lab/countries/migrations/default.default.sql Die Anweisungen pro Quelle ausgeben, ohne sie anzuwenden: lambdaorm push -w lab/countries -e lab/countries/.env -o [ { "source": "default", "sentences": [ "ALTER TABLE Countries ADD phone VARCHAR(20)" ] } ] Eine Spalte umbenennen Um eine Spalte umzubenennen, setzen Sie previousMapping im Mapping der Eigenschaft ( { name: icon, mapping: icon_name, previousMapping: icon } ) und entfernen Sie es, sobald die Änderung angewendet ist. Das Umbenennen von Tabellen wird nicht unterstützt.

docs.text: Script Führt ein Skript aus: mehrere Abfragen in einer Transaktion . Das Skript ist in 3xpr geschrieben, und alle seine Aufrufe von orm.execute(query, data, options) laufen in derselben Transaktion, auch über Quellen hinweg. Die Transaktion wird bestätigt (Commit), wenn das Skript endet, und bei jedem Fehler zurückgerollt (eine fehlgeschlagene Abfrage oder ein throw ). Das Ergebnis ist der Wert der letzten Anweisung (oder von return ). Es läuft lokal mit dem Workspace ( -w ) oder auf einem Data Gateway ( -u , über POST /script ); das Gateway muss scripts.enabled haben, und die Zugangsdaten müssen die Berechtigung script besitzen. Optionen Option Kurz Beschreibung workspace -w Projektpfad (Standard: das aktuelle Verzeichnis). stage -s Name des Stages (Standard: der erste Stage des Schemas). script -x Skript (3xpr-Anweisungen, die orm.execute(query, data, options) aufrufen). file -f Datei mit dem Skript (anstelle von -x ). data -d Variablen des Skripts: JSON oder der Pfad einer JSON-Datei. envfile -e Liest eine Datei mit Umgebungsvariablen. output -o Ausgabeformat: json , beautiful , light oder yaml . url -u URL des Schemas auf einem Data Gateway ( POST /script ). Beispiele Inline lambdaorm script -w lab/northwind -e lab/northwind/.env -o beautiful \ -x 'orm.execute("Orders.update(p => ({ freight: freight })).filter(p => p.id == id)", { id: id, freight: freight }); orm.execute("Orders.filter(p => p.id == id)", { id: id })' \ -d '{"id": 10248, "freight": 40}' Aus einer Datei create-quote.3xpr : account = orm.execute("Accounts.filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId }); if (account.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "account not found" }; } orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" }); for (line in lines) { orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, quantity: line.qty }); } orm.execute("QuoteEvents.insert()", { quoteId: quoteId, event: "created" }, { stage: "insights" }); quoteId lambdaorm script -w . -f create-quote.3xpr -d quote.json orm.execute(…, { stage: "insights" }) läuft auf einem anderen Stage und nimmt an derselben Transaktion teil (seit @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0). Auf einem Data Gateway Die URL enthält die Route des Schemas (hier crm ): lambdaorm script -u http://localhost:8080/crm -f create-quote.3xpr -d '{"quoteId": 10, "accountId": 1, "lines": []}' Hinweise Sprache: Variablen, if / else , for , for … in , while , switch , try / catch , throw , return ; es gibt keinen Operator ? : , kein ++ / -- (verwenden Sie i += 1 ) und keine benutzerdefinierten Funktionen. Siehe Skript . Das Skript arbeitet auf einer Kopie der Daten und kann keine Umgebungsvariablen lesen ( $VAR schlägt fehl). Fehler werden als error: … ausgegeben, und nichts, was das Skript geschrieben hat, bleibt erhalten. Mit -u benötigt ein Data Gateway mit Bearer-Authentifizierung das Token in der Umgebungsvariablen SERVICE_TOKEN der CLI (gesendet als Authorization: Bearer ; seit @lambdaorm/cli 1.6.3). Der Befehl endet mit Exit-Code 1, wenn das Skript fehlschlägt (seit @lambdaorm/cli 1.6.3).
